t: Why email can't practically be made secure
w: Email is default-plaintext, lacks forward secrecy, leaks metadata, and webmail exposes plaintext to providers.

t: Why Nagle and delayed ACKs interact badly
w: Delayed ACK bets on a fast reply and loses in send-send-reply patterns, adding about 200ms stalls.

t: Why phones shut off at apparent 20 percent battery
w: High current causes voltage sag that worsens with age, so cutoffs use measured voltage, and percentages mislead on worn batteries.

t: Why a positive test is often a false positive
w: With rare disease prevalence, a 99%-accurate test gives mostly false positives: about 100 false versus 1 true positive per 10,000 tested.

t: Simple bearer tokens beat JWTs for most APIs
w: Use 16+ byte random tokens stored server-side as bearer tokens; avoid JWTs, OAuth and custom crypto unless delegating access to third parties.

t: Why astronomy time conversions are painful with leap seconds
w: Astronomy converts UTC to TAI and TT, depends on leap-second tables and Earth velocity for TDB; UTC exists to hide this from ordinary users.

t: How WhatsApp group encryption works and its limits
w: Server controls membership; an attacker who joins can't read past messages, but members see the join notice. Telegram group chats lack e2e encryption entirely.

t: Why JWT is a poor cryptographic design
w: Most crypto failures are implementation mistakes, so misuse-resistant designs matter; JWT's kitchen-sink complexity invites them.

t: Why drowning victims climb and how to rescue
w: Drowning people grab and climb anything they touch, pushing rescuers under; hand them a pole or buoy instead of swimming in.

t: Calculating whether 8K is visible at normal distance
w: At 6.5 feet from a 65-inch TV, 20/12.5 vision resolves about 3840 pixels across, matching 4K; low-contrast video hides even that.

t: Why Rust's polling futures are not the io_uring problem
w: Polling versus completion is orthogonal to io_uring; the real difficulty is lifetime-bound buffers crossing the syscall boundary, and Pin enables single-allocation state machines.

t: Why gravity propagates at the speed of light
w: A change in gravitational interaction propagates at light speed, so a falling body responds after a delay set by light travel time, not instantly.

t: How the SHAttered PDF collision was constructed
w: Both PDFs share a prefix and suffix; the collision lives in JPEG data, with misaligned comment fields hiding two different image streams.

t: WebAssembly's original encoding was an AST, not a stack
w: A Wasm designer explains the first format was a pre-order AST, then post-order encoding decoded faster; multi-value returns shaped the design.

t: Windows file locking: rename, delete and hardlinks
w: Windows locks file objects, not names: open files can often be renamed but not deleted unless FILE_SHARE_DELETE is set; hardlinks follow the same rules.

t: Why QUIC costs more CPU than TCP for bulk transfers
w: QUIC's anti-middlebox design blocks TSO, LRO and kTLS offloads, and userspace 1500-byte packets mean far more syscalls.

t: Why C# compiler uses handwritten recursive-descent parsing
w: Hand-written recursive descent enables AST reuse for incremental reparsing, better errors, and resilient trees that let IDEs autocomplete invalid code.

t: Computed goto dispatch removes branches from VM loops
w: A goto dispatch table leaves one indirect jump per instruction, avoiding the switch, break and loop branches of a standard dispatcher.

t: Low-latency Java practices from HFT engineers
w: Measure tail latency rather than averages, avoid GC pauses, keep call stacks short, pin one thread per core, and use non-locking data structures.

t: Why word processors need custom text layout
w: Word processors need layout details browsers do not expose, like bidi selection geometry and reflowing only the current line while typing, so apps render text on canvas.

t: Why iMessage stays closed: hardware-attested anti-spam
w: Apple bans spamming devices by serial number, which needs attested hardware; that trust chain is why iMessage cannot easily go cross-platform.

t: Why prefix varints decode faster than LEB128
w: Putting length in a UTF-8-like prefix means decoders branch less and use native loads, while encoded size matches LEB128.

t: Why JWT's design invites cryptographic failures
w: Algorithm negotiation and mixed metadata create own-goals; modern protocols like Noise fix algorithms statically with good defaults.

t: Why Protobuf can't be truly zero-copy like Cap'n Proto
w: True zero-copy means reading fields without parsing; Protobuf's variable-width tag-value encoding forces a linear scan, so only strings can point into the buffer.

t: Why Robinhood halted GME buys: margin crunch
w: Margin lines drained as traders bought before funds settled; T+2 settlement made proceeds margin-funded, so buys were throttled to avoid insolvency.

t: Docker punches holes past ufw firewall rules
w: Docker inserts iptables allow rules that bypass ufw, so a container can be publicly reachable despite an active firewall.

t: Why summing median task times underestimates projects
w: Task durations are right-skewed; summing medians gives a far too optimistic total because long tails dominate the sum.

t: Why PAM exists: login's customization problem
w: Before PAM, each site patched /bin/login for Kerberos, LDAP or NFS; PAM made authentication modules pluggable.

t: Continuations explained as VM snapshots and dynamic-wind
w: A continuation is a frozen program snapshot; dynamic-wind reinitializes resources like connections when execution re-enters the computation.

t: Why C++ builds are so slow
w: Inline functions and class layouts sit in headers, so changes trigger large recompiles and the linker discards duplicated code.

t: GC pause math for game frame budgets
w: At 144 fps a frame has about 7ms; a 200 microsecond GC pause uses under 3% of it, so 'GC cannot work in games' needs real latency numbers.

t: How clearinghouse collateral works in settlement
w: Trades settle days later; collateral needs rise with volatility, which can squeeze brokers like Robinhood.

t: Solidity's surprising default behaviors
w: Mutable-by-default state, silent integer wraparound, literal-dependent division and implicit copy semantics cause subtle bugs.

t: Why CBC mode leaks information to online attackers
w: CBC chains blocks to fix ECB's replay and pattern leaks, but an online attacker can still run slow dictionary attacks against earlier ciphertext blocks.

t: Why zero-cost abstractions leak complexity upward
w: Optimal performance needs static specialization, and that compile-time knowledge spreads through call stacks, making the accidental complexity viral.

t: Why arbitrary display scaling is hard to get right
w: Affine transforms can render at any scale, but 1px lines at 1.5x fall on partial pixels, causing antialiasing, redraw costs and centering problems.

t: How rainbow tables compress password hash lookups
w: Chaining one-way function outputs lets one stored endpoint cover many hashes, trading lookup time for much smaller tables.

t: Why ML overfits in statistical arbitrage
w: Market signals have R-squared near 1%, so simple linear models often beat complex ones; complexity must come from structure or features.

t: Wait before extracting repeated code
w: Let duplication survive a few changes first; either it stops looking repetitive, or a missed edit shows which parts truly need extraction.

t: Why generics are hard to add to Go
w: Type inference and annotation rules get complicated fast, and mistakes in generics designs get locked in permanently.

t: Work-sample tests beat conversational interviews for engineers
w: Friendly conversations poorly predict skill; Matasano's work-sample tests surfaced capable candidates interviews rejected, so every candidate should go through the same process.

t: Why Chrome has no master password
w: The OS user account is the only real boundary; inside it, extra protections are theater, so Chrome uses OS encryption.

t: Cheap LED bulbs flicker at 120 Hz
w: Poor rectification and smoothing make many LEDs pulse twice per mains cycle; slow-motion filming reveals it, while some brands smooth DC properly.

t: Why Go built its own toolchain
w: Standard C ABIs lacked segmented stacks and precise GC stack maps, so Go needed a custom toolchain from day one.

t: How Hacker News front page ranking works
w: Score is divided by age raised to a gravity exponent, with penalties for no-URL posts, buried stories and lightweight content.

t: Why compilations can be copyrightable even if parts are not
w: Individually uncopyrightable items like method signatures can form a copyrightable work through creative selection and arrangement, as cookbooks show, complicating Google's API defense.

t: Why JavaScript not Python or Lua won the browser
w: Insider explanation: mid-1990s Python and Lua could not change incompatibly for browsers, so JS evolved in standards, with interoperation requirements driving its spec.

t: Why mmap alone is unsafe for databases
w: mmap alone is unsafe for a database: it needs write-ahead logging and control over when data persists, or the OS flushes garbage.

t: Why process lead matters more than RISC vs CISC
w: Instruction decode costs are similar for both; Intel's manufacturing process advantage has historically mattered more than ISA encoding.

t: How Geneva drives and heart cams work in watches
w: A trained watchmaker explains the Geneva drive smoothing mainspring power, heart cams resetting chronographs, and instantaneous date wheels.

t: Complex numbers as ordered pairs of reals
w: Defining complex numbers as pairs with explicit addition and multiplication shows real arithmetic embedded inside, so the imaginary unit follows naturally.

t: Why renting hash power enables double-spend attacks
w: If hash power can be rented at market rates, a 51% attack earns fees and enables double-spends, so no fee level alone deters it.

t: How phone location data is collected and resold
w: Chip, OS and app makers share GPS data by contract; supposedly anonymized five-second traces are easy to rejoin and sold to hedge funds.

t: Why 1.1.1.1 skips EDNS client subnet data
w: EDNS client subnet leaks requester IP to authoritative servers; DNS-based load balancers need it, so privacy and geo-accuracy conflict.

t: How Aldi achieves fast checkout and low labor
w: Barcodes on many sides, distinct packaging for similar items, shipping boxes as shelves, deposit carts, and no bagging cut labor and scan time.

t: Mixing old material into homework beats cramming
w: Incremental homework and a question period led students to retain material months later, even after an easy-seeming exam.

t: Fair use is an exception to copyright, not a license
w: A license grants permission; fair use is an independent exception, so copying can be lawful without a license, as Google Books showed.

t: Why IoT firmware hardcodes DNS servers
w: ISP-provided DNS may ignore TTLs and rewrite NXDOMAIN answers; hardcoding known resolvers avoids that, but DNS-over-HTTPS will defeat Pi-hole-style redirection.

t: Scaling a 50M-user app one bottleneck at a time
w: Growth came from adding indexes, switching MyISAM to InnoDB, tuning MySQL's 64MB default, then splitting tables across machines; fix bottlenecks as they appear.

t: Why encrypted email struggles against modern realities
w: Encrypted email leaks metadata, lacks browser support, archives plaintext widely, and conflicts with search; sensitive chats belong in dedicated messaging apps.

t: Why Tesla Autopilot drove into a stationary barrier
w: Vision tracks lanes and car rears while radar ignores stationary objects, so a gore area that looks like a lane leads into the barrier.

t: State curiosity matters more than trait curiosity
w: Task-specific curiosity is linked to better learning and recall, while trait curiosity adds little; curiosity itself still lacks a consensus definition.

t: How DynamoDB really stores data internally
w: Insider: hash keys map to three-replica quorum groups with one master for writes; underneath, the storage is many MySQL instances with JNI bridges, not LevelDB.

t: Scaling a web stack one bottleneck at a time
w: Load balancing, read replicas, sharding, memcached and reverse proxy caches each answer a specific bottleneck that appears as load grows.

t: Why visual polish makes products seem more usable
w: Users tolerate usability flaws in attractive interfaces, which can mask problems in testing; the effect is documented by Nielsen Norman Group.

t: Modernize legacy code piece by piece with tests
w: Avoid full rewrites. Build end-to-end tests as a baseline, then change or delete code freely, respecting the team that keeps it running.

t: Hidden costs of hiring remotely across countries
w: Employment law, holidays and termination rules vary per country, so global remote hiring needs local legal structures.

t: How the Great Firewall detects and blocks VPNs
w: Traffic analysis flags VPN-like flows by packet patterns, so encryption alone fails; tools must mimic ordinary HTTPS traffic shapes.

t: Why esbuild's author chose Go over Rust
w: Go compiled far faster; Rust's large stack frames in big switch statements overflowed on deeply nested JavaScript.

t: How FedEx weighed hub airport candidates
w: Hub siting weighed runway layout, weather, ramp space, labor, fuel and truck access, so overnight sort needs many constraints.

t: Why FoundationDB is a general storage primitive
w: An ordered, transactional key-value core lets other data models and APIs like Zookeeper or SQL sit on one scalable, fault-tolerant store.

t: Why broad ad audiences beat hyper-targeting
w: Tiny targeted audiences are expensive; ad systems aim for the largest pool with one or two filters, reaching the same people far more cheaply.

t: Why tolower breaks identifiers in Turkish locale
w: Locale-dependent case mapping makes INFO lowercase differently under Turkish rules; use ASCII-only case folding for identifiers like HTTP headers.

t: Row polymorphism versus structural subtyping explained
w: Row types let a function accept any record with a required field without subtyping, preserving the other fields' types through inference.

t: Why Nagle and delayed ACKs interact badly
w: The fixed 200ms ACK timer was borrowed from X.25 for Telnet; today disabling delayed ACK usually helps since ACKs are tiny.

t: Knuth vs McIlroy: the famous word-frequency duel
w: Knuth wrote a literate program for word frequency and McIlroy answered with a Unix pipeline; the criticism was unfair because Knuth wrote the program he was asked for.

t: Why 56k modems don't break the Shannon limit
w: The 35 dB noise floor assumed an analog network; digital telco trunks reduced noise, so the limit's inputs changed, not the law.

t: Why early Linux RNG focused on entropy estimation
w: The maintainer explains 1990s export controls and distrust of NSA-designed SHA-1 led PGP and Linux to focus on entropy estimation.

t: How Kademlia uses XOR distance to route
w: Node and key hashes share one space; XOR gives a distance metric so lookups greedily approach the target instead of searching exhaustively.

t: What SQLite WAL mode guarantees on crashes
w: WAL keeps commits across app crashes and never corrupts, but recent commits may roll back after power loss.

t: Why AlphaGo's moves defy human Go chunking
w: Human players reason with chunked group abstractions; AlphaGo seems to evaluate stones more individually, producing moves outside classical theory.

t: Why exact belief updating in Bayes nets is NP-hard
w: Updating beliefs over a Bayesian network is NP-hard, and even approximating it within 0.5 minus epsilon is NP-hard, so brains must use heuristics.

t: Why auto suppliers were squeezed in the chip shortage
w: Carmakers cancelled 2020 orders and pushed risk onto chip suppliers, who had cut capacity just as demand rebounded.

t: Why Tesla's crash-rate comparison is misleading
w: Autopilot miles are easier than average and disengagements before crashes go uncounted; mismatched datasets make the comparison a Simpson's paradox.

t: Why Apple's M1 is fast: width and balance
w: M1 speed comes from very wide decode, a 630-entry reorder buffer, large caches and high memory bandwidth, balanced to keep power low.

t: Dark matter is an inconsistency, not a discovered substance
w: Dark matter and dark energy name mismatches between predicted and observed motion. The names imply a known substance, when the real finding is a gap in theory.

t: Why rental car reservations don't guarantee cars
w: Rental firms don't enforce reservations and plan fleets around expected no-shows, so customers with bookings often get no car.

t: Why most outages come from changes, not failures
w: Code, config and schema changes cause most outages; disk exhaustion and expired certificates are slow killers to automate.

t: Why tiny-volume quantitative blood tests are hard
w: Microliter samples suffer evaporation and localization variability, so quantitative blood chemistry is implausible while yes-no detection tests are feasible.

t: Why bug impact differs from exploitability
w: Exploitability depends on feasibility and required conditions, not how easily laypeople grasp a bug; the iOS TLS flaw needed specific circumstances to reach code execution.

t: Carbon cenospheres as a marker of industrial civilization
w: Combustion-engine cenospheres could persist in the geological record as a durable signature of industrial civilization for millions of years.

t: Netscape server enabled HTTP DELETE by default
w: Netscape Enterprise Server allowed HTTP DELETE out of the box, and a vulnerability scan deleted sites until it was disabled.

t: Why fitness function design dominates genetic algorithms
w: The fitness function defines the search space; evolutionary methods are hard to explain and often lose to direct approaches.

t: Why China's maps use GCJ-02 coordinates
w: China requires the obfuscated GCJ-02 offset of WGS-84, so satellite overlays misalign by 50-500m unless coordinates are converted.

t: How to charge Li-ion batteries for longer life
w: Li-ion cells degrade faster at high state of charge, so keeping them around 50-80% and avoiding deep cycles extends battery life.

t: Why modern construction projects stall on approvals
w: Detailed drawings and contractor liability fear push every question into formal RFIs, adding delays and change-order premiums.

t: Why AltaVista lost: stale index, lost focus
w: A months-stale primary index full of 404s let Google's fresh index win; HITS and PageRank-style link analysis were parallel ideas.

t: Why Emacs needed a dumper: PDP-10 workspace history
w: Early PDP-10 systems kept a program's halted memory image intact, letting you resume it; Emacs's dumper recreates that workspace model on Unix.

t: Alan Kay on objects: messaging, encapsulation, virtual computers
w: Kay's core idea of objects is loosely coupled, encapsulated messaging between virtual computers, not data modeling or inheritance.

t: Why optional typing creates an uncanny valley for users
w: Retrofitting types onto dynamic APIs breaks idioms like tuple indexing; static typing needs different API design, not just annotations.

t: Enumerating rationals lazily with a Calkin-Wilf tree in Haskell
w: A binary tree unfold plus breadth-first traversal yields every rational without repeats; laziness makes it both elegant and efficient.

t: GADTs explained: type-refining constructors in Haskell
w: Algebraic data types combine sums and products; GADTs let each constructor refine the type index, enabling type-safe evaluators for ASTs.

t: Meta-analysis of which hiring methods predict performance
w: Schmidt and Hunter's 1998 meta-analysis summarizes which selection methods, such as interviews and tests, actually predict job performance.

t: Static generics versus dynamic trait objects in Rust
w: Generic bounds generate a copy per type at compile time; dyn trait objects dispatch at runtime, so prefer generics unless you need mixed collections.

t: Oracle-to-Postgres SQL translation cheatsheet
w: Concrete mappings: nvl to coalesce, rownum to LIMIT, merge to INSERT ON CONFLICT, sys_guid to gen_random_uuid, pivot to unnest.

t: AlphaFold is homology modeling, not folding physics
w: AlphaFold matches sequences to known structures, roughly twice as accurate as older methods, but reveals little about how proteins fold or predict novel folds.

t: Why 00000-prefixed LinkedIn hashes were pre-cracked
w: Entries starting 00000 are cracked markers; hashing common passwords and checking truncated hashes reveals them.

t: Lindy effect: old low-level tech outlives new tech
w: Technologies that have lasted longer are likely to last longer still, and widely adopted low-level plumbing like TCP/IP tends to persist.

t: Insecure products persist because customers don't pay for security
w: Security costs time and money, so vendors optimize for what customers buy; this explains insecure IoT and rushed ML deployments.

t: Outdoor light is far brighter; childhood myopia link
w: Outdoor light is often over 100x brighter than indoor light, and childhood outdoor exposure is strongly linked to lower myopia rates.

t: Why Uber's self-driving software failed to brake
w: Object classification flip-flopped between types, and a hardcoded one-second braking suppression masked it. A patch over a deeper classifier flaw.

t: How HN gives overlooked stories a second chance
w: Reviewers pick overlooked stories into a pool; software randomly lobs them onto the front page for minutes of attention.

t: How big-company software buying really works
w: Purchasing departments negotiate discounts by default, and 80-question checklists come from junior staff who hand evaluation to vendors who answer yes.

t: Why edge runtime cold-start comparisons mislead
w: Fastly's 35 microsecond figure was a hot start with code loaded; Workers' 5ms includes loading code from disk.

t: Practical digital security checklist for activists
w: Prefer TOTP over SMS 2FA, enable full-disk encryption, avoid email for sensitive data, use Signal and a local password manager.

t: Using arbitration and state UDAP laws to win claims
w: State deceptive-practices laws can treble damages and award attorney fees, which pressures companies toward early settlements.

t: Why lab replications fail: unwritten experimental conditions
w: Methods sections omit tacit controls like noise, cage cleanliness and handling; failed replications often reflect unrecorded variables, not falsity.

t: Self-hosting email splits into three separate choices
w: Domain ownership, mailbox hosting and sending are separable; sending needs a stable IP with ongoing reputation monitoring, the hardest part.

t: AlphaGo's edge-case play and optimization
w: Strong optimizers pick strategies that look balanced to humans while shrinking the opponent's win probability; optimal solutions often sit at extreme corners of the space.

t: Turn off delayed ACKs with TCP_QUICKACK
w: Delayed ACKs suit Telnet echo but stall request-response traffic; TCP_QUICKACK or TCP_NODELAY on Linux avoids it.

t: Burnout as a learned link between work and failure
w: Repeated high-risk failures condition the brain to associate work with failure; small guaranteed wins restore the reward signal and prevent burnout.

t: Studies find no cognitive effect of CO2 at high levels
w: Military studies found no cognitive effects from CO2 up to 40,000 ppm; exhaled breath already reaches about that, so office levels are unlikely to matter.

t: How display ads and the Like button track users
w: Display targeting depends on publisher inventory; the Like button works as a cross-site tracking cookie, and advertisers pay for audience access, not raw data.

t: Silicon Valley was built on ex-employees' trade secrets
w: Fairchild, Intel, MOSTek and early Unix all leveraged departing engineers' knowledge; California's non-compete ban helped shift innovation from Boston.

t: Why some processors cut off scaling merchants
w: Traditional processors underwrite first; some newer ones approve anyone and underwrite only at revenue thresholds, so keep backups.

t: Why clients must store reversible saved passwords
w: Clients must replay plaintext or reversible credentials, so hashing is impossible; a hard-coded key is weak but beats plaintext, and DPAPI is better.

t: Why language string representations age badly
w: Languages designed when Unicode fit in 65536 characters chose 2-byte encodings, the worst of both worlds; UTF-8 is the modern choice, and C strings already fit it well.

t: Wait before extracting repeated code
w: Duplication that looks identical may be incidental; keep it until changes reveal the true shared shape, then refactor when a bug shows the same edit is needed in many places.

t: Why low interest rates inflate house prices
w: Buyers are sized to a monthly payment; cheaper loans let lenders push bigger balances, so payment caps push prices up, not down.

t: Why app-level defenses cannot stop OS rootkits
w: Hypervisor and SMM rootkits defeat application-level antivirus; defenses calibrated to userland tools are playing to lose against real attackers.

t: Why astrophysicists still need dark matter
w: Structure formation and galaxy evolution depend on dark matter; even MOND-style alternatives must mimic it to reproduce observed structure.

t: How TIL cell therapy rebooted a patient's immune system
w: Patient's own tumor T cells were isolated, expanded to 130 billion in the lab, and reinfused after chemotherapy suppressed the native immune system.

t: Running at scale without containers, using Nix
w: Containers give reproducible deployments but not builds; Nix pins full build dependencies, and Kubernetes mostly helps stateless apps, not databases.

t: SEPA transfers are push, direct debits are pull
w: SEPA credit transfers push money; SEPA Direct Debit is the revocable pull mechanism, and instant payments are a separate, often costly service.

t: Why small farm trials mislead on yield claims
w: US corn yields are roughly three to four times sub-Saharan maize; fertilizer and modern practices close the gap, so small trials need scale context.

t: Why self-signed certificate warnings matter
w: Encrypted connections without verified identity can still be intercepted, so browsers treat unverified encryption as an error, not a mere warning.

t: Reading slopes to see rent-versus-buy sensitivity
w: Slope signs show how buying cost responds to each variable; a flat down-payment slope reflects Modigliani-Miller.

t: Designing content to survive 500 years
w: Use archival materials, multiple languages with dictionaries, and copies in stable regions like nuclear repository sites.

t: Why detailed commit messages pay off long-term
w: Context fades over time; clear commit messages record why a change was made, which future maintainers need most.

t: Distance from a point to a line segment
w: Project the point onto the segment direction with the dot product and clamp the parameter to [0,1] so endpoints give distance to the ends.

t: Derivatives as linear approximations, not gradient functions
w: Viewing a derivative as the tangent-line linear map at a point makes forward and reverse algorithmic differentiation easy to grasp.

t: Why restarts beat exceptions for error handling
w: Lisp conditions let code handle errors without unwinding the stack, using restarts that Java and Python's try/except lack.

t: Michael Jordan's statistics and ML reading list
w: Casella and Berger for inference, Ferguson and Lehmann for asymptotics, Gelman for Bayes, Robert and Casella for Monte Carlo.

t: Build habits with the Tiny Habits recipe
w: Shrink the habit until it needs no willpower, anchor it to an existing routine, then celebrate right away; this worked where earlier attempts failed.

t: How MLS feeds make real estate data hard to aggregate
w: Listings live in regional MLS systems only brokerages can access, with no standard format or API, so aggregators like Zillow must integrate each region separately.

t: Why user-agent-based bot detection fails
w: User agents are self-declared with no standard bot flag, so substring blacklists are slow and easily spoofed; reliable detection needs behavioral signals.

t: Buffett's institutional imperative explains bad corporate decisions
w: Organizations resist change, absorb available funds into projects, back leaders' whims with analysis, and copy peers regardless of rationality.

t: Why publishing Google's index wouldn't break its monopoly
w: Indexing is the easy part; CommonCrawl gives cheap web corpora (about $50 per grep), and habit plus click data keep Google dominant.

t: How a small fiber ISP is actually built
w: Firsthand guide: pick a backhaul point, run fiber to customers, and work around rights of way and monopoly rules; money is the main barrier.

t: Why sensor data breaks standard data architectures
w: Industrial sensor streams reach millions of events per second per server; generic platforms fail, forcing bespoke systems.

t: Why key-change warnings defend against messenger MITM
w: Any public-key system is open to MITM; key-change alerts are the defense, but most users never verify keys, so design around that.

t: Why Apple's SSD stores firmware and boot images
w: Since T2, the SSD holds firmware that BridgeOS loads, so bad EFI flashes cannot brick the machine, and DFU mode restores writable firmware.

t: How physics replicates results without rerunning experiments
w: Big experiments can't be repeated, so physics relies on cross-checks between detectors, many observations and systematic-bias hunts.

t: Why Bitcoin's energy use tracks coin price, not transactions
w: PoW miners spend energy until mining cost equals coin value; transaction count barely changes the energy a block consumes.

t: Phone security depends on baseband and enclave isolation
w: Modern basebands are isolated like USB peripherals; secure enclaves and audit depth matter more than code openness for security.

t: Use em and rem for fonts, not pixels
w: Pixels ignore user and platform text-size settings; em/rem scale to the platform default, and containers should be sized by characters per line.

t: Bitcoin's 2017 SegWit user-activated soft fork explained
w: Nodes rejecting non-SegWit-signaling blocks would split the chain; miner opposition made the UASF's success unlikely.

t: Why hospital IT is hard to secure
w: Custom EMRs built on decades-old systems, vendor lock-in, and fax-based exchange make modern security patches and upgrades difficult.

t: CHERI pointers carry bounds and permissions
w: CHERI packs address, bounds, and permissions into one pointer, making every access bounds-checked; 64-bit addresses cover 16 EiB.

t: Null references versus logical missing-value sentinels
w: Hoare's criticism targets null references, not logical missing values; without nulls, programmers reinvent them with flags or sentinel values.

t: Fix configs instead of watching logs for attacks
w: Logs flag problems you should not have; remove the attack surface, then keep structured audit trails of admin and authorization events.

t: Why Node.js succeeded: non-blocking I/O with no legacy
w: Java and Python used threads, so non-blocking libraries clashed with blocking code; JavaScript had no legacy I/O, so all packages became non-blocking.

t: Back-of-envelope cost of gravity-based grid storage
w: E=mgh means storing 12 hours of California power by rail cars needs over a billion kilograms, costing far more than pumped hydro.

t: How Latin word order enacts meaning
w: Latin's flexible word order lets Ovid place 'exilium' in isolation, so syntax mirrors the described exile.

t: Why registrars show taken domains as available
w: Registry lookup false positives, aftermarket premium listings, and drop-window buffers explain availability errors.

t: Source code and courses worth studying
w: Study xv6 and MIT 6.824 labs for OS and distributed systems, Tarsnap for C style, and Arc for implementing a Lisp.

t: Why Firefox couldn't evolve its old extension API
w: Breaking an internal API means porting code, shims, chasing add-on authors and maintaining both APIs for a year, which blocked optimizations like Quantum.

t: Why real-time equity settlement breaks market making
w: Real-time settlement forces institutions to hold cash rather than Treasuries, which removes market makers' buyer-of-last-resort capacity.

t: Traits of programmers who stay excellent long-term
w: Master a small technology subset, understand data structures and algorithms, structure data well, and go deep into the domain.

t: Classic MVC was unidirectional, not Rails-style
w: Original MVC on desktops had views query the model and controllers update it, a unidirectional flow closer to Redux than Rails' per-entity pattern.

t: Why an inverted yield curve signals recession fears
w: When the economy looks weak, investors rush into long treasuries for safety, pushing long-term yields below short-term ones, so the curve inverts.

t: Why home robots face brutal cost competition
w: Home robots must beat cheap human labor; early buyers are wealthy, so $5,000 price targets remain far from humanoid costs.

t: Why the melanoma AI study was flawed
w: On imbalanced data use precision-recall, not ROC; test on balanced sets and measure clinicians by referral decisions, not eyeballed diagnoses.

t: Where C# falls short for systems code
w: No inline fixed arrays, no addressable value elements without pointers, and generation-checked collections make stdlib operations linear.

t: Why $5 VPS hosting is hard to sustain
w: A $5 plan must cover hardware, SSD wear, support tickets and abuse cleanup, and noisy-neighbor CPU and disk contention is hard to prevent.

t: Why faces cannot reliably reveal emotions
w: Emotions unfold over time, use the whole body, overlap heavily in expression, and are culturally modulated, so single-frame classifiers face a hard ceiling.

t: What to really assess in engineering candidates
w: Hiring should test naming, maintainability, careful review, and team impact rather than algorithm puzzles.

t: What NFTs actually point to: usually off-chain files
w: An NFT is a token ID in a contract; the image usually lives on a centralized platform, so the NFT breaks if that host disappears.

t: The 2013 Bitcoin lock-limit incident explained
w: Bitcoin's real protocol was Core's actual behavior; nodes with different Berkeley DB lock limits accepted or rejected the same transaction, splitting the chain.

t: How auto order cancellations triggered the chip shortage
w: Automakers cancelled orders in 2020, vendors lost fab slots to other customers, then demand rebounded and fabs could not restore capacity quickly.

t: Estimating HN's active posters from logs
w: Two proxy estimates gave 0.8% and 8% posters; the ratio depends on unknown distinct-user counts, showing how measurement assumptions dominate.

t: Why solid-state battery energy claims need weight context
w: Volumetric density flatters solid-state cells; they are smaller but about 2.5x heavier, and 2.5V nominal voltage limits specific energy versus Li-ion 3.7V.

t: Why equity crowdfunding hurts small investors
w: VC returns depend on large portfolios where outliers pay for losers; retail investors lack portfolio size and access to good deals (lemons effect).

t: Why CSV resists parallel parsing unlike JSON Lines
w: Quoted newlines and commas mean CSV rows can't be found lexically; you must parse serially. Compressed JSON Lines is a strong alternative.

t: Why short interest can exceed 100% of float
w: Each short sale is matched by a buyer, and borrowed shares can be re-lent, so short interest has no fixed cap relative to float.

t: Why oil is priced in dollars
w: Oil is priced in dollars because dollars dominate trade and finance, fueled by American consumers' spending and dollar markets, not a petrodollar deal.

t: Why zero-confirmation Bitcoin payments can be double-spent
w: Unconfirmed transactions can be replaced via RBF with a conflicting spend, so merchants must wait for block confirmations.

t: Why 432 Hz tuning claims do not hold
w: The 432 Hz appeal depends on the arbitrary second; a 2% pitch gap is trivial next to DJs' routine plus or minus 10% pitch control.

t: Cooling a house with ventilation instead of AC
w: Tall ceilings, windows on every side, and an upper attic vent drive stack-effect airflow that pulls hot air out at night.

t: Why Lisp macros let you add language features
w: Macros let programmers define abstractions like dolist in libraries, avoiding the multi-year language-committee process Java needed.

t: Why Norvig chose Python over Lisp
w: Python matched textbook pseudocode best; at scale, architecture and team process matter more than language choice.

t: Annotated reading list for application security
w: Recommends the Web Application Hacker's Handbook, Practical Reverse Engineering, and Cryptography Engineering, with notes on what to read first.

t: How Dropbox placeholder files differ from network filesystems
w: Cloud files show real sizes instantly and cache on open; unlike SMB or NFS over WAN, offline and pinning work.

t: Why price discrimination can clear markets
w: Student rates capture demand that would otherwise go unserved, so discrimination can create value rather than just extract it.

t: Why terminal rendering latency is hard on macOS
w: Core Text can take over 150ms per frame on a 4K display, and low latency means the next frame must include the new prompt.

t: Why origin IP allowlisting alone isn't enough
w: Origins must also check the Host header or use authenticated origin pulls or Argo Tunnel, since CDNs cannot verify origin ownership.

t: Why early employees need a large exit to break even
w: Forgone salary and investor preferences push the required sale price for early employees from millions into the $10-15 million range.

t: Rules-based versus principles-based regulation
w: Principles-based regulation gives regulators latitude to resist rules-lawyering and regulatory capture, at the cost of predictability; rules-based is the opposite trade.

t: Pointer-to-pointer removes linked list special cases
w: Storing the address of the link pointer makes deletion a single assignment, removing the head-versus-middle branch from the code.

t: Why cold water can preserve brain after drowning
w: Cold slows cell damage, so long submersions can allow full recovery; hyperbaric oxygen claims lack solid evidence and the press overstated them.

t: Why velocity becomes a four-vector in relativity
w: Relativity merges scalars and vectors into four-vectors; velocity's temporal partner is change in coordinate time per proper time.

t: What battery defects cause phone cell fires
w: Deflected electrodes, thin insulation tape and welding burrs can cause internal shorts; a battery engineer notes Samsung's candid report was rare.

t: Prerequisites before adopting microservices
w: Microservices require monitoring, CI/CD, API contracts and tooling that monoliths let you skip.

t: Energy per capita shapes farming and fertility
w: Below about 1 MWh per capita, a country lacks nitrogen and steel production, so farming stays labor-heavy and families have more children.

t: The practical problems that break CSV data exchange
w: Encoding is unknowable, Excel mangles numbers and dates, BOMs vary, and most CSV libraries fail the spec in different ways.

t: Why idle Claude Code sessions cost full re-caching
w: Prompt cache expires after an hour idle, so resuming rewrites the full context; eliding old thinking performed best among fixes tried.

t: Practical advice for blind developers
w: Learn NVDA, VoiceOver or Orca, use only the keyboard, and expect inaccessible tools that need workarounds like command-line Git.

t: How a hidden div broke Edge video acceleration
w: A hidden empty element over YouTube videos made Edge's hardware fast path bail, hurting battery life.

t: Why blockchains make poor general-purpose databases
w: Blockchain trades throughput and simplicity for decentralization; Bitcoin handles far fewer transactions per second than real databases, and blockchain is largely a marketing term.

t: Server relief: cheap server-side password verification
w: Store SHA256 of the scrypt hash so clients pay the scrypt cost while the server verifies cheaply; a stolen database is useless for login.

t: How TACK extends certificate pinning to all sites
w: TACK lets sites pin certificates on first visit like HSTS, so rogue CA interception of ordinary sites becomes detectable without manual browser pinning.

t: Events and jobs are different messaging problems
w: Events fan out to every subscriber while jobs go to one worker, so job queues need completion and state tracking that pub/sub lacks.

t: How missing technical data rights create sole-source lock-in
w: Waiving technical data rights lowers upfront cost but lets the contractor become the only source, so later parts cost far more.

t: Why bright indoor light needs an evening cutoff
w: Clocks handle photoperiods of about 14-15 hours; 18 hours under bright light lengthens the internal day and cuts sleep, so evening dimming matters.

t: Why cloud-backed secrets force a security trade-off
w: Encrypting cloud-backed passwords with a device-only key breaks restore on new devices; using the account password exposes them to the provider.

t: What Google interviewers actually want
w: Interviewers want candidates to succeed; they need evidence for a clear positive or negative score, so they seek signal rather than trick questions.

t: What W3C's EME does and doesn't do
w: EME doesn't put DRM in browsers; it lets them call decryption modules already present elsewhere, with a clear-key mode for platforms that lack one.

t: Why 'no evidence of efficacy' isn't 'no efficacy'
w: Relative risk 0.61 with CI 0.13-2.89 from 3 vs 4 deaths fits anything from large benefit to large harm; small trials can't detect moderate effects.

t: How Glacier achieves cheap storage with custom hardware
w: Low-RPM spin-down drives in custom racks trade throughput for power and cost; retrieval is slow because only a limited number of drives can spin up per rack.

t: Rob Pike's case against generics in Go
w: Containers of ints or strings are less burdensome than claimed; Go favors simple types over inheritance taxonomies, a stance that shaped the language's design.

t: Prioritize statelessness, then coupling, complexity, duplication
w: Optimize in order: reduce state, coupling, complexity, then duplication; stateless code is easiest to reason about, test, and scale out.

t: Why publication bias, not the p=0.05 cutoff, is the problem
w: Publishing only significant results distorts the evidence; with fair coins, some runs look significant by chance while null results never appear in the literature.

t: Why parser generators catch grammar ambiguity
w: Building LL or LR tables reveals ambiguous grammars at build time; general parsers and PEG prioritized choice hide those ambiguities.

t: Why Netflix uses React for signup pages
w: Heavy A/B testing, localization across about 200 countries, and shared components make React valuable even for a simple landing page.

t: Why S3 is a poor fit for serving websites
w: S3 returns transient 50x errors that browsers never retry, so static sites see random broken images and pages.

t: Why Romans lacked steel quality, not converters
w: A Bessemer converter was buildable by Romans; the hard part was consistent steel, via controlled manganese and carbon additions.

t: Why .htaccess-based upload protection silently failed
w: Apache 2.3.9+ ignores .htaccess by default; relying on it to block PHP execution in uploads left the hole open.

t: Detecting GPS jamming from aircraft ADS-B data
w: ADS-B broadcasts self-reported accuracy fields like NACp; mapping aircraft with poor values reveals regional GPS interference.

t: Treat leap seconds like timezone offset changes
w: Store timestamps in TAI and apply leap seconds as offset changes, like DST, avoiding the repeated-second ambiguity of UTC.

t: Why e-ink devices cost more than expected
w: E Ink sells proprietary film, not displays; makers must reverse-engineer drive waveforms, and that cost lands in the device BOM.

t: Why the Uber rider app has thousands of scenarios
w: Regional features, experiments and 40-50 product teams multiply flows, so a few visible screens hide huge complexity.

t: Decoding a dense k one-liner step by step
w: k has few syntax forms: applying functions, infix operators, bracket argument lists and adverbs; a short line decodes once these rules are known.

t: Deduplicating encrypted files via content-hash keys
w: Encrypt each file with a key derived from its own hash: identical files produce identical ciphertext, so the server deduplicates without seeing plaintext.

t: Why batch auctions don't end high-frequency racing
w: Batch matching forces a tiebreak: first-arrival priority rewards speed, while pro-rata filling invites inflated orders, so both schemes have gaming problems.

t: Why crypto composition matters more than primitives
w: Secure primitives are undermined by how they are composed; homemade KDFs and unusual modes are red flags, and vetted designs like the Axolotl ratchet exist.

t: How ad impressions are valued by audience match
w: Remnant ad value depends on matching quality, purchase intent, customer value, and audience desirability by geography.

t: How registrar access enables domain hijacking
w: Hijacking needs registrar access to change nameservers and a full copied zone; AXFR-disabled setups make unnoticed takeover very hard.

t: Timing caffeine around adenosine to shift sleep
w: Caffeine blocks adenosine, which builds up while awake; delaying the first coffee to late morning and cutting off by afternoon helps shift sleep.

t: Practical habits for exploring unfamiliar code
w: Start with file sizes and the dispatch loop, single-step the main flow, and track data structures passed through many functions.

t: Why MessagePack rarely beats JSON in browsers
w: Native JSON.parse is fast and msgpack is slower to encode and decode; gzip erases most of the size savings.

t: Why media players need broad permissions when sandboxed
w: Playing files, optical discs, webcams, GPU and audio stacks needs device, file and network access that undermines sandbox models.

t: What 'zero knowledge' storage actually requires
w: Zero-knowledge storage needs client-side key management; vendors' transport and at-rest encryption claims can together create false privacy impressions.

t: The 10x programmer claim has weak evidence
w: Tracing citations behind the 10x claim finds no replications, dated data, and no valid measure of individual productivity.

t: Why FISA courts differ from Article III courts
w: FISC is a congressional creation without lifetime tenure or adversarial hearings, so claims about Roberts' lifetime surveillance power misread the structure.

t: Why Bitcoin transaction IDs can change
w: Transaction IDs derive from malleable content, so the correct way to find a sent transaction is scanning history for matching parameters.

t: How the mining boom hollowed out Australia's economy
w: Resource windfall lifted the dollar and hollowed out manufacturing; without a sovereign wealth fund, budgets fell into structural deficit.

t: Why Intel missed mobile: margins, not ISA performance
w: x86 translation logic is now a tiny share of die area; Intel's refusal of low-margin mobile chips, not ISA performance, explains its miss.

t: Why SCADA systems need one-way data diodes
w: Industrial control systems send data two ways to IT historians; software rules alone cannot stop backward flow, so physical one-way data diodes are the verifiable fix.

t: Real architectural differences between ARM64 and x86
w: x86 decodes variable-length instructions at every byte offset; ARM64's fixed width makes wide decode simple, with weaker memory ordering needing explicit fences.

t: Why Law of Demeter limits object navigation
w: Chaining getters through Chapter to Section to Paragraph couples callers to internals; restructuring the book then breaks every caller.

t: How Google's engineering raised surveillance costs
w: Forward secrecy, Curve25519, certificate pinning and Chrome's sandbox made mass surveillance expensive, beyond what Google needed internally.

t: Why overriding methods in subclasses breaks invariants
w: A subclass that overrides push and pushAll double-counts when the base pushAll calls push; prefer composition or interfaces over implementation inheritance.

t: Why electromagnetism follows from local phase symmetry
w: Demanding that the wavefunction phase can change independently at each point forces a gauge field, which is electromagnetism.

t: Why lenses cannot heat past the source temperature
w: A lens cannot heat a target above the radiation source's temperature; moonlight is reflected sunlight, so the Moon's own temperature is irrelevant.

t: How a Roth IRA can hold a huge tax-free gain
w: Roth IRA growth is tax-free if invested within the account; contributions are locked until retirement age and cannot be borrowed against.

t: Why training AI on code may be fair use
w: Courts have not tested it, but training on copyrighted code is likely fair use, and users are not liable for accidental minor copies.

t: How GNU readline pressured CLISP into GPL licensing
w: RMS released readline under GPL so linking software had to be GPL; CLISP relicensed in response, showing copyleft used as leverage over other vendors.

t: What hiring research says about predictors
w: Summarizes Schmidt and Hunter's meta-analysis of selection methods, showing research, not intuition, should guide which hiring criteria a company uses.

t: Why ripgrep beats ag: regex, line numbers, mmap
w: Ripgrep's speed comes from DFA-only Rust regexes, skipping line-number counting by default, and avoiding mmap; ag's author explains the trade-offs.

t: How custom curve parameters break ECDSA signature validation
w: Attacker-chosen base point lets someone craft a second private key matching a victim's public key using a signature, without the original private key.

t: Why version control fails for law documents
w: Conflicting legislative branches can't simply be merged; systems keep parallel versions until a court or legislature decides, which takes years.

t: Why host-pathogen relationships tend toward truce over time
w: New hosts first see messy mortality; ill-adapted viruses spread poorly, so pathogens gradually adjust and may become symbionts, a process called détente.

t: How Payment Request and Payment Handler APIs fit together
w: Payment Request lets sites invoke installed payment apps; Payment Handler lets those apps register, with the browser matching supported methods and prompting the user.

t: How Yale's admissions committee actually evaluates applicants
w: Reviewers spend ~20 minutes per file; clear rejects and admits are filtered early, and a committee debates the rest.

t: Why Bluetooth struggles through the human body
w: Water absorbs 2.4 GHz, so indoor reflections help while outdoor headsets need strong antennas; higher Bluetooth 5 power improves range.

t: Why iCloud sync struggles with Core Data
w: A file-sync service has no server that resolves conflicts, so clients replaying diffs cannot agree on a canonical database state.

t: Why hyper-growth companies keep rewriting their stacks
w: Founders pick a fast-to-build stack, then successive hires rewrite it, stalling development; Google, eBay, Facebook and Reddit followed this pattern.

t: Why xip.io's DNS setup is technically broken
w: Low TTLs on CNAME chains add latency; missing NS records and refused zone transfers to backups show custom DNS daemons often break standards.

t: Why shifting traffic can mislead experiments
w: Time-based site changes correlate with the variant receiving more traffic, so one arm can swamp results.

t: C prototype and struct-return gotchas
w: Use f(void) to forbid arguments in C; C lacks return-value optimization, so returning big structs costs copies.

t: Practical sysadmin tips for a first VPS
w: Use shell aliases, tmux for persistent sessions, rsync for file moves, and nginx to serve several apps from one VPS.

t: Most mismanaged plastic comes from Asia and Africa
w: Paper bags need about 43 reuses to match plastic energy; North America is about 3% of mismanaged plastic, Asia and Africa 86%.

t: Why Windows UI designers overrode usability data
w: Insider account: designers without Windows experience overrode usability-tested decisions, and backlash forced reversals.

t: Why server-side bugs pay less than exploit markets
w: Vendors can patch server bugs instantly, so no grey market exists; exploit buyers pay more for reliable chains they can resell.

t: How lens choice shapes 3D storytelling tension
w: Wide and long lenses change perspective and depth; integrating 3D with lens language lets filmmakers build tension, such as a long lens slowing a runner.

t: How Apple hardened the MacBook camera LED in hardware
w: A dedicated always-on PMIC enforces a minimum LED on-time and duty-cycle floor, so no firmware or power cut can defeat the camera indicator.

t: Why a Solaris kernel engineer left illumos
w: Linux closed its 2010-era performance gaps (BKL, mutexes, ext4, TCP), so the faster-kernel rationale behind illumos no longer justifies its cost.

t: How time-lock puzzles force sequential computation delay
w: Sequential hash chains run in parallel force a fixed compute delay; obfuscating chain starts hides the key until the work is done.

t: Why automotive code uses unlocked shared globals
w: With fixed RAM, no malloc and no blocking, single-writer global variables are a fast, safe way to share state between components.

t: Compiling to C inherits undefined behavior risks
w: Null dereferences, signed overflow and oversized shifts are undefined in C, so optimizers can remove checks and break memory safety.

t: Why N:M green threads cost more than they save
w: Userspace schedulers struggle to beat Linux's, need cross-thread synchronization, and cause subtle bugs with third-party code.

t: Ordering JS code to improve gzip compression
w: Clustering similar fragments by edit distance or an LZ-based metric keeps repeats inside gzip's 32K window, shrinking output.

t: Babbage's method of differences behind his engines
w: Babbage generated log and sine tables mechanically with finite differences, the principle that drove his difference and analytical engines.

t: How FRAND licensing differs from ordinary patents
w: Standards-essential patents must be licensed on fair, reasonable, non-discriminatory terms, so Apple's suit enforced those terms rather than claiming feature patents.

t: React Native skips the DOM for native performance
w: A React team member explains that React Native renders native views with no DOM, and that good mobile UX still requires deliberate performance work.

t: How cross-signed roots keep new CAs trusted
w: Cross-signed roots let old clients trust a new CA via an older signature; sending the self-signed root in chains only slows TLS.

t: Why Shenzhen's manufacturing edge is not just labor
w: Hukou rules keep local advantages tied to birthplace; Shenzhen's migrant talent pool and infrastructure drive its manufacturing lead.

t: How delta hedging amplifies stock moves in squeezes
w: Market makers hedge delta; as price moves, gamma forces buying into rallies and selling into drops, which amplifies squeezes.

t: Offline-first setup to limit surveillance
w: Use kiwix for local Wikipedia, install offline docs, and fetch RSS server-side so reading habits stay private.

t: Why defer breaks when cleanup is refactored
w: Scope-based defer runs cleanup when the creating function returns, so moving creation into helpers breaks; value-based destructors travel with the object.

t: How to post a good Show HN
w: Use Show HN only for tryable projects, link the site not text, state what it does, and avoid marketing language.

t: How tech companies claim employee side-project IP
w: Most companies claim work on own time; Google's process lets most work be open-sourced after review, a useful industry benchmark.

t: Bacteria don't want; resistance is selection
w: Resistance arises through selection across lineages, not intent; many antibiotics come from fungal and microbial chemicals.

t: IRV versus Borda count for polarization
w: Instant runoff ignores a centrist who is everyone's second choice, while Borda count rewards broadly acceptable candidates over extremes.

t: Completion-based async I/O versus Unix readiness multiplexing
w: VMS and NT link I/O completion to follow-on computation, letting the kernel notify on completion; Unix forces manual multiplexing and thread management.

t: How governments actually buy exploits
w: Governments buy exploits through contractors like Raytheon rather than individual developers; the grey market is legal, long-standing, and sustained by reliable payment.

t: How to read a line of K array code
w: K reads by applying verbs and adverbs to what follows; views update automatically like spreadsheet cells, here tracking the offsets of newlines in a file.

t: How Israeli airport security screens passengers, not bags
w: Screeners probe story consistency through layered conversations, trading time and profiling for depth, unlike US bag-focused screening.

t: Porting Metal Gear Solid to PC in 1999
w: Textures covered body parts, allowing 16-colour palettes; music fit a 512KB ADPCM buffer; the executable swapped overlays around a shared 600KB core.

t: Why rotating video artifacts reveal gimbal lock
w: Near 90 degrees pitch, gimbal lock forces a roll flip; if only the object spins while background stays still, it is attached to the camera.

t: Lower network update rates work in fast games
w: Descent-style games play well at 20 updates per second with interpolation; 60 Hz wastes bandwidth and lag compensation covers latency.

t: How the Seawater Greenhouse cools crops
w: Air is drawn through a seawater-wetted honeycomb, cooling it by evaporation and trapping insects in salt water while the greenhouse stays open.

t: Why Erlang isolates failures better than Go
w: Erlang's isolated process memory lets one crashed process be killed cleanly; Go's shared memory means a panic leaves overall program state unknown.

t: Writing a whole OS in a garbage-collected language
w: AOT-compile a managed runtime to machine code, bootstrap with a tiny assembly loader, and mark GC methods as compiler intrinsics for raw memory access.

t: Why early 4K monitors needed display-driver hacks
w: HDMI and DisplayPort 1.2 couldn't drive 4K at 60Hz natively; drivers faked it as two tiles, causing window-spanning problems on Linux and ChromeOS.

t: Postgres full-text search limits versus Solr
w: Postgres hard-codes its tokenizer and lacks faceting, so configurable engines like Solr or Elasticsearch are needed for many search workloads.

t: Four cases the 'this' rule misses in JavaScript
w: 'this' also binds via bracket calls like o['foo'](); forEach gets undefined unless thisArg is passed; DOM listeners get the element; strict-mode plain calls undefined.

t: Why angled solar arrays cannot beat optimal orientation
w: Independent panels' energy adds linearly, so each off-optimal angle yields less than one optimally oriented panel; no free energy.

t: How a pre-blockchain digital notary chained hashes
w: Client hashes are batched into a Merkle tree whose root links into a super hash chain, so certificates prove a document existed at a timestamp.

t: Why Korean stops are hard for English speakers
w: English treats aspirated and unaspirated k as one sound, but Korean separates normal, aspirated and tense velar stops into distinct words.

t: Why signed overflow UB enables loop optimizations
w: Assuming signed overflow never happens lets compilers unroll loops and precompute bounds; wrapping semantics would block many optimizations.

t: Measuring ripgrep against GNU grep fairly
w: With equal parallelism and file coverage, ripgrep is about 2x faster than GNU grep; bigger gaps mostly come from default filtering or Unicode.

t: How fiber taps evade OTDR fault detection
w: A small beam splitter diverts photons without a break, while cutting the fiber triggers OTDR repair alerts, so taps must avoid a detectable fault.

t: Why runaway trim is hard to correct on the 737
w: Tailplane loading from elevator input fights manual trim, so pilots must offload the yoke to regain trim control.

t: How to vet a claimed P vs NP proof
w: Simple combinatorial approaches are known not to work, so a credible proof needs new techniques; check credibility and peer review.

t: How transaction malleability freezes spendable bitcoin change
w: Unconfirmed change cannot be spent until its parent confirms; a mutated transaction ID can make a payment silently fail.

t: Why TPMs make poor DRM
w: TPMs attest boot-stage hashes, not device identity, so firmware updates would revoke licenses; DRM needs device-bound keys.

t: Why a Brompton beats other folding bikes
w: Brompton rides like a real bike with gears and large-enough wheels; cheaper small-wheel folders compromise ride quality and gearing.

t: Dynamic languages in large teams: a double-edged sword
w: Hyper-dynamic languages suit small projects and disciplined teams; with juniors and no architectural owner, flexibility creates staggering tech debt.

t: How public company valuation actually works
w: A company's valuation is the last traded share price times shares outstanding, even if few shares trade.

t: Why Copilot can seem to emit private code
w: Context comes from open local files, and frequently repeated patterns get reproduced; the team says such repeats occur in under 1% of suggestions.

t: Private contact discovery between two users
w: Explains private set intersection: parties learn only shared elements, so Signal users can compare their own contacts without a server seeing them.

t: How JavaScript was designed under Netscape pressure
w: Eich explains JS's Scheme-inspired first-class functions and the Java-driven mandate to make objects without classes, from an insider view.

t: Why startup options have a 90-day exercise window
w: Law requires ISOs to be exercised within 90 days of leaving; AMT on the exercise spread often makes exercising costly.

t: Restricted stock taxes and the 83(b) election
w: Without a timely 83(b) election, restricted stock is taxed as ordinary income at each vesting; electing at grant makes later gains capital gains.

t: Why HTML's promises fell short in practice
w: Device independence, user style control, and accessibility rarely materialized, so apps get rebuilt per platform and ARIA is bolted on later.

t: What separates expert hackers from experienced ones
w: Experts ask what caused a bug and how to prevent it, then build test fixtures and clear interfaces to make testing feasible.

t: Why big FIFO queues wreck network congestion
w: Datagram networks lack backpressure, so large FIFO queues cause bufferbloat; per-flow fair queuing is the classic remedy.

t: Linguistic method for teaching children to read
w: Bloomfield and Barnhart's Let's Read teaches phonics-based reading through daily lessons a parent reads aloud, a practical guide from long experience.

t: How Tcl beat Java in Sun's internal bake-off
w: Insider account: Sun's 1995 internal language review chose Tcl over Java, and the Java (Live Oak) team was scrapped at fiscal year end.

t: Maintaining Python across Google's monorepo
w: Google upgraded Python from 2.7 to 3.11 over years, since committers own breakages, while tooling kept thousands of third-party packages patched and current.

t: Raft is MultiPaxos, not a rival consensus algorithm
w: Paxos is a family of ideas, and standard Paxos decides one value. Raft is a concrete specification of MultiPaxos ideas, so comparing them is misleading.

t: Why small startup teams show misleading outcome variance
w: Small samples produce extreme results by chance; the hospital example shows people routinely ignore sample size.

t: Practical pitfalls and advice for using asyncio
w: Use asyncio only when network IO is the bottleneck, prefer aiohttp over raw asyncio, and turn on debug features outside production.

t: Why iCloud struggles with Core Data stores
w: Core Data stores are SQLite databases that can be large, and iCloud replicates whole files, so syncing them clashes with its file-level model.

t: Why infringement is not theft in law
w: Explains that theft and copyright infringement are distinct legal categories, both framed as alienable rights, which makes the stealing debate legally irrelevant.

t: Why unzeroed disk blocks leak data across VMs
w: Sparse virtual disks look zeroed but are not; hypervisors must zero or map freed blocks, or tenants can read prior data.

t: Curated resources on the Nile graphics system
w: Links to Nile, Gezira, Ohm, Maru, KScript and VPRI reports document Alan Kay's dense graphics DSL stack.

t: Why baseband isolation matters for phone security
w: A baseband with USB access exposes kernel USB drivers, while memory-firewalled basebands have a smaller attack surface.

t: Why game lighting models don't match reality
w: Shading formulas like lighting times diffuse plus ambient look right but ignore light transport, which is why physically based rendering matters.

t: Why a hash digest is not an authenticator
w: Anyone can recompute a plain SHA1 digest, so it authenticates nothing; use HMAC, and avoid archaic modes like IGE that were reinvented and broken.

t: Speed-reading papers with timed summaries
w: Read papers in 12-minute slots, writing a three-point summary of questions, results or techniques, then revise a week later and deep-read only key papers.

t: Linux RNG maintainer rebuts /dev/random attack paper
w: Since 2012, Linux keeps gathering entropy even when the pool looks full; the paper's attack assumes wrong entropy estimates.

t: Monads explained as a generalized None-handling wrapper
w: A monad is an interface wrapping values so chaining functions handles failure, like None, automatically, removing nested checks and making error handling compositional.

t: Practical Haskell performance rules for large data
w: Avoid thunk buildup in long loops, use Text and ByteString instead of String, prefer Vector for finite data, and stream large inputs.

t: GC closing a file descriptor breaks SQLite locks
w: A garbage-collected file object closed a descriptor SQLite shared, so later flock calls failed; reused fds cause subtle bugs.

t: Why dense math notation is precise, not obfuscated
w: Terms like absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure are compact definitions; each word carries a precise mathematical meaning.

t: Startup lecture notes on ideas and markets
w: Pick a fast-growing small market first, build what you need, expect naysayers, and have a clear answer to why now.

t: Residual stream keeps consistent representations across layers
w: Logit-lens observation: GPT-style layers share one representation, so the output head can decode intermediate layers into words.

t: Why TARP and QE differ in government accounting
w: TARP ran through Treasury and profited; QE was Federal Reserve asset purchases, with profits remitted to Treasury by statute.

t: ORM overhead can rival database time in web apps
w: Time spent in ORM and driver code is application CPU, not waiting on the database; well-indexed reads are fast, so translation often dominates latency.

t: Why an invasion of Japan was logistically daunting
w: Invasion needed air control, naval gunfire, landing craft and supply chains; the Soviets lacked these, so the Soviet threat alone cannot explain surrender.

t: Collapsing a server stack into one executable
w: Replacing TCP with UDP, bypassing the kernel for Ethernet and using memory-mapped lmdb reads let a startup serve reads in under 3 microseconds.

t: How dbus was adopted by KDE and GNOME
w: dbus succeeded by meeting the stated requirements of KDE and GNOME developers, solving real problems instead of hypothetical ones, after many earlier IPC attempts.

t: Annotated shortlist of essential programming books
w: Opinionated list of classic CS books with reasons to prefer particular editions, such as Effective STL over other Meyer titles.

t: Why systemd beats shell-script init systems
w: Shell-script init spawns many processes per service; systemd forks services and gets kernel notice of exit instead of polling.

t: Why phishing training fails against replayed emails
w: Attackers copy genuine transactional HTML and change one link, so fakes look identical and blame-the-user training stops working.

t: Setting up a US C-corp from abroad, practically
w: Delaware C-corps suit future VC rounds; expect lawyer costs near $300/hr, an EIN, a US bank partner, and local counsel for any IP transfer.

t: JS-first versus DOM-first component models
w: React treats JS objects as primitives and the DOM as artifact; Web Components invert that, making DOM elements primitive.

t: Hidden factors in S3 versus owned storage
w: Cloud storage replicates across regions, reprices instantly, and avoids capex; leaving costs about one month's rent.

t: Spotting weak evidence in an alcohol treatment study
w: One significant result among many nulls, pooled from two trials and uncorrected for multiple comparisons: a fragile finding despite 'high certainty' labels.

t: How neural network compressors achieve lossless coding
w: Model predicts next-byte probabilities, arithmetic coding spends about minus log2 p bits, and the decoder trains identically so no weights are sent.

t: How ANITA detects neutrinos and cosmic rays by radio
w: Neutrinos in ice emit coherent Askaryan radio pulses; cosmic-ray air showers emit horizontally polarized radio via Earth's magnetic field.

t: Kendall notation for queues: arrivals, service, servers
w: Classify queues by arrival process, service process and server count using D, M or G distributions; D/D/1 and M/M/1 show how they differ.

t: Lymph is blood-derived fluid cycling through tissues
w: Lymph is essentially blood minus red cells, becoming interstitial fluid in tissues, cycling like the water cycle.

t: Runescape botting arms race and bytecode binding
w: Powerbot bound game objects via bytecode and reflection, surviving Jagex obfuscation until a web-walking API arrived.

t: Employee rights to concerted action under NLRA
w: Section 7 protects collective workplace complaints, so discipline over such activity can violate Section 8(a)(1) even without a union.

t: How promotion incentives drive Google product shutdowns
w: Insider explains promotion criteria reward launches over maintenance, so teams abandon upkeep and products get shut.

t: Housing costs are concentrated in a few elite metros
w: Inflation-adjusted new-home cost per square foot is roughly flat nationally; high costs cluster in high-wage metros, and newer homes also carry more amenities.

t: Why nuclear plants lost cost competitiveness
w: Cooling and build costs make nuclear more expensive than solar and wind, and storage now shifts grid economics, so cheap renewables plus batteries set the benchmark.

t: Replacing the README's examples with sed and find
w: Each README example maps to sed -r with find and xargs; standard Unix tools cover bulk edits, file filtering and previews.

t: The couldn't-you-just test for disruptive technology
w: When technical people dismiss an idea with couldn't you just, it may be friction removal that makes the technology explode, like blogs and YouTube.

t: How Tether's dollar peg could fail
w: Tether issues tokens claimed fully backed by dollars, but Bitfinex cannot clear wires, so redemption depends on trust.

t: How checking accounts make money for banks
w: Checking accounts earn through fees and debit interchange, and low balances keep interest cost minimal.

t: Why renewables raise grid costs without storage
w: Renewables generate when weather allows, not when demand peaks, so surplus is sold cheaply or negatively while balancing costs rise.

t: Why annual renewable share misleads about grid reality
w: Annual percentages hide that wind often exceeds demand, causing negative prices, while inflexible nuclear makes surplus management hard.

t: How a convincing bank phishing call manipulated a target
w: Scammers spoof the bank's number, call back immediately to create urgency, and exploit reset codes; banks should explain why codes are sent.

t: Why TOTP authenticator apps create recovery problems
w: TOTP secrets don't migrate between phones, so losing a device means re-enrolling every account; backup codes reintroduce password-like risk.

t: Why fusion's tritium problem isn't solved
w: Practical fusion plants need tritium breeding, and tritium is hard to contain, so fusion's stigma and proliferation issues aren't obviously smaller than fission's.

t: Why decentralized networks drift toward centralization
w: Running a node costs time and money, and unequal spending lets a few providers dominate even under decentralized protocols, as GitHub does for Git.

t: Why beneficial ownership thresholds exempt operating companies
w: Tracing owners of operating companies through funds is costly; disclosure targets shell companies, which otherwise let anonymous owners hide behind layers of entities.

t: Rule for deciding what needs a unit test
w: Write one test per desired external behavior of a unit plus one per bug fixed; testing every public method couples tests to implementation.

t: Daily accessibility failures seen by a blind developer
w: Mouse-only controls and inaccessible sites block screen reader users; accessibility bugs make people give up on basic tasks.

t: Why Rust rejects borrowed data in spawned threads
w: Walks through the 'static error from thread::spawn and how Arc or scoped threads fix sharing data safely.

t: Why Google UX changes move in small steps
w: Redesigning products used by billions triggers backlash, so UX evolves incrementally and ends up as a hodgepodge even with skilled designers.

t: Why merchants need card imprints to win chargebacks
w: Issuers side with consumers in fraud disputes unless the merchant has a physical swipe plus an imprint; without one, chargebacks are often lost.

t: Why large corporations flattened income inequality mid-century
w: Large firms hid pay gaps in benefits and resisted measuring individual output; after 1980, ambitious people leaving the ladder reversed that flattening.

t: Practical cooking techniques that transform home meals
w: Rinse rice and keep the lid on at low heat; room-temperature eggs cook better; bake batter promptly since baking powder reacts quickly.

t: Why tech hiring grew to many interview rounds
w: Companies add interviews to avoid trusting one evaluator, cover multiple skill dimensions, and justify interviewer cost, so the logic compounds over time.

t: Linux tools for running a business
w: Xournal, LibreOffice, OBS, Audacity, Tesseract, QEMU/KVM and GnuCash cover contracts, OCR, accounting and virtual machines on Linux.

t: Why Homebrew mirrors older macOS package managers
w: Easy relocatable installs solve only 5% of the problem; native builds, prefixes, and versioned Cellar symlinks drove the complexity that Fink and MacPorts faced.

t: Checking the Mel legend against manuals
w: Manuals suggest Nather's Mel story misremembers the machine: the RPC-4000 index tag sits at word end, so the trick needs an unusual field overflow.

t: Rust's objects, traits and lessons from Go
w: Rust dropped prototype objects for typeclasses after finding them unused, then re-added objects for reuse; Go's interfaces closely resemble typeclasses.

t: Mutable and immutable variables are equivalent under SSA
w: Shows that in a single execution, mutable reassignment can be rewritten as SSA fresh variables, so the mutable/immutable distinction is not observable.

t: How the DES cracker book evaded export controls
w: Historical account: the EFF book printed DES cracker source as scannable, checksummed text, exploiting the paper publishing exception to circumvent digital export restrictions.

t: Measuring run queue latency with runqlat histograms
w: Run queue latency is the key scheduler metric; a BPF histogram shows how long runnable threads wait, exposing scheduling bugs that averages hide.

t: What USB-C cables actually carry: power, USB2, lanes
w: USB-C cables always carry at least 60W power and a USB2 pair; high-speed lanes and eMarker chips vary by cable, affecting speed and 100W support.

t: 5G sub-6GHz versus mmWave explained
w: Sub-6 5G shortens the transmission interval from 1ms to 100us and uses finer subchannels, helping small packets; mmWave is a separate, shorter-range band.

t: HATEOAS describes how websites already work
w: Following links and submitting forms drives state changes in a browser, which is Fielding's hypermedia-as-engine-of-state idea; most REST APIs omit it.

t: Why US high-speed rail struggles beyond regulation
w: HSR needs grade-separated right-of-way and long straight track; FRA rules aren't the main obstacle, and Acela's weight isn't why its service lags.

t: Lessons from a rejected YC interview: bring a demo
w: Clinging to one idea and lacking a working demo sank the team; YC expects a demo and openness to their suggestions.

t: How pitot-static failures mislead airspeed and altitude
w: Airspeed uses pitot and static pressure; altimeter and vertical speed use static port alone, so blocked pitot tubes show as airspeed drops.

t: Stock option taxes: NQOs, ISOs and 83(b)
w: NQOs tax the spread as income at exercise, ISOs can trigger AMT, and early exercise with an 83(b) election can defer tax on restricted stock.

t: Python's built-in exception hierarchy
w: Lays out the full tree of built-in exceptions under BaseException, showing which categories to catch and how they nest.

t: Deep nets as learned compact representations
w: Deep layers turn raw pixels into compact, task-specific features like edges and curves, discarding redundancy the classifier does not need.

t: Why Turing machines model all computation
w: A finite brain and finite paper have finitely many distinguishable states, so any mathematician's procedure reduces to a table of transitions.

t: Why starving cancer cells is hard in practice
w: Cancers reroute to anaerobic glycolysis and compete for blood supply, while replication-targeting drugs also hit skin, gut and immune cells.

t: Algorithmic execution is not high-frequency trading
w: Algo trading means executing a large order over hours, like a pension buying AAPL; HFT is different, and critics are often misinformed.

t: Why network drives feel slow, and Dropbox's approach
w: Apps assume local disk; serial small accesses over high-latency links freeze UIs, so local folders with background sync hide latency.

t: Reversing modem firmware with binwalk
w: Binwalk finds embedded filesystems and compression signatures; squashfs can be extracted using the offsets it reports.

t: Why Lisp compilers work on individual forms
w: Lisp compiles top-level forms incrementally, enabling REPL development and immediate macros; circular multi-unit references are a different problem.

t: Why the TRS-80 initially outsold the Apple II
w: Radio Shack's retail reach gave the TRS-80 early dominance, but Apple's reliable Disk II and documented expansion slots won out.

t: Programming as teaching a running system
w: Common Lisp treats programming as teaching a running system incrementally, with standard hooks like CHANGE-CLASS so live objects adapt without restarts.

t: Why Hare lacks built-in hash maps
