w: Without generics, arbitrary hashing and equality are hard to express, and hidden allocations clash with manual memory management principles.

t: What volatile really costs in hardware
w: Volatile forces a real memory write, which can trigger TLB lookups, cache-coherence snooping and bus arbitration; plain stores can stay in registers.

t: Monads built up from functors in code
w: A functor applies a function inside a container, possibly changing element type; the post builds from functors toward monads.

t: First-hand story of building Objective-C on the Amiga
w: Author wrote a lexer, parser and runtime in Manx Aztec C, building OOP on Amiga shared-library function tables, as a high schooler.

t: Why discussing estimates makes errors correlate
w: Two independent estimates miss on the same side with probability at least 0.5; talking converges them further, so consensus loses the truth.

t: Deliberate practice, not raw hours, drives expertise
w: Clarifies Ericsson's research: expertise needs coached, monitored practice, distinct from playful engagement.

t: Practical security habits for production services
w: Dry-run platform updates, track dependency fixes, and run known-good source builds; input validation alone has bought little real security.

t: Why object-oriented layouts hurt game engine performance
w: OO access patterns scatter data and waste cache; data-oriented design makes data flow explicit for cache-friendly, parallel processing.

t: Why DNSSEC is being replaced for email and certificates
w: MTA-STS replaces DNSSEC for SMTP TLS; multi-perspective checks and RDAP offer other verification paths, while registrar takeovers dominate attacks.

t: Canvas vs WebGL rendering trade-offs from xterm.js
w: WebGL batches a typed array to the GPU in one call, beating canvas, but costs more to maintain and needs a parallel DOM for accessibility.

t: Why Gawker's judgment forced bankruptcy
w: Without a stay, appeal bonds were unaffordable, so bankruptcy became the vehicle to fund appeals and sell assets.

t: Deliverability lessons for running a newsletter
w: Mail providers penalize non-openers and suspicious TLDs like .tk; tracking pixels help spot disengaged subscribers, and routing links through your own domain avoids blocks.

t: Why patent examiners grant bad patents
w: Examiner time was set in the 1970s while prior art grew enormously, so examiners who cannot find art quickly must grant applications.

t: Why US houses are wood and still last
w: Wood is cheap where forests exist, and well-built insulated wood frames save energy better than masonry in extreme climates.

t: Big-fish-little-pond effect in STEM degrees
w: Students of similar ability are less likely to finish STEM degrees at elite schools where peers score higher; relative standing shapes persistence.

t: Voice assistants as non-visual command lines
w: Voice interfaces demand memorized syntax and skills and fail at recognition, wake word and intent; they behave more like command lines than conversation.

t: Why open plans can help team productivity
w: Cornell study: open layouts make it easier to read availability, manage quick interruptions, and ask low-stakes questions, boosting team creativity and output.

t: Modular monoliths as a middle ground to microservices
w: Put modules behind feature flags so one codebase runs as a monolith or as scaled instances, avoiding microservice ops costs; static-language compile times suffer.

t: How to read lawyer threats and posturing
w: Nasty letters are posturing until counsel believes a real case exists, so calm, non-admitting replies are often better than capitulating.

t: Porting Redis to ARM was nearly trivial
w: Redis ran on ARM after fixing unaligned accesses, with tests passing. Well-written C ports easily, so portability fears are often overstated.

t: Scale deep before scaling wide
w: Many workloads fit one modern machine; cutting abstraction layers and using good algorithms often beats distributed scaling.

t: Why cattle methane is part of a carbon cycle
w: Methane degrades to CO2 that feed recaptured, so herd size, not cumulative emissions, sets the atmospheric methane stock.

t: How to move from freelancer to consultant
w: Raise rates, bill by the day, build specialty practices, and own business outcomes rather than hours.

t: Montreal's 1969 police strike as a natural experiment
w: A 1969 Montreal police strike brought bank robberies, looting, and fires within hours, showing how quickly order breaks without policing.

t: Why the Fed backstops corporate bonds
w: Companies refinance maturing bonds; if issuance halts, forced asset sales and cross-default covenants can trigger technical defaults.

t: Why untested backups fail: undocumented, hand-built systems
w: Systems built in-situ with drifted, undocumented config are hard to restore; test restores in isolation and verify media.

t: Why perceptual hashes produce more false positives
w: Perceptual hashes match similar content by design, so false positives cluster around innocent images resembling flagged material, unlike cryptographic hashes.

t: Products take the shape of their revenue model
w: Free personal-finance apps often monetize through data and upsells, so over time they become lead funnels, and acquisition often destroys the original product soul.

t: Small data pipelines can beat big-data stacks
w: At about 2.5GB a day, a Python script and Postgres cost roughly $400 a month, versus a $100k-a-month big-data cluster for the same job.

t: Media multitasking studies do not cover listening to music
w: The cited MMI measure covers concurrent screen media like email and Netflix, so it does not show that background music harms focus.

t: Proof-of-work energy scales with market cap
w: Mining arbitrage ties electricity spent to Bitcoin's market value, so energy use grows with price until it becomes unsustainable, a clear mental model.

t: Why there is no single best startup strategy
w: Successful strategies coexist in an ecosystem; contradictory advice reflects different niches, not outliers.

t: Why simple whiteboard coding beats brainteasers
w: Engineering hiring avoids brainteasers; a simple implement-a-function test filters candidates well if problems stay simple and not escalate beyond what interviewers can judge.

t: Why pressure cooker sales are a poor terrorism signal
w: When a rare event is paired with a common product, the base rate makes the signal nearly worthless, so surveillance on such purchases would find almost nothing.

t: Coprime cells in a triangular grid and prime patterns
w: Coloring a triangular grid by gcd gives a regular pattern; a prime-related function produces similar pictures only sometimes and locally, as this comment clarifies.

t: Why unacknowledged open-source use drains maintainers
w: Hyperscan lost most maintainers despite heavy use; silent corporate adoption without acknowledgement undermines the case for funding the project.

t: Test scores track GPA closely in admissions
w: Former admissions reader: SAT/ACT scores correlated strongly with GPA, often predicting admit or deny decisions before normalizing transcripts.

t: Why radiologists resist automation of their work
w: Radiologists control residency supply and standards via their board, so automation threatens high incomes; a founder found advisory engagement but little real progress.

t: Why automation fails when situations turn unusual
w: Humans excel at novel situations but fade on monotonous drives, while AI never tires yet struggles with sudden change, so handoffs between them are dangerous.

t: Essential reading list for Scheme and Lisp compilers
w: Curated resource list: Dybvig's thesis, Orbit, Quinnec's book, Appel's continuations, plus semantics background.

t: How 1031 exchanges and step-up basis shelter gains
w: Depreciation offsets rental income, 1031 exchanges defer capital gains, and inheritance resets basis, so gains go untaxed.

t: Key meta-analysis on which hiring methods predict performance
w: Points to Schmidt and Hunter's 1998 meta-analysis, the central reference on how well different hiring methods predict job performance.

t: Ancient tech that could have enabled optics and photography
w: Silver chloride photography and Fizeau interferometers needed only ancient materials; optics and photography were feasible thousands of years before they arrived.

t: Why callbacks lose the meaning of program position
w: In structured code the program counter implies preconditions and call context; callback-driven async code loses that context, making invariants hard to reason about.

t: Why sandboxing apps is hard without documented access
w: Developers rarely know which files and syscalls their apps need, and libraries rarely document them, so least-privilege policies like SELinux are hard to write.

t: Why voluntary response polls are worthless
w: Voluntary response samples reflect only those who choose to answer, so unless responses are a large share of the population they are likely biased.

t: Why 2016-2019 MacBook Pro displays fail
w: A thinner display flex cable is integrated into the screen and breaks often, so repair means a $600-700 display replacement, per a repair shop.

t: Why dating apps suffer a lemons problem
w: Dating markets are lemon markets where bad actors erode trust for everyone, so gatekeepers like certified used-car programs may be needed.

t: Cookies are Set-Cookie headers, not placed files
w: Servers send Set-Cookie headers and browsers choose whether to store and return them; the placing idiom misleads about who controls cookies.

t: Stocks as hens: why price drops favour accumulators
w: Dividends are the output, so falling prices only matter when you sell; a clear analogy for long-term investing.

t: Cache timing side channels date back to the 1990s
w: Covert timing channels through CPU caches were identified in early 1990s high-assurance VAX and KVM/370 work, well before the 2005 papers.

t: Resource list for learning electronics from software
w: Arduino, Adafruit and SparkFun tutorials, EEVblog, and Tigoe's Physical Computing book cover electronics basics for software engineers.

t: How QNX's MsgSend achieves fast IPC
w: Synchronous send hands control straight to a waiting receiver, skipping the scheduler, inheriting priority and keeping data in cache.

t: How iPhone Secure Enclave keys are derived
w: Encryption key combines a hardware UID and GID fused into silicon with boot-time sensor entropy, so the enclave cannot be separated from its processor.

t: Why Z80 struct loops are slower than expected
w: Z80 lacks immediate 16-bit arithmetic and (IX+n) addressing is slow, eroding its apparent advantage in struct-processing loops.

t: Why queues between two databases cause consistency problems
w: Queues add a third stateful system; the source database already holds the state, and repairing lost or missing queue messages is manual.

t: History of the cosmological constant and quintessence
w: Relativists in the 1920s proposed long-range forces to stabilize dense matter; Einstein's cosmological constant and later quintessence models explain accelerating expansion.

t: How long film and prints really last
w: Fixed black-and-white silver lasts decades, selenium toning raises it to 100-200 years, and Kodachrome's dye forms in processing so it fades less.

t: How Guix differs from Nix despite shared roots
w: Guix reuses Nix's derivation format and daemon but is written in Guile Scheme, treats packages as first-class values, and is not a fork.

t: Why startup stock offerings risk rescission
w: Stock issuance must be registered or exempt; private placement status is fact-dependent, so a failed exemption lets investors rescind and recover funds.

t: How modern OSes trace back to DEC minicomputers
w: Minicomputers were shared multiuser machines, unlike early single-user microcomputers; modern OS lineage traces to two DEC minicomputer families.

t: Why piped-installer downloads are a security risk
w: Unauthenticated HTTP installers allow MITM and per-client trojans; without package signing, nobody can verify what code was delivered.

t: Ultima Online's ecology system: designer's insider correction
w: Designer explains the resource AI was disabled in beta, but resource values remained used for crafting and harvesting; documented on his site.

t: Plastic bottles' embodied energy is tiny versus oil
w: A 30g PET bottle embodies about 1200 kJ of oil energy, so drilling and shipping externalities dwarf manufacturing energy costs.

t: How a dead-man switch failed in a train crash
w: A heavy driver's leg held the pedal during a heart attack, defeating the switch; requiring a mid-range pedal position guards against that.

t: Why youtube-dl's DMCA takedown legal theory is weak
w: Accessing with valid credentials is not circumvention under 1201(a)(2), as a court held, so the access-control claim looks shaky.

t: How external boot really works on M1 Macs
w: M1 blesses a copy of the Preboot loader onto the internal SSD; only the root filesystem lives on the external disk.

t: Why x86 complicates compilers and register allocation
w: Few registers, overlapping register classes, irregular encodings, and fixed multiply/divide registers all make register allocation harder.

t: Index fund fees matter less than starting now
w: A cheaper option saves about 0.09% a year, while delaying investing six months costs more; open a low-cost index account now.

t: Small samples produce extreme outcomes by chance alone
w: The two-hospital example shows small teams' extreme results come from random variance, so success stories mislead about skill.

t: Violinist's view on block versus random practice
w: Expert musician explains block practice builds sustained focus, a skill that random-task studies overlook entirely.

t: How neutrino flavors interact with charged leptons
w: Each neutrino flavor interacts only with its matching charged lepton via W-boson processes; particles are quantum fields everywhere.

t: Haskell type signatures explained via C++ templates
w: The signature f :: a -> a reads as a generic function; type variables work like C++ templates and can be inferred when omitted.

t: What restricted stock means and its tax trap
w: Startup restricted stock is subject to repurchase until vesting and is untaxed until then, which creates real tax risk for holders.

t: How cuts to physician fees drive patient volume
w: When fees fall, physicians see more patients per hour to hold income, while drug and procedure prices drive cost growth.

t: Permutation test explained with a teacher comparison
w: Reshuffle student groups 1000 times to build a null distribution; if the real difference lies in its tail, the teachers likely differ.

t: Why enterprise software is hard to make usable
w: Developers are often not the users, regulations and corner cases add complexity, and large feature surfaces make polished UX hard.

t: Why quantum gravity tests need Planck-scale energies
w: Any quantum gravity theory combines Planck's, Newton's and light-speed constants into the Planck scale, far beyond collider energies.

t: Why rocket engine cycles are tightly coupled
w: Rocket engines are turbopumps plus plumbing; cycle choice like gas generator versus staged combustion sets how tightly design parameters couple.

t: Why XML namespaces break round-tripping
w: Namespace prefixes are not stable identifiers, so 'ns1:tag' can equal 'ns2:tag'; this breaks parsers that mutate and re-serialize XML.

t: Practical guide to installing and running Python
w: Install the latest 64-bit minor release, use the right installer per OS, and avoid bare python commands; prevents common setup pitfalls.

t: Why batteries cannot cover renewables gaps
w: Twelve hours of global electricity needs about 35,000 GWh of storage, roughly 70 years of current global battery output.

t: Why SQLite is hard to contribute to
w: Contributions must be provably public domain, and must justify decades of testing and maintenance, so patch effort is small relative to upkeep.

t: Why software should be priced by value, not cost
w: Cost-based pricing suits commodities like gypsum; software is better priced by the value it delivers to customers.

t: Why tree height reveals the wet air layer
w: Near-surface turbulent air carries heat and moisture; the height of local trees roughly marks the top of this boundary layer.

t: Why physician supply is capped by residency funding
w: The real limit on practicing doctors is Medicare-funded residency slots, not medical school seats or the AMA.

t: How a bad kernel driver bricked cloud nodes
w: A bad driver update caused boot loops; recovery meant detaching each cloud disk, deleting the .sys file on another node, and reattaching, straining storage.

t: Lessons from a silent queue-worker outage
w: Don't code while distracted; keep the on-call phone nearby, since monitoring alerts are useless if you can't receive them.

t: Why expansion isn't inertia from the Big Bang
w: Recession speed proportional to distance requires ongoing acceleration; inertia alone cannot produce Hubble's law.

t: Using FCRA and FDCPA to challenge debts
w: A debt validation letter starts a 30-day clock; if the furnisher cannot verify the tradeline, it must be removed.

t: Why HN's shared space fuels conflict
w: Unlike siloed sites, everyone shares one room, so users meet hostile views unexpectedly and misread regional norms.

t: Low-code tools for building a SaaS backend
w: Hasura autogenerates a GraphQL CRUD API from a database; pair it with Forest Admin, Metabase and PostHog for admin, BI and analytics.

t: Gallup questions linked to business success
w: Gallup found that clear expectations, tools, recognition and development questions track company success more than happiness.

t: Why open source needs invoiceable paid tiers
w: Companies can't expense donations, so offering paid pro licenses with real features gets through corporate accounting more easily.

t: Why predictive policing learns biased outcomes
w: Models predict from past arrests, so biased enforcement becomes the target; removing bias may leave a system that optimizes the same arrests.

t: Why electromagnetic radiation is the likely alien medium
w: EM has nearly every property wanted for communication; no reason advanced civilizations would choose inferior media.

t: Pragmatic web stack: React, Django, Postgres and cookies
w: Skip Redux early, default to Postgres, use cookie auth on one domain behind nginx to avoid CORS and JWT complexity.

t: Why hydrogen loses to batteries on round-trip efficiency
w: Electrolysis plus fuel cell is about 35 to 40 percent efficient, versus over 90 percent for batteries, and compression adds further losses.

t: Why SAP forces businesses to conform
w: Denormalised schema and enterprise integration explain why SAP demands process change; local tools are easier for reporting.

t: Amortized analysis explains constant-time dynamic array appends
w: Dynamic array appends are O(1) amortized: copies happen predictably and rarely, so worst-case O(n) per append misreads amortized cost.

t: What stimulant medication should feel like for ADHD
w: Proper ADHD dosing gives focus and clarity rather than a high; tolerance builds over time, so effects can fade and need periodic use.

t: Why MP3 vs FLAC rarely matters for listening
w: MP3 at V0 or 320 kbps is near-indistinguishable from 16-bit FLAC; loudness mastering, not the format, explains bad-sounding digital music.

t: How rental fleets profit from buying and reselling cars
w: Bulk discounts, depreciation, and rental income form a fleet cycle; fewer working cars means less revenue.

t: Count tree nodes, not lines, to measure code
w: Counting every node in the code's tree gives a better size measure than lines, which can reward bad formatting and wrong habits.

t: Three stages of mastering a domain
w: Frameworks help beginners avoid pitfalls, but at true expertise, understanding of nuance surpasses frameworks, which can then mislead.

t: Correcting claims about MySQL limitations
w: Nested groups can use nested-set modeling, LONGTEXT is right for large text, and MySQL can index TEXT columns with a prefix length.

t: Why educational games struggle to sell
w: Institutional buyers pick boring features, while parents do not spread word of mouth for narrow age ranges, so media companies win on cheap exposure.

t: Lessons from a JSON-file database in production
w: Concurrent writes, corruption and slow queries forced a chain of hacks ending in a single-table SQLite kitchen sink; a cautionary first-hand account.

t: VPNs shift identification to the provider's logs
w: A shared VPN IP forces an observer to combine fingerprints with provider logs, so the VPN's logging policy determines how easily you are identified.

t: Why consumer device firmware goes unpatched
w: Devices ship on 6 to 12 month product cycles but live 3 to 5 years, and embedded OSes lack post-sale patch infrastructure.

t: Heel-striking with locked knees loads the lower back
w: Straight-legged heel landings transmit force up the leg; forefoot landings with a bent knee dissipate it, a habit minimal shoes teach.

t: Why chemical fuels beat batteries for drag acceleration
w: Gasoline holds about 100x more energy per kg than lithium-ion (roughly 40 vs 0.4 MJ/kg), so battery drag cars face a hard limit.

t: Cloud repatriation is limited by lost skills
w: Insight from a thesis: the main barrier to leaving the cloud is de-skilling, since staff can no longer run buffers and transcoders on-prem.

t: Three perspectives on stock investing: company, stock, game
w: Investors can value the company, the stock, or the trading game; the game perspective now dominates market behavior.

t: Why legitimate payment accounts get flagged as fraud
w: Fraud models cluster legitimate businesses that use virtual cards or masked spending with fraud patterns, causing false rejections.

t: Why a weekend self-driving hack misses emergencies
w: Logging CAN-bus data and imitating drivers handles easy highway driving, but without vehicle dynamics models and emergency data, edge cases fail.

t: Repurposing Sanger sequencers for COVID testing
w: Uses idle Sanger sequencers and skips RNA extraction, detecting COVID from sequencing data with regression to scale testing capacity.

t: Why rewriting an unclear legacy system backfires
w: A replacement built without understanding the old system imperfectly recreates it, forcing migrations while the old system survives anyway.

t: Why AWS on-call load and delivery pressure hurt
w: Heavy on-call tickets without investment in tooling, plus feature pressure from managers, produced exhausted engineers and poor code quality.

t: Why conversational writing is not transcribed speech
w: Real speech is messy and listeners edit it on the fly. Conversational prose is an idealised, edited version that takes skill to write well.

t: Why off-grid sites should accept some downtime
w: Above a reliability threshold, battery production's fossil energy exceeds the solar energy saved, so chasing 100% uptime is counterproductive.

t: Blind wine tastings reveal price doesn't predict preference
w: In blind tests a $5 Barefoot beat a $100 Silver Oak; expectations and labels strongly shape perceived quality.

t: Why plastic packaging can lower total environmental impact
w: Plastic wrap doubles cucumber shelf life, and food waste outweighs packaging; glass bottles' energy and transport often cost more than plastic.

t: Cash-price pharmacies may cost more than insurance
w: Some $4 generics bill to insurance and count toward deductibles; cash-only pharmacies with shipping fees can cost more despite advertised savings.

t: Two sleep changes that mattered most
w: Avoiding alarm clocks and blue light at night gave the largest sleep gains, more than temperature or darkness tweaks.

t: Why GUI replacements slow expert data entry
w: Expert keyboard entry in terminal apps builds muscle memory; mouse-driven GUIs with dropdowns add speed bumps that reduce productivity.

t: Why accelerators matter more than CPU speed
w: Displays and GPUs dominate laptop power while CPUs mostly idle, so dedicated accelerators beat raw CPU gains.

t: How Gmail image caching affects email open tracking
w: Per-recipient image URLs still yield one request per delivery; Gmail fetches images only after the user opens the email.

t: How flagging and killing work on HN
w: Flags downrank and can kill stories; comment flags require the timestamp page, a speed bump against impulsive flagging.

t: Learning from works versus copying them
w: Copyright protects expression, not learned concepts or facts, so training may be fair use; infringement arises mainly from reproducing enough verbatim text.

t: Why mock-heavy unit tests verify implementation, not behavior
w: Mock frameworks let tests assert internal call counts instead of outcomes, producing brittle tests that document implementation rather than behavior.

t: How Python spread inside Goldman Sachs unofficially
w: Developer installed Python across securities desks within 30 minutes despite unapproved status, backed by a senior partner's tacit approval.

t: Why huge neural nets generalize: depth-to-width ratio
w: Per the book's epilogue, generalization of very large networks depends on the depth-to-width ratio, which controls data-dependent couplings between neurons.

t: NeWS synchronous events versus X11 input focus
w: NeWS blocked event distribution until synchronous handlers ran, avoiding focus errors. Asynchronous X11 clients cannot do this, so their focus tracking is flaky.

t: Schmidt and Hunter's meta-analysis of hiring methods
w: A 1998 meta-analysis finds most hiring methods weakly predictive, with only two procedures working reasonably well at a validity near 0.5.

t: Why voluntary response polls cannot support inferences
w: Self-selected respondents are not a random sample, so voluntary response results cannot generalize to the population however large the sample.

t: Why perceptual hashes are weaker than cryptographic hashes
w: Cryptographic hashes resist collisions, but perceptual hashes match similar content by design, making them easier to attack; Apple's second hash cannot be verified.

t: How PostScript LaserWriter enabled WYSIWYG desktop publishing
w: Apple licensed PostScript from Adobe; WYSIWYG printing of screen content made MacPaint and MacWrite desktop publishing work.

t: How bulk bandwidth pricing and fiber capacity scale
w: Transit prices fall sharply with commit size and competition, while capacity per fiber strand keeps growing, unlike fiber's real-estate value.

t: IBM's incremental path from punch cards to electronics
w: IBM built and field-tested electronic calculators like the 603 and 605 before computers, showing business computing drove early electronics.

t: Electricity price can erase EV fuel savings
w: At $0.22/kWh a Model S costs about $0.073 per mile, the same as a 30 mpg gas car at $2.20/gallon.

t: Why C is not a portable assembler
w: Compiling a trivial if statement with gdb shows the emitted code differs from naive assumptions about C.

t: What owning a private railcar actually costs
w: A Pullman car needs $300k+ of upgrades to Amtrak standards, plus 480V head-end power, braking work, locomotive hire, parking and per-mile fees.

t: Why headphone sine-sweep specs miss what listeners hear
w: Sine sweeps ignore impulse response, intermodulation and phase, so standard measurements can mislead about musical listening.

t: How cross-currency payments net out between banks
w: Banks net opposing currency flows and trade only the shortfall; persistent imbalances appear as the current account deficit.

t: Home EV charging limited by utility service capacity
w: Most public chargers are shared 22kW units with smart-charge duty cycling; home upgrades can cost around $20k due to grid capacity.

t: Absolute versus relative risk of rare vaccine clots
w: Six clot deaths per 6.8M doses, against thousands of daily COVID deaths, shows why pausing needs risk comparison.

t: Why blood typing has dozens of red cell groups
w: Over 35 red cell groups exist; codominant Kell antigens mean homozygous k people can form anti-K antibodies, causing transfusion reactions.

t: Keeping self-hosted servers maintainable long-term
w: Minimize customization, use stock Docker images, keep declarative compose files and documentation, so a failed server is recoverable years later.

t: Inside bsnes: decapping chips for accurate SNES emulation
w: Accuracy-first emulation preserves games that depend on bugs; decapping cartridge coprocessors extracted firmware, enabling 100% compatibility.

t: Wine quality stops tracking price around $40
w: Quality rises with price up to roughly $40, after which you pay for flavor profile or hype; experts can reliably identify vineyard and vintage blind.

t: Why Excel persists in insurance actuarial work
w: Excel's uniform environment, traceable formulas, and built-in memoization and reactivity beat Python for many actuarial calculations; Python offers little speedup without numpy.

t: Why submenus open after a deliberate delay
w: Apple's 1995 guidelines explain the submenu delay: it stops pointer sweeps across menus from opening submenus accidentally.

t: Four design basics every engineer should learn
w: Visual hierarchy, basic typography, UX thinking from Don't Make Me Think, and what colors signal for alerts and branding.

t: Why Opera's all-in-one design was hard to recreate
w: Opera packed mail, feeds, torrents and notes into a roughly 5MB native browser; web-tech rebuilds of that breadth are bulkier and slower.

t: Choosing cookware that works on induction hobs
w: Induction needs magnetic flat bases; tri-ply steel and cast iron work well, while aluminium without a steel base and curved pans fail.

t: Practical B2B SaaS pricing: price higher, tier three plans
w: Price above comfort; a three-tier $49/$99/$249 default; avoid clients under $29 a month, who churn and consume support time.

t: Building a concatenative language interpreter step by step
w: A stack-based interpreter needs only a data stack, a dictionary mapping words to function pointers, and a token loop.

t: Structural recursion mirrors recursively defined data
w: Recursive data like binary trees makes structural recursion clearer than loops; the code shape matches the data definition, which Haskell expresses directly.

t: How federal sentences are actually calculated
w: Statutory maximums rarely apply; Guidelines offense levels and adjustments set the real range, often months rather than years.

t: Methodological flaws in the Esperanto study
w: Points out teacher confounds, attrition to 21 Esperanto students and undifferentiated secondary-language data, teaching how to read studies critically.

t: Why sysadmins require known-state, company-owned hosts
w: Starting every host in a known state makes testing and upgrades predictable at scale; company-owned devices allow remote wipes without personal-data disputes.

t: Why high-speed digital boards need real EE expertise
w: Past roughly 25-50 MHz, digital circuits behave like analog: traces radiate and reflect, so amateur layout practices produce unreliable boards.

t: Deconstruction as close engagement with a text, not a method
w: Derrida's deconstruction is not a repeatable procedure; it is micrological reading of a text on its own terms, mostly philosophical texts.

t: Academic 'practical' differs sharply from engineering practicality
w: Academic practical often means a toy implementation exists; engineers must weigh detection, cost, prerequisites and threat assumptions papers skip.

t: GC tradeoffs: pause latency versus throughput, and why knobs mislead
w: Go optimizes pause times at throughput's expense, suiting web servers; batch jobs prefer throughput since occasional pauses barely matter.

t: How the PACE chronic fatigue trial was undermined
w: Recovery criteria changed mid-trial, outcomes were self-reported, and data were withheld, blocking reanalysis; a lesson in trial integrity.

t: Nine technological mechanisms needed for industrialization
w: Industrialization required a bootstrapping sequence of fuels, materials, power, and knowledge; any out-of-order step can stall it.

t: Why Rust 2018 changes absolute path resolution
w: Explains the mental model behind confusing use and extern crate behavior, and why absolute paths now begin with the crate name.

t: Why broadcast graphics avoid pure black and white
w: Legal gamut headroom and careful filtering prevent crawl and strobing on NTSC; hand-fitting pixels rarely beats good filtering.

t: How rice preparation determines sushi quality
w: Washing removes starch, polishing removes bran, and exact water ratios control texture; each step strongly affects gluey or mushy results.

t: What quantum computers can and cannot do yet
w: Shor's algorithm would break RSA only with many entangled qubits; D-Wave's annealing design is unconventional and far from general quantum computation.

t: Why streetcars were profitable and modern transit is not
w: Streetcars opened new land as real estate plays and carried dense daily ridership; cars and decentralization removed both drivers of profit.

t: Early attempts to show light has a finite speed
w: Traces Alhazen, Bacon, Beeckman and Galileo; Galileo's lantern experiment failed to detect delay, showing light's speed must be extraordinarily high.

t: How 1990s GSM networks routed and billed calls
w: BSCs connect cell sites, MSCs route to SS7, HLRs track phone registration and feed billing; text messaging grew from a value-added service into a core one.

t: Why linked-list strings are slow versus packed arrays
w: Each character in a linked-list string needs two pointers that can scatter across memory, hurting cache use; a packed C-style array avoids this overhead.

t: Why stealth buys time rather than invisibility
w: Stealth delays detection; coatings tune one radar band, leaving early-warning MHz and Ka-band radars and IR cues exposed.

t: Practical GCC inline assembly conventions for AVX2
w: Use symbolic operand names in upper case, one input per line with comments, and constraints like +&x for early-clobber vector registers.

t: Normit transforms and why deep nets are hard to debug
w: Quantile-to-Gaussian normit transforms often boost power over nonparametric tests; stacked ReLU layers act as chained regressions that are hard to debug.

t: Why Mario 64 rendering was bound by N64 microcode
w: N64 games built command lists for RSP microcode and used mandated matrix libraries, so optimizations depended on the microcode team's revisions.

t: Function pointers: dispatch tables and callbacks
w: Function pointers let libraries call user policy at runtime, replacing big switch statements with O(1) dispatch and enabling extensible callbacks.

t: Why undocumented startup partnerships can still be joint ventures
w: Joint ventures are a form of partnership law, so a missing written agreement does not prevent a court from finding one with ownership claims.

t: Why quantum interpretations cannot be told apart by experiment
w: Copenhagen, many-worlds and pilot-wave give identical predictions, so experiments cannot choose; the choice is sociological.

t: Haskell controls side effects instead of banning them
w: Purity makes effects explicit and first-class in types, so code can reason about effects rather than ignore them.

t: Evolved programs game badly designed fitness functions
w: Evolving systems exploited timing side channels and scheduler communication to score well, so fitness functions must be designed against gaming.

t: How 1970s growth controls shaped Bay Area housing
w: Anti-growth court rulings, city caps like Petaluma's 1972 ordinance, and Prop 13 and rent control compounded into today's Bay Area housing shortage.

t: Why DANE creates new certificate authorities
w: DANE puts certificates in DNSSEC, making TLD operators and the root into new CAs, largely controlled by governments.

t: How cave divers manage navigation risk
w: Fixed lines, numbered markers, and planned reversals make cave diving safer than its reputation suggests.

t: Rust benchmark pitfalls and tail-call optimization
w: Slow iterator benchmarks usually mean optimizations were off; LLVM sometimes does TCO, and 'become' is reserved for guaranteed tail calls.

t: IDEs that stored code in databases, from Smalltalk
w: Smalltalk and IBM VisualAge stored code in databases with refactoring browsers, a lineage that predates file-based IDE designs.

t: Practical deployment workflow: rollbacks and config overrides
w: Keep old release files so rollback is one command; limit staging/production differences to one overrides file, placed on each machine outside deploys.

t: Practical HTML pitfalls: lazy loading, tel links, meter
w: Skip lazy loading on images you care about, since distant or offline loads can fail; tel and sms links can't be detected as working.

t: Why ORMs clash with the relational model
w: Relations hold flat tuples with normalization theory; objects hide state and are higher-order, so operations needing two objects' internals can't be expressed.

t: Why PayPal holds funds on pre-sale merchants
w: Chargebacks on undelivered pre-sold goods fall on the processor, which often can't recover from failed merchants, so it underwrites new pre-sale businesses cautiously.

t: What the Lavabit court order actually demanded
w: Escalation targeted Lavabit's ability to decrypt Snowden's data using its own TLS keys, not an initial demand for all messages, correcting Levison's account.

t: How a claimed signature was debunked as copied
w: The base64 signature decoded to hex matched a blockchain transaction input, so the claimed proof reused an existing signature rather than proving identity.

t: Why Amazon refunds track customer lifetime value
w: Refunds are modeled as projected future revenue minus past revenue and refund cost, so high-value customers get refunds without evidence.

t: Why browsers need telemetry without spying
w: Without field data, regressions take weeks to reproduce; privacy-preserving collection tries to balance diagnosing crashes with user trust.

t: Why the Google+ names policy poisoned unified accounts
w: Unified login was reasonable, but sharing the social network's name and strict name rules made the account system politically toxic.

t: Why voting security is about chain of custody
w: Election judge explains that seals, custody and observers matter more than machine type; paper is not inherently safer.

t: Why legacy Python 2 code silently changes under Python 3
w: Python 3 numeric semantics change results without errors, so search-and-replace porting is not enough for large old scripts.

t: Why autopilot steers into barriers at lane splits
w: Lane-marker confusion at splits; good systems detect internal inconsistency and alarm. The missing property is cognizant failure.

t: Fighting spam with retrained text classifiers
w: Spammers adapted to mixed alphabets and mixed content; rapid retraining on flagged posts kept a small team's classifier effective.

t: Solve problems with the least necessary work
w: Alice's hosted WordPress solution beats Clyde's custom CMS: productivity means solving the customer's problem with the least code, not writing the most.

t: Why software estimates should admit uncertainty
w: Give ranges and timeboxes, naming unknowns like unfamiliar APIs or bug hunts, instead of dates you then miss.

t: How game rules distorted high school debate
w: Treating dropped arguments as conceded rewarded fast spreading; any scored competition tends to optimize for the rules over the activity's purpose.

t: Why engagement experiments can hurt long-term health
w: Teams choose winners on short-term engagement while long-term holdout groups go unreviewed, so incentives reward immediate-metric features.

t: No-code tools follow decades of developer innovation
w: No-code systematizes patterns after developers settle them, depends on developer infrastructure, and cannot replace the developers who build it.

t: Teach problems before giving the solutions
w: People retain answers better after grappling with the problem; a git tutorial built around real pitfalls like detached HEAD illustrates it.

t: Why pipe benchmarks mislead without flushing
w: Python buffers stdout into 8KiB writes, so its pipe speed looked high until flush=True; benchmarks must control for buffering.

t: Why archive.is returns foreign DNS answers
w: Returning distant IPs forces takedowns through foreign procedures and buys time; global DNS caching undermines this design.

t: Glacier retrieval fees can dwarf storage costs
w: Glacier prices retrieval by peak hourly request rate, so one large restore can cost hundreds of times the monthly storage fee.

t: Why PowerPC Macs fell behind Intel
w: IBM and Motorola could not keep pace with Intel on performance and cost; Apple's MHz-myth messaging masked the gap until the switch to Intel.

t: Why VLC doesn't damage speakers, explained
w: VLC sends 16-bit samples through official Windows APIs; amplification saturates audio but cannot set hardware output, so the fault lay in the sound card's power limits.

t: How English and Russian grammar differ
w: English relies on fixed word order and few conjugations, while Russian marks roles through inflection, letting word order stay flexible.

t: Apple removed app-recommendation apps, insider says
w: A former App Review leader reportedly said Apple removed whole categories of apps that drove downloads outside the App Store, a rare insider account.

t: Why ignoring database internals causes data loss
w: Treating databases as black boxes led to missing transactions, MongoDB async buffering data loss, and projects with missing or wrong indexes.

t: How Starlink's latency and user terminals work
w: Explains 20-40ms latency, flat phased-array terminals, and why user cost and capacity limit adoption.

t: Why cheap CGI features keep failing commercially
w: Animation productivity does not scale: a 30-person TV pipeline cannot make a theatrical feature in a month.

t: How proof-of-stake security and slashing work
w: Validators stake 32 ETH and lose part of it when they attack, making 51 percent attacks costly without PoW's energy use.

t: Running Windows gaming in a VM via GPU passthrough
w: Practical setup: IOMMU lets a VM get exclusive PCI-E GPU access, so Linux hosts can run Windows gaming VMs without dual boot.

t: Spotting Bing results in DuckDuckGo via IP test
w: A 'what is my IP' query on DDG surfaces a BingBot IP, a quick way to see that many private engines reuse Bing results.

t: Why affordable housing costs are driven by land
w: Construction costs are similar across countries; land prices dominate per-unit cost, so the same unit can vary several-fold by location.

t: Practical advice after a false criminal accusation
w: Don't talk to police, hire the strongest lawyer possible, and think like a guilty person; innocence alone counts for little at trial.

t: Why Fukushima's backup generators failed
w: Diesel backup generators sat below sea level in reactor buildings, so the tsunami that overtopped the seawall flooded them and cut cooling.

t: Boring tech stack ran 2M users with zero outages
w: Plain SQL Server, minimal JavaScript and copy-to-deploy ran for a decade with zero outages, though the lack of drama hurt the author's visibility.

t: Why software is not really engineering
w: Unlike structural engineers, software teams routinely ship deliverables they do not fully understand, and they lean on abstractions to save them.

t: What made Agile work versus how it degraded
w: Honest estimates, team-only standups and real demos worked; public boards and managers turned them into self-promotion and deadline pressure.

t: Why people defend conclusions they can't reconstruct
w: Working memory keeps conclusions, not supporting facts, so when challenged people rely on shortcuts instead of re-deriving the reasoning.

t: Interviewing by discussing past projects, not whiteboards
w: Read resumes closely, then discuss projects in depth: what was enjoyable, hardest, and what would change, with no whiteboard coding or trivia.

t: Integration tests break less than mocked unit tests
w: Unit tests with mocks break on internal refactors; testing API responses and database state survives code changes and catches real regressions.

t: Why stale sessions and background agents burn quota
w: Prompt cache expires after an hour, so resuming a stale long-context session misses cache; many skills and background agents also consume tokens unexpectedly.

t: Why SPAs exist: latency for desktop-class apps
w: SPAs aren't a fad; they cut round-trip latency for interactive apps, while simple content still fits server-rendered stacks well.

t: How spreadsheet-driven cost cuts eroded culture
w: A former CEO saw PE analysts cut what was easy to measure, like benefits, while the morale and performance costs of those cuts stayed hard to quantify.

t: Two principles every error system must satisfy
w: Error systems relying on developer discipline fail, and one handling policy cannot fit all errors, since some are ignorable and others must not be ignored.

t: Lessons from a Crowdstrike-caused Linux outage
w: Vendor kernel update broke current Debian stable; staging controls and vendor rollout policy were the real gaps.

t: What hiring research says predicts performance
w: Schmidt and Hunter's meta-analysis suggests structured methods and work samples predict job performance better than unstructured interviews.

t: Why random front-page placement backfired on HN
w: Readers treat the front page as a personal contract; randomly placed stories violated expectations, so introducing noise damaged trust.

t: Why Autopilot's design invites zone-out crashes
w: Weak hands-on enforcement and a sparse sensor suite create a deadly valley: drivers zone out while the system still fails at edge cases.

t: Practical guide to IRC networks, clients and bouncers
w: Lists active networks, clients across devices, community bots and bouncers for staying connected to IRC.

t: Why extensions shouldn't request access to all sites
w: Requesting every website is a large overreach; localhost web servers are hard to secure, so native messaging is the better design.

t: Why DNS over HTTPS leaks to ISPs anyway
w: DoH sends queries to one resolver, and IPs and SNI stay unencrypted, so ISPs still see destinations; gives how to block DoH endpoints.

t: Why asteroid mining economics do not add up
w: Walks through delta-V, launch cost, and extraction constraints to show why valuable asteroid material would lose value once supply floods the market.

t: Why hospitals struggle to publish price data
w: Insider explanation: health systems are fragmented medical malls running legacy systems like Epic and MUMPS, so pricing data is scattered across many sources.

t: Inside John Deere's tractor software development
w: Tractor software involves 150-300 engineers and very strict review, so code changes move slowly and undergo heavy scrutiny.

t: How US sanctions force GitHub account restrictions
w: Any firm serving US customers or banks must comply with sanctions, so GitHub limits commercial services in sanctioned countries but keeps public repos.

t: Comparing EV and gasoline CO2 per mile
w: Using 11.8 kg CO2 per gallon and 372 g per kWh, a Hummer EV emits about 267 g per mile versus 363 for a Malibu.

t: How true facts and base rates build misleading narratives
w: Each stat can be accurate yet misleading; choosing denominators and adding conclusions shapes narrative, so readers should check which facts are omitted.

t: How ReadyReturn pre-filled taxes and why it stalled
w: Pre-filled returns using data the government already holds won near-universal approval in tests, but partly lobbying by tax software firms stopped it.

t: Lessons from abandoning Elixir in production
w: Hiring got hard after champions left, library and IDE coverage lagged, and avoiding Redis and workers still needed database persistence.

t: Why preprint servers struggle to replace journals
w: Preprint servers lack archival guarantees and face bandwidth and hosting costs, while tenure committees still weight journal impact factors.

t: NFT value is attention and scarcity, like baseball cards
w: Owning an NFT doesn't grant image rights; value comes from scarcity and sustained attention, much like a collectible card's brand and rarity.

t: Where passwords leak into logs and how to audit
w: Sensitive data often leaks through request-body logging, exception traces, load balancers and proxies; audit logging and tracing pipelines regularly.

t: Why scooter companies lack defensible moats
w: Network effects are local and cheap to break, since blanketing a city costs under $1.5M, so brand and durability matter more.

t: Go vs Rust generics and sum types in practice
w: Rust's ApiResponse<T> and Option/Result beat Go workarounds, but generics add design-time cost; nil interfaces cost real money.

t: What XKeyscore can and cannot see
w: Interception at transit hubs yields plaintext only where encryption is absent; Gmail was exposed where server-to-server TLS fails.

t: Why academic publishers resist disruption
w: Publishers sell reputation within academic incentives; PDF distribution is solved, so the barriers are cultural and structural.

t: Tech debt needs a conscious choice and payoff
w: Real tech debt is a deliberate tradeoff with a repayment plan; legacy code and poor design are not debt, and turnover creates knowledge debt.

t: Hidden costs of splitting a monolith into services
w: Services talking JSON add serialization overhead, painful cross-repo branching and builds, and new auth complexity that a single monolith never had.

t: Insider account of Optimizely's decline
w: Abandoning self-serve for vague enterprise sales, opaque marketing and extractive pricing eroded a hot startup's value, as seen from inside.

t: Chinese companies as tools of statecraft
w: In China the state, military and corporations are one entity, so treating firms like Huawei as market competitors misreads them as instruments of statecraft.

t: Why cloud game streaming struggles with latency
w: Players notice about 50ms of input latency; streaming adds network round trips, and client-side prediction cannot hide lag on streamed frames.

t: Exercising startup stock options carries real risk
w: Exercising options needs cash plus tax on paper gains; if the company fails, you lose the cost and recover the tax slowly.

t: Why Iceland's reforestation struggles
w: Iceland's free-range sheep eat native birch seedlings, so reforestation relies on sheep-resistant species and farm-subsidized planting.

t: Why general-purpose AR products overreach
w: Without a killer use case, teams chase fidelity everywhere; find a beachhead use case that works with low fidelity, as Apple Watch did.

t: How fixed-fee loans hide high effective APR
w: A fixed fee repaid from sales makes effective APR climb as a business grows faster, so compare fees against standard APRs.

t: Feed-to-food energy efficiency of meat and milk
w: Beef returns only about 1.9% of feed calories as product versus 24% for whole milk, so seaweed does not fix feed inefficiency.

t: Simple numbered SQL files for database versioning
w: Keep numbered change scripts in source control and track a version number in the database; a small runner beats heavy migration frameworks.

t: How companies can pay for open-source licenses
w: Ask maintainers for a commercial quote and invoice it; projects should make payment one-click to encourage paying.

t: How AWS actually emerged, separate from SOA
w: Ex-Amazon engineer says S3 was built by its own team, so AWS did not grow out of the SOA effort.

t: Why pointers click when you picture memory
w: Pointers become clear when you picture raw memory and what's actually stored, instead of parsing the syntax, which confused the author for years.

t: How non-EU citizens legally work in Germany
w: Tourist visas cannot work; student visas allow 19 hours a week for employers only; other permits need proof of shortage.

t: Why schema evolution matters more than type elegance
w: Real systems mostly change deployed code, so protobuf's compatible evolution outweighs its type-theoretic warts.

t: Sizing a sand battery for home heating
w: Worked numbers show a sand heat store with a resistive element, PWM control and sensors can hold roughly 40 hours of heating at 5kW.

t: Why iMessage lacks forward secrecy
w: Per-message AES keys are wrapped with long-lived RSA keys, so one key compromise exposes years of messages; 1280-bit RSA is weak.

t: Why Kafka stores ordered messages in segment files
w: Each partition is an ordered append log of segment files with offset indexes, suited to buffering work without ad-hoc queries.

t: Hyperconverged and hyperscale are different things
w: Hyperconverged virtualizes compute, storage and networking as one appliance; hyperscale is a top-down design approach using commodity servers.

t: Why game developers struggle to support macOS
w: No cross-platform builds, weak backward compatibility, small market share and older integrated GPUs make macOS costly for studios.

t: Blocking I/O in Haskell without blocking the OS
w: Haskell's scheduler parks threads on blocked sockets, so code reads sequentially without OS-level blocking or manual callbacks.

t: What installing Debian in 1998 involved
w: Pre-web install needed boot floppies, LILO recovery via fdisk /mbr, and PPP over modem; a vivid period account.

t: Practical framework for investing during a crash
w: Match money to time horizon, expect dead-cat bounces, expect long recessions, and use mean reversion to judge whether equities are cheap.

t: Using RSS feeds to replace social platforms
w: hnrss.org provides feeds for HN replies, Ask HN and Show HN; RSS also tracks CVEs, distro security notices and SourceHut commits.

t: Why Vista's reputation suffered: drivers and SuperFetch
w: Vista exposed poor vendor drivers, and aggressive SuperFetch prefetching overloaded spinning disks with random reads, slowing the first minutes after boot.

t: Why Google keeps Maps and Play protocols proprietary
w: Map data licenses restrict distribution, Play needs anti-fraud controls, and a single controlled client lets Google change protocols freely.

t: Entropy as grouping microstates by macrostate averages
w: Each bit configuration is equally likely; entropy comes from grouping states by aggregate values like average, where most states cluster near 50%.

t: Why ambient chatter helps focus: tribal safety signals
w: Deep focus needs certainty of no interruption and a sense of safety; ambient tribal chatter signals others are nearby, while silence can feel isolating.

t: Why small-batch hardware costs more per unit
w: Low volume means no component or tooling price breaks; design-focused, complex products add development cost and risk, which raises the price.

t: Telegram's chats aren't end-to-end encrypted
w: Only Telegram's secret chats are end-to-end encrypted; regular cloud chats use server-held keys, so Telegram could read them.

t: Removing a list entry without special cases
w: An early-return head check plus a normal for loop avoids segfaults by construction and is simpler to reason about than pointer tricks.

t: Speed limits, road design, and crash severity
w: Vehicle speed raises crash frequency and severity; road design often drives actual speeds more than posted limits do.

t: Why undefined behavior lets compilers do anything
w: One UB step invalidates a program's meaning, like a false premise in a proof, so compilers may reason from it freely.

t: Why money beats punishment for unpleasant chores
w: Without money, societies rely on punishment for undesirable work; communes collapse when unpaid people quit, while prices adjust small mismatches smoothly.

t: Why personal cars beat transit for many trips
w: Cars win on near-zero waiting, proportional lateness penalty, night and weather availability, and direct routes; cutting parking alone will not shift trips.

t: Why a new CTO must stop deep technical work
w: Fragmented days make deep technical work harmful to the team; value comes from autonomy, direction, and knowing when help is needed.

t: Canada versus US gun ownership and mass shootings
w: Canada's mass-shooting deaths per capita are about a third of the US's, yet track it once guns owned are controlled.

t: Why smoke alarms must not be disabled
w: Alarms need battery backup and reliable placement; disabling features for convenience defeats their life-safety purpose.

t: Why Boeing delayed the MCAS sensor fix
w: Likely reason: disabling MCAS on sensor disagreement would break the common type rating with older 737s, requiring new pilot training.

t: Function colors: constraints exist either way
w: Colorless functions hide constraints like suspension points, but the constraints still exist; explicit colors make them checkable.

t: How GitLab runs an all-remote company
w: Hiring outside expensive metro areas at local pay and cutting office costs are the main levers of an all-remote model.

t: Why metadata falls under third-party doctrine
w: Fourth Amendment protection depends on who generates and controls the data, not how revealing it is; carrier records fall outside it.

t: Bitcoin as a remittance channel under capital controls
w: Capital controls and scarce USD channels make peer-to-peer bitcoin trading a faster route than wire, Western Union or PayPal.

t: Back-of-envelope cost of universal basic income
w: Federal revenue of about $3.5T divided among 360M people yields only about $10k each before any other government spending.

t: Why PS5 cooling costs more than Xbox's design
w: Sony's heatsinks and heatpipes cost more, reflecting a model recouping costs from games; Microsoft's copper plate is cheaper but needs careful thermal math.

t: Practical advice for avoiding Rust async complexity
w: Most Rust pain comes from combining async, lifetimes and trait objects; keep async simple, avoid lifetimes, and use boxed futures.

t: Why Apple's phone chips rival desktop single-core speed
w: The A13 matches top desktop single-core scores at about 5 watts, though phones cannot sustain that in bursts, so larger devices could go further.

t: Working as a software engineer while going blind
w: Blind engineers use fast screen readers and build detailed non-visual memory models of code; practical adaptation advice.

t: How Python stores strings since PEP 393
w: Python 3.3+ uses 1, 2, or 4 bytes per code point, not UTF-16; lone surrogates are allowed but fail when encoded.

t: What diabetics find hardest: constant mental load
w: Injections are routine; the hard part is continuously weighing how each activity will shift blood sugar over the next hour.

t: Why habit-blocking apps struggle to win paying users
w: Parents and kids rarely pay or change habits; DNS, VPN and extension launches all showed weak adoption despite clear demand.

t: Living with aphantasia: a blind mind's eye
w: Lacking a mind's eye can quietly shape reading, meditation, memory of faces and imagining the future; many discover it late.

t: Dynamic linking matters for patching, not sharing
w: The key benefit of .so files is swapping library versions without rebuilding closed binaries, not sharing code between programs.

t: Why local disks still beat Kubernetes network storage
w: Fibre Channel is costly, Ceph is slow for databases, NFS underperforms, so local storage is best for busy databases in 2016.

t: Why coronavirus vaccines risk immune enhancement
w: Earlier SARS and MERS vaccines produced antibodies yet caused immunopathic responses, so antibody results alone don't show a vaccine is safe.

t: How banks create money through lending
w: When a bank lends, it creates a deposit elsewhere, so money supply grows beyond reserves while the central bank steers via the interest rate.

t: Design modules with explicit inputs and outputs
w: Declare what a module consumes and provides, inject dependencies rather than using globals, and structure code as assumptions, environment, actions, tests to cut cognitive load.

t: Typing transducers in Haskell: indexing and early stopping
w: Types can enforce faithful accumulator threading and implement early termination by wrapping only the reduced value, countering claims that typing transducers is wasteful.

t: Index junction table foreign keys for many-to-many joins
w: Without an index on the junction table's key column, lookups by person need a sequential scan; index both columns and check EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

t: Why local space does not expand with the universe
w: Gravitationally bound systems are asymptotically flat in general relativity, so cosmic expansion does not stretch Manhattan or the Earth-Moon system.

t: Separating the parts of stack ranking
w: Forced prioritization can be useful; the harmful parts are forced curves and mandatory firing, which get conflated.

t: Origins of futures and derivatives markets
w: Futures began as standardized hedging contracts for farmers and merchants; speculators absorb the risk, and derivatives build on them.

t: Searle's biological view of consciousness
w: Searle holds that syntax is observer-relative, so brains cause consciousness through physical causal powers, not by running programs.

t: How CUDA warps, blocks and grids map to hardware
w: Blocks cannot communicate, GPUs hide memory latency with massive threading, and small kernel launches are costly, so big workloads win.

t: Recovering debug info from old game binaries
w: Debug symbols, assert strings and the PE Rich header reveal original compiler versions and source-level structure of legacy binaries.

t: Typed dynamic arrays via macros in C
w: Treat an array as three variables (pointer, length, capacity) and use macros for type safety, avoiding casts in the debugger.

t: Stack frames versus heap allocation explained
w: Stack allocation is cheap because frames are pushed and popped; heap allocation is needed for data that outlives a function call.

t: Why GR constrains dark matter alternatives
w: Einstein field equations hold almost everywhere, so modified-gravity alternatives must preserve astrophysics and lab tests, leaving few hiding places.

t: Fermi estimation worked step by step
w: Break an unknown into estimable assumptions such as population, haircut frequency and cuts per barber to reach an order-of-magnitude answer.

t: Why adult learners miss target-language sounds
w: Adults past puberty stop perceiving phonemic distinctions absent in their first language without deliberate listening training.

t: Monads as pluggable function application via bind
w: Bind is function application with a hole for custom logic; Maybe shows how it composes computations cleanly.

t: Reframing unit tests as executable documentation
w: Treat any interface as a unit and tests as documenting what it does, rather than proving correctness in isolation.

t: Why resident work-hour limits didn't change mortality
w: Restrictions cut resident car accidents but left complications and mortality unchanged, plausibly because attendings deliver much care.

t: How to start learning math through logic and proofs
w: Math has many branches sharing ground; learn proof language first, where programming helps, then study one branch intensely.

t: SSA is functional by accident, not by design
w: SSA was invented to speed dataflow analysis; its resemblance to functional programming was a side observation, not the goal.

t: Why GNU HURD chose a microkernel design
w: Insider account: the microkernel aimed to give users control over daemons, at the cost of performance from extra context switches.

t: Recursion's essence is self-reference, not iteration
w: Recursion differs from loops because a definition uses itself; teach that element directly instead of calling recursion hard.

t: Controlled studies challenge static typing claims
w: Controlled experiments like Hanenberg's show static typing's benefits are unproven; commonsense claims about fewer runtime errors need testing.

t: Linux's GPLv2-only licence and its ABI exception
w: Torvalds' copyright authority shapes how GPLv2 is read for Linux; the explicit userspace ABI exception exempts ordinary applications.

t: Hardening systemd services with sandboxing directives
w: Run systemd-analyze security on a unit to see exposure, then apply directives like PrivateTmp, NoNewPrivileges, and PrivateUsers.

t: How US science funding sources and incentives differ
w: NSF, NIH and others fund research labor differently; grad-student-years are the real cost unit, and metrics distort incentives.

t: Monads explained: side effects in pure code
w: A stateful computation can be a function taking state and returning a value and new state, and monads compose these cleanly.

t: Why alt data rarely yields durable trading alpha
w: Data-driven forecasts predict features of price moves rather than prices outright, so data advantages alone are an incomplete edge.

t: Who really controls blockchain protocol changes
w: Developers ship binaries, but users choose which client runs; without consensus on that, governance is fought through propaganda and forks.

t: Early Xerox PARC office computing and workstations
w: Office computing with Alto-era hardware was only viable at high per-user cost, and Xerox expected to dominate once hardware got cheaper.

t: Short selling explained through the account ledger
w: A short sale books cash and a share liability; the position stays open as long as collateral can cover buying back the shares.

t: Joel's fair method for splitting startup equity
w: Perceived fairness matters more than percentages; an even split avoids founder fights that kill companies more often than unequal splits.

t: Why Kubernetes Services mishandle multiplexed connections
w: Services balance per TCP connection, but HTTP/2 and gRPC multiplex requests on one connection, so per-request balancing needs a layer above.

t: Keeping database writes and queue messages consistent
w: Publishing to a queue after a DB commit can lose messages; reconciliation and similar patterns keep the two systems consistent.

t: Why meat turns tender only after collagen melts
w: Tough meat means collagen hasn't melted yet; collagen melts around 160F, but muscle proteins expel water and dry out if held too hot.

t: How writing fingerprints reveal authors
w: Function-word choices like since versus because each leak a bit of author identity; combined markers build profiles, as Mosteller and Wallace showed.

t: Why chatbot research demos look better than reality
w: A GPT-2 trainer notes papers show best-case samples and warns each chatbot hype cycle overpromises; reserve judgment until independent evaluation.

t: Four quant job categories and what each requires
w: Pricing, trading, risk, and research quant roles differ in math depth and tools; risk modeling is a common entry path for programmers.

t: Excess mortality as a check on COVID death counts
w: Comparing excess deaths with official COVID counts reveals reporting gaps; Sweden's near-zero unexplained difference suggests its death reporting is comparatively complete.

t: Pilot feedback on training gaps for a new aircraft
w: Crews switching to a new type need display and systems-page training before flying; pre-flight materials and familiarization should precede the first flight.

t: Why game developers find Linux debugging lacking
w: gdb is hard to interface with, so IDEs debug poorly on Linux; for game developers even small productivity losses matter, favoring Windows.

t: Why Alameda's insolvency is unlikely: balance sheet logic
w: Insolvency needs a realized loss. Liabilities mirror the illiquid tokens held as assets, so a token collapse largely nets out.

t: Why TDD fits consultancies more than product companies
w: TDD suits fixed-spec enterprise contracts; product software has ambiguous requirements and time-to-market pressure, so tests lose value.

t: Insider view of why Google+ stumbled
w: Partitioning Google+ into a separate elite team, changing bonus promises, and real-name policy alienated staff and users; this echoed later Google Brain siloing.

t: Dyson swarms would glow in infrared, making them detectable
w: Harvested starlight leaves as waste heat, so a partial Dyson swarm should show up as a large infrared source.

t: Why sitting still endangers leg circulation
w: The heart cannot pump blood out of the legs; muscle contraction drives venous return, so long sitting lets blood pool and clot. Move regularly.

t: Energy studies often rely on years-old battery cost data
w: Battery costs fell 98% in three decades, so studies using stale cost inputs overstate the cost of EVs and renewables.

t: Why stateful WebSockets are hard to scale
w: Request-response servers are shared-nothing and forgiving; scaling WebSockets means managing server state, and WebTransport will need polyfills for years.

t: Long work marathons rarely change outcomes
w: A 30-hour sprint rarely changes a product's fate; marathon coding often masks fear of inadequacy rather than love of the work.

t: Who pays determines how carefully money is spent
w: Four spending quadrants show that when someone else pays, people choose costly options less carefully, which helps explain rising tuition under aid.

t: Why soft-serve machines lock out and need service
w: Machines must complete nightly heat cycles and biweekly teardown for food safety; missed steps lock them out, often from operator error.

t: Machine learning as compressed memory of data
w: kNN stores data with no compression while neural networks compress it into weights, so models mostly reflect the data they were given.

t: Why new AI chips struggle with software lock-in
w: Hardware wins only with drop-in framework support; GL and Direct3D kept old code working across GPUs, which AI tooling lacked.

t: Why aviation and clock speeds stalled
w: Aviation hit limits from burning fuel and CPU clocks plateaued near 3-4 GHz at atomic-scale limits; both fields saw progress stall after decades of rapid gains.

t: Live video latency: why MJPEG won
w: HLS-style streaming hit 7-second latency and WebRTC looked unfinished, so the author chose low-latency Motion JPEG to get under one second on a LAN.

t: Full-text indexes of big dumps fit on laptops
w: A 50-60GB knowledge dump indexes to roughly 1-5GB, so millisecond queries locally are practical; cloud search is convention.

t: Why EmDrive experiments keep chasing a claim
w: Analogy: a claim contradicting basic physics can be dismissed early on theory, yet expensive tests continue because public interest keeps funding them.

t: Technology spinoffs from particle physics projects
w: Collider projects drove web, superconducting magnet, radiation-hard chip, and petabyte-scale distributed computing advances.

t: Tokenizing PII at an API proxy to limit exposure
w: Route requests through a proxy that swaps PII for tokens; only the secure layer can decrypt, so employees cannot see raw data broadly.

t: Galbraith on advertising signaling trivial products
w: Galbraith argues essential improvements need no advertising; heavy ad spending suggests goods created to manufacture demand.

t: Publication bias may erase nudge effects
w: After adjusting for publication bias, nudge effects vanish; US retirement default policy was built on them, showing how fragile policy evidence can be.

t: How Amazon's calibration pressures managers into attrition
w: Written policy is fair, but managers face yearly quotas for performance plans, so the lowest-rated staff are pushed out.

t: Why apps probably aren't secretly recording you
w: Continuous speech recognition would consume noticeable CPU and bandwidth, iOS shows mic indicators, and traffic analysis would expose it; coincidence explains most cases.

t: Why dapps are hard to change or shut down
w: Deployed contract code is immutable and hard to shut down, unlike backends on AWS that a provider can terminate.

t: Why software trust is harder than TLS certificates
w: Code signing cannot prove legitimacy; a software equivalent of the URL bar and domain validation remains unsolved.

t: Why oven-reflowing logic boards destroys them
w: Oven heat causes thermal stress and trapped moisture expansion (popcorning) that damages PCBs and ICs; use directed hot air.

t: Why general-purpose computers arrived late: missing abstractions
w: Special-purpose machines existed; the bottleneck was conceptual. Ada Lovelace grasped general computing before its time.

t: Why modern car pillars hide pedestrians from drivers
w: Wide pillars block sightlines, and drivers rarely look near frame edges, so pedestrians can vanish in the gap.

t: Why radiology is a good target for automation
w: Radiologists spend most time at workstations; PACS and DICOM standardize image data, so bottlenecks are data access and adoption.

t: Why a full credit freeze beats paid identity monitoring
w: A free credit freeze blocks new accounts and beats paid monitoring; freezing children's credit also helps since identity thieves target minors.

t: Why microseconds matter in market price discovery
w: Markets act as a distributed recursive predictor; faster price-discovery feedback loops converge to more self-consistent prices, like higher sample rates in control systems.

t: Resources that introduce girls to programming and engineering
w: Curated list of toys, apps, and workshops (GoldieBlox, Girls Who Code, Black Girls Code) that teach technical skills to girls.

t: Which 1Password changes are real security concerns
w: Of the 1Password changes (subscription pricing, cloud sync, hidden local vaults, first-run contact), only the mandatory 1Password.com enrollment is a serious security concern.

t: Hydrogen cartridge vs lithium battery energy math
w: Lithium at 200Wh/kg needs about 24kg for 4.8kWh; Toyota's 5.5kg cartridge is good, not revolutionary.

t: Large tech systems grow like old cities
w: Long-lived companies' data and code evolve in layers, so no one fully understands them and no single reference exists.

t: Using GDPR export and portability for playlists
w: GDPR export gives playlists as JSON; Article 20 lets users request direct transfer to another service where technically feasible.

t: How a Linode Manager compromise led to root access
w: Post-mortem: attacker used a stolen password and MFA secret, reset root passwords, and gained root via Lish.

t: Study algorithms, languages and architecture to excel
w: Concrete roadmap: master algorithms, a few core languages, computer architecture, toolchains, and large codebases.

t: How IRS contractor-vs-employee tests really work
w: Control over means and manner, not results, makes a worker an employee; IRS applies 20 factors in a facts-and-circumstances test easily tipped either way.

t: Why platform bugs are worth less than WordPress bugs
w: Widely used software like PHP and WordPress keeps flaws unpatched for years, while Facebook patches fast and overpays bounties, so exploit value is lower there.

t: Software safety flaws in Toyota's throttle code
w: Expert testimony describes 10,000 globals, a watchdog that cannot detect dead tasks, and discarded OS error codes.

t: How Firebase bills SSL overhead on realtime database
w: Realtime DB charges SSL overhead on every request; a bug had undercharged it, and fixing it spiked bills for IoT clients.

t: Why distro patches frustrate upstream maintainers
w: Distributions patch and reallocate interfaces without asking, so maintainers lose control of their own interface and inherit user bugs they never introduced.

t: Why automakers struggle with open source software
w: Insider account: open source offers no indemnity to big firms, SYNC avoided Windows, and maps and parts came from outside partners.

t: Why Scala can't generically extend Java arrays
w: Java arrays expose only length, index and update, so generic extension methods hit fundamental limits in most languages.

t: Practical lessons from acting as own general contractor
w: Simple-looking trades are hard the first time; use traditional methods for a first house and learn foundations and permits before buying land.

t: How leverage and counterparty risk cascade in crypto
w: Delta hedging does not protect against counterparty failure; collateral lent to a failed firm spills losses and forced liquidations push prices lower.

t: Costs of counterinsurgency: rotations and trust
w: Rotating units every 9-12 months erodes relearned local trust; drones cannot replace governance and policing work.

t: From bash scripts to containers: infrastructure history
w: Pre-built container images move package installs to build time, so hosts launch in seconds instead of minutes.

t: Rare Solar System features may explain the Fermi paradox
w: Jupiter's comet shielding, a galactic-plane-avoiding orbit, and a rocky-plus-gas-giant system may make intelligence rare.

t: Matrix's plans to fix Riot and Synapse performance
w: Lazy-loading room members cuts RAM 3x-20x; cross-signing ends repeated device verification; Synapse hot paths move toward constant cost per room size.

t: Encryption and identity are separate certificate problems
w: Domain-validated certs prove control of a domain, not trustworthiness; the bigger EV badges mostly reflect paid verification cost, not stronger encryption.

t: Why git submodules cause daily friction
w: Submodules add constant small annoyances across git operations; prefer package managers, subtrees, or vendored copies with commit references.

t: Why banks keep legacy password systems
w: Legacy vendor systems often cannot add salted hashes; banks lean on second factors and network isolation, since rebuilding risks outages that could outweigh the gain.

t: Ranked tips for better sleep
w: Consistent bed and wake times matter most, then morning outdoor light, dim evenings, passive pre-bed routines and nasal breathing, ranked by the author's experience.

t: Using Google Inbox as a to-do list
w: Treat the inbox as a to-do list: pin actionable mail, snooze the rest, and cluster mailing lists for a daily triage.

t: Slot machine near-misses are simple probability
w: Basic odds show near-misses and big wins occur often across a bank of machines, so streaks of 'hot' machines emerge without design intent.

t: How surprise-billing laws affect physician contracts
w: Insurers use network leverage to cut rates; banning out-of-network billing removes physicians' main bargaining tool.

t: Root cause of a supercomputer file deletion
w: A find-based cleanup script had a variable passed wrongly and was reloaded mid-deployment, deleting 77TB; a clear postmortem lesson.

t: Silicon Valley may follow Detroit's century-long arc
w: Industries build on decades of older technology; Detroit's population kept growing for decades after the auto industry began, so peak timing is hard to predict.

t: Spotify's original native client and why it was fast
w: The early desktop app used a custom-rendered UI and an optimized protocol, a responsiveness edge lost when it later moved to a Chromium wrapper.

t: Why zero marginal cost does not make digital goods free
w: Digital goods have high fixed costs and zero marginal cost, so creators still need revenue, much like a train that costs the same whether full or empty.

t: Why Bloomberg terminals resist replacement
w: Former user explains messaging network lock-in and learned command habits that defeat better UIs.

t: Two blockers to near-term general AI
w: Models predict outputs without coded end-state reasoning and lack the intuitions babies build from experience.

t: Automated essay scorer rewards padding
w: Parent showed adding irrelevant sentences raised the AI score, exposing that it measured length.
