t: Why keeping margin percentage misprices offshoring
w: Preserving margin percentage raises profit; matching offshore profit needs only a small price increase.

t: Why Linux GUI toolkits seem fragmented
w: Most drivers ship in the kernel, but GTK and Qt break compatibility across versions, unlike Win32's decades of binary compatibility.

t: Polished how-to videos are often less accurate
w: A finish carpenter found polished how-to videos often less accurate than shaky jobsite clips; judge expertise, not production quality.

t: Why built-in webcams look bad and what fixes it
w: Small sensors and lenses limit quality regardless of 4K specs; a used DSLR with clean HDMI and a capture card works.

t: Teaching computational thinking before any code
w: CS Unplugged activities build computational thinking first; block languages feel fake to teens, so teach text code afterwards.

t: Why iOS parental apps relied on abusable MDM access
w: Parental apps used enterprise MDM and VPN APIs for deep device control; Apple removed them since that access is a privacy and security risk.

t: Why iOS parental apps relied on abusable MDM access
w: Parental apps used enterprise MDM and VPN APIs for deep device control; Apple removed them since that access is a privacy and security risk.

t: Cookware materials ranked by food-leaching risk
w: Glass is safest, then commercially pure titanium, then stainless steel; new stainless leaches more nickel and chromium, used pans very little.

t: Why the Oracle v. Google fair use verdict surprised
w: Two of four fair use factors weigh against Google, so the verdict is surprising; Oracle's appeal will argue no rational jury could find fair use.

t: Why removing senescent cells could extend healthy lifespan
w: Clearing senescent cells extended mouse lifespan 30-40% and improved late-life health, though other aging causes would still eventually kill.

t: Many mocks signal code that needs restructuring
w: A unit test needing many mocks usually means the function should be split; restructure the code rather than the test strategy.

t: Why Java's verbosity pays off at scale
w: Java keeps all code in classes, avoiding top-level script ambiguity; explicit types and visibility help large codebases.

t: Why HN timestamps look inconsistent after re-ups
w: Re-upped stories get timestamps chosen to match their front-page rank; original submission times are on other pages.

t: Why corporate politics emerges from incentives
w: Politics arises from emergent incentives rather than villains; managers grow teams to run bigger groups.

t: Why MongoDB write acknowledgement is configurable
w: Write concern lets drivers choose acknowledgement levels, such as waiting for replicas across data centers.

t: Why deleting public forum comments breaks conversations
w: Public comments are part of a shared conversation like a newsgroup; deleting them damages other users' posts, so the norm is a balance of deletion and anonymity.

t: Amazon's non-compete enforcement rarely succeeds in court
w: Washington courts rarely grant injunctions against engineers changing jobs, and a non-compete often covers narrower activity than it appears, depending on state law.

t: Why early employee equity shrinks through dilution
w: A 1% grant can fall to 0.2% through investor and employee dilution; the company's eventual value is unknown, so negotiate protections.

t: The Great Filter argument for the Fermi paradox
w: If probes are never seen, some step is an extremely hard filter; easy abiogenesis on Mars would move that filter toward the future.

t: Why stop-and-go driving drains Tesla range
w: Brakes dissipate energy and regenerative braking recovers only part of it, so city driving hurts efficiency more than cruise control.

t: Why phone numbers make weak account recovery
w: Phone-based recovery is exposed to SIM-swap attacks; authenticator apps and recovery paths independent of phone numbers are safer.

t: Why EmDrive claims clash with momentum conservation
w: A closed resonant cavity cannot push itself without momentum going somewhere; the FAQ's explanation quietly conserves nothing new.

t: Why YAML's design is stuck: history from a creator
w: YAML predated JSON and was shaped by XML's peak; multiple implementations and volunteer work make its spec slow to change.

t: Why confiscated wealth yields far less cash
w: Founder stock is illiquid; forced sales crash the price, so confiscation yields much less than the stated wealth.

t: How Facebook's XCheck exemptions arose
w: Large systems accumulate edge cases; XCheck let integrity teams shield subpopulations from other teams' automated penalties.

t: Why medical AI is essentially regression
w: Clinical AI infers rules from data like regression; the real question is whether it helps clinical decisions at all.

t: Why single-person building illness claims need skepticism
w: One symptomatic unit out of 1800 makes soil contamination unlikely; check unit-specific materials first, and beware attention-seeking online patients.

t: Why semi-autonomous units end with overpriced shared services
w: Semi-autonomous units often must buy shared services like IT from a captive internal vendor with no competition, producing poor service and duplicated overhead.

t: Why Stack Overflow answers are freely licensed
w: Answers are a shared resource read by thousands, unlike Experts-Exchange's one-to-one model; CC licensing rejects the paywall approach.

t: Deep learning as learned input-to-output mapping
w: Deep learning is a black box mapping input numbers to output numbers; the hard part is encoding your domain problem as inputs and desired outputs.

t: Practical rules to reduce code cognitive load
w: Favor declarative code, shallow call chains, separated business logic, composition over inheritance, and greppable names to cut the mental cost of changes.

t: Why trustless systems still rely on courts
w: Trading is fast because a trusted legal layer is abstracted away; tokenized houses still need courts and LLC wrappers to enforce.

t: Napkin math on 10-minute EV charging cables
w: Charging 100 kWh in 10 minutes needs about 1000 A; copper cable mass, heat and connector force make such cables impractical.

t: Handwrite for memory, type for searchable storage
w: Memory formation and long-term searchability compete; handwriting aids recall while typed notes aid retrieval, so using both fits a tradeoff.

t: Why published synthesis yields are hard to reproduce
w: Novel syntheses often drop from grams to micrograms, and reported yields like 75 percent can be unreproducible even by experienced chemists.

t: Why ship steering and speed should share one controller
w: Splitting control across roles and hidden backup modes causes mode confusion; unified controls prevent the mismatch behind ship collisions.

t: A body-scan routine for falling asleep
w: Lie still, scan the body slowly naming sensations, and count breaths when thoughts drift; this holds attention and helps sleep.

t: Essential developer tools most CS curricula skip
w: Shell, version control, and editor skills are rarely taught, costing students time; the published lecture notes cover them.

t: GPL versus permissive licenses: different goals
w: GPL maximizes free software; MIT and BSD let authors share generously, but permissive licenses enable proprietary forks, creating frustration.

t: Why the UK has so little forest cover
w: UK forest cover is about 13%, below most of Europe; clearing for farmland began about 5,000 years ago, and mountains protected forests elsewhere.

t: Why fundamentals outlast the libraries you learn
w: Languages and libraries churn, while data structures, algorithms, and design principles stay stable; learning those makes new frameworks quick to pick up.

t: Insurance is for ruinous losses, not expected value
w: Insurers profit on average; buy cover for losses you can't absorb, not to beat expected value.

t: Why HN threads are driven by waves of objections
w: Clear model: early reflexive objections trigger second-wave defenses, so top comments often complain about the thread.

t: Build relationships inside platforms you depend on
w: Platform support inboxes often fail. Find a human inside the platform early and spread relationships so a reassignment does not cut you off.

t: What 'protein folding solved' means for practitioners
w: Practitioner says structure from sequence is useful for engineering insight, but benchmarks do not show that.

t: When ORMs stop being worth it for Postgres
w: ORMs only support the lowest common denominator of database features; advanced Postgres features and analytical queries need hand-written SQL.

t: Air-FI: noise-based covert channel from air-gapped PCs
w: The Air-FI channel encodes data as noise in Wi-Fi bands, readable by Wi-Fi chipsets at ~10 bits/s, but needs malware already on the target.

t: A biologist on why engineered super-pathogens are hard
w: Biologists know little about dynamic, redundant systems, so whether lethality, long incubation and transmissibility can coexist is unknown.

t: Why encrypted leak dumps eventually become readable
w: Delayed-release encrypted files rely on today's algorithms staying secure; advances or quantum computers can break them later.

t: Sloppy-but-fast vim navigation with H, M, L and f
w: Use H/M/L and counted f/t motions to approximate position quickly, combine c2f with repeated j, and favor fluid navigation over precise counting.

t: Why small napkin machines cost far more per unit
w: Matching one industrial machine needs 175 small machines and about 700 workers, so labor and capital dominate while power costs stay minor.

t: Why SMS is weak for account recovery
w: SMS alone can reset passwords; require a second factor, and add porting delays with alerts to the old SIM.

t: Prompting GPT-3 with an internal monologue
w: Asking GPT-3 to write a parenthetical reasoning step before answering helped it recognize nonsense questions and give more accurate, hedged answers.

t: Why a $1 app price is a trivial decision
w: Marginal utility explains pricing: a dollar is trivial to someone who casually spends on things they would discard, so small app prices sell easily.

t: Adam Smith's game analogy for Stoic indifference
w: Stoics treat life as a game of skill and chance; judge yourself on playing fairly and well, since outcomes beyond your control should not decide happiness.

t: British views of the American Civil War
w: Parliament debated recognition and the Trent affair nearly drew Britain in; Confederate networks in Britain shaped pro-South sentiment.

t: Why search ads beat social ads: user intent
w: Search users express intent; Facebook users browse friends' posts without seeking things, so targeting data helps less.

t: Experienced dev finds AI code needs heavy rewriting
w: On a 15-year-old Java and React system, AI-generated code often needed about 70 percent rewriting after self-review because of architecture issues.

t: How a poison pill blocks hostile takeovers
w: A poison pill issues discounted shares to other holders, diluting a 51% attacker and making the hostile takeover ruinously expensive.

t: Six ways open-source projects make money
w: Open-core companies, hosting, support, employer funding, crowdfunding and patronage each trade autonomy for revenue.

t: Steps to register a German GmbH or UG
w: Notary, bank account, then tax advisor; a UG is optional and mainly serves a tax-motivated intermediary role.

t: Why privacy hardening triggers endless CAPTCHAs
w: Blocking fingerprinting and CDNs makes Google CAPTCHAs escalate; fingerprint protection itself seems to raise red flags.

t: Email hosting options, prices and migration tips
w: Google Takeout exports mail as mbox for migration; several providers offer custom domains for a few dollars a month.

t: How timeshare sales pitches hide the real loan cost
w: Pitches quote pennies a day; the real cost is a 12-13 percent APR loan on a roughly $40k purchase.

t: Why Google requires JavaScript at login
w: JavaScript lets Google detect automated browsers, so requiring it removes bot signals and blocks mass account hijacking attacks.

t: Most homeless are transient, not chronically addicted
w: About two-thirds are transiently homeless, often employed; preventing loss of stable housing is the most effective intervention.

t: Why software estimates stay wrong: misses don't cost developers
w: Estimates stay wrong because misses rarely hurt the estimator; managers pad the worst estimators, and developers explain overruns rather than anticipating complexity.

t: Why Mozilla's Persona login failed to take off
w: Insider explanation: three-way cold start across users, providers and sites, plus hard federated-login UX, sank Persona.

t: Kay on Dijkstra and 1960s research culture
w: ARPA-era researchers explored without consensus; Kay explains that OOP at PARC meant something different from today's usage, and that Dijkstra's critiques were useful when heeded.

t: Engineering lessons from Cycorp's symbolic AI
w: Trading completeness for answers most of the time made the inference engine practical, but unresolved views on AI goals hurt the company.

t: How advertising builds associations via co-activation
w: Ads link concepts through co-activation and priming; liking is a decision heuristic, so warmth-based associations reliably increase purchase likelihood.

t: Why corporations cannot represent themselves in federal court
w: Under N.D. Cal. Civil Local Rule 3-9(b), corporations must appear through a bar member, so a self-represented corporate plaintiff risks procedural dismissal.

t: The 'bump the lamp' principle for hidden details
w: Roger Rabbit's moving shadow shows that invisible craft compounds: extra effort most users never notice still shapes overall quality.

t: How banks reorder transactions to maximize overdraft fees
w: Processing largest debits first triggers repeated $35 fees; chronological posting would have avoided most of them.

t: Why Common Lisp development feels so productive
w: Incremental REPL-driven development with Emacs and SLIME yields safe, performant code quickly; the editor setup is the main barrier for newcomers.

t: Why ARM on Windows lacks a forcing commitment
w: Chipmakers, OS vendors and software firms each wait for others to commit; without a forcing commitment like Apple's, ARM-on-Windows stalls.

t: Sales fundamentals from a veteran sales leader
w: Sell aspirin, not vitamins. People buy time, money, sex, or peace of mind, and being useful builds the trust that drives sales.

t: How adverse selection can cause an insurance death spiral
w: Without healthy people enrolling, insurance becomes a subscription for the sick, so premiums rise and more healthy people leave.

t: Fitness matters more than obesity for longevity
w: A 1999 study of 32,000 people found aerobic fitness predicted lower death rates more strongly than obesity did.

t: Structural reasons US medicine costs so much
w: Insurance tax treatment, restricted foreign doctor licensing, and long residencies each inflate US medical costs.

t: Why anecdotal cures mislead: spontaneous remission
w: People in remission credit whatever they tried; spontaneous recovery is common, so anecdotes cannot separate treatment effects from coincidence.

t: Why mature markets differentiate through marketing
w: In mature markets products are technically equivalent, so brands differentiate on positioning and image; engineers often overlook that lever.

t: Screen engineers with practical design questions
w: Probe real experience and design ability, like source-control tradeoffs or class modeling, rather than language trivia or puzzles.

t: Readline keybindings work across most macOS apps
w: Ctrl-based readline keys (ctrl-a/e/f/b/p/n/k/u) work in shells and most text fields; remapping Caps Lock to Control makes them fast.

t: GNU grep beats BSD grep by 30x on logs
w: On a 1.5GB log, BSD grep on macOS took 37s versus 1.3s for GNU grep via Homebrew; the grep implementation matters for large files.

t: Why researchers must never dump user data
w: Exploits should stop at proof of existence; pivoting to dump sensitive data creates legal and employment risk for the researcher.

t: Deleted Reddit posts remain traceable via archives
w: Archives like pushshift keep deleted posts searchable by username, so throwaway accounts can be tied back to real identities.

t: Why players exploit safe doorway combat
w: Players minimize risk by luring enemies to doors; rewarding risk-taking or punishing retreat, as Ninja Gaiden did, counters that low-risk path.

t: Practical methods for learning Chinese efficiently
w: Modern tools like SRS flashcards, Pleco OCR and free grammar resources make Chinese literacy far faster than in the 1990s.

t: Manual requirement traceability in DO-178B avionics
w: DO-178B requires tracing requirements to code, and doing it by hand was a mess; tooling for traceability would help.

t: Why Minix stalled after grant-funded work
w: Without bug trackers or ownership, grant-funded projects stall; NetBSD userspace and clang slowed builds to hours.

t: Red flags that expose fabricated SaaS revenue
w: Real revenue leaves traces in contracts, infrastructure load, sales activity, and expansion; a long tail of tiny customers with no growth is a warning sign.

t: Why need-blind colleges can cost less than state schools
w: Need-blind schools act as price discrimination: full-pay families subsidize aid, so net cost for many students can match or beat in-state tuition.

t: OptiBay SSD upgrade tips
w: Put the SSD in the 3 Gbps optical bay, keep HDD internal, and install Boot Camp before removing the drive.

t: Why rigid types can hinder changing deployed code
w: Real-world cost is changing deployed code, not writing it; types catch breakage from changes but overly rigid types block common, needed changes.

t: Which hiring methods actually predict job performance
w: Points to Schmidt and Hunter's meta-analysis of 85 years of selection research as the evidence base for interviews, tests and resume screening.

t: Why Linux overtook Solaris technically and commercially
w: Linux won on performance, observability, drivers and contributor count; ecosystem, staff skills and TCO outweigh a once-superior incumbent.

t: Curated starting resources for learning Clojure
w: Concise wikibook intro, clojure.org rationale, Emacs setup guides and Rich Hickey videos; many tutorials assume a Java background.

t: What Google Cloud Messaging actually carries in Signal
w: Signal uses GCM only as a wake-up push on Android; no message data goes over it, and the app fetches messages from Signal's server.

t: Practical public speaking tactics for nervous speakers
w: Pause instead of filler sounds, anchor to three audience members, open with self-deprecating humor; audiences remember your voice more than content.

t: How tax rules push firms toward buybacks and debt
w: Interest is deductible while dividends are taxed twice, so debt and buybacks win; this drives leveraged buyouts and the shareholder-value focus.

t: Why Theranos's microfluidics claims were overstated
w: Clinical analyzers already use microliter assays with fast results; reducing dead volume is incremental rather than revolutionary.

t: Quant's risk comparison of bitcoin and gold ETF
w: Near-zero correlation with GLD; MtGox/USD had about 1.3pp daily volatility and a 36% worst day vs 5.5%, and gold gave 2.7x return per unit risk.

t: How Google handles employee open-source copyright
w: Employment agreements claim competing work; Google releases code under Google copyright and cleared about 75% of requests, explaining the tradeoff.

t: Why Apple's App Store trademark is weak
w: Explains trademark registrability: generic terms cannot be registered, and the arbitrary-meaning argument for app is the key legal question.

t: Why Node's single event loop suits app developers
w: Single event loop per process trades raw power for simplicity and low cognitive overhead in concurrent servers.

t: Why subsidized loans inflate tuition prices
w: Discount government loans shift capital into education beyond the efficient level and, with weak collection, push prices up.

t: US adopted metric legally in 1866 and 1875
w: The US authorized the metric system in 1866 and joined the Treaty of the Meter in 1875, yet customary units persist in everyday use.

t: IETF's crypto review board chaired by an NSA employee
w: The IETF's CFRG reviews cryptography for other standards; its chair was an NSA employee, a conflict that raised trust questions about standards review.

t: Why carbon and silicon differ for alien chemistry
w: Carbon's four bonding slots and mid-sized atoms enable stable chains; silicon is too large and inert, so carbon-like chemistry is favored.

t: Why coroutines beat callbacks for async I/O
w: Callback chains get unwieldy at scale; coroutine libraries like gevent, eventlet and Erlang or Haskell's runtimes give async I/O in blocking-style code.

t: Why parties converge and politics stays contentious
w: Parties act as brands that cut voter effort, and Hotelling convergence plus narrow majorities keeps US and Australian politics close and bitter.

t: Signed web packages and hidden URLs in Chrome
w: Web Packages let certificate-signed content render offline and show the publisher origin, changing what the address bar means.

t: Type with wrists aligned to forearms
w: Relax wrists so hands sit at forearm angle rather than bent straight forward; the author reports decades of trouble-free typing.

t: Why allocations and GC break 16ms frame budgets
w: At 60fps a frame has about 16ms; per-frame object allocation triggers GC pauses that wreck performance in game loops.

t: Containers are isolated processes, not virtual machines
w: Docker containers are ordinary processes isolated with namespaces and cgroups; the core value is isolation, with packaging layered on top.

t: How Dutch rail crew schedules are computed
w: NS's TURNI solves about 1,000 driver duties from 15,000 trips in 24 hours; rail crew problems are far harder than airline ones.

t: Why FAANG lawyers avoid AGPL software
w: AGPL's Corresponding Source definition could reach software that merely uses the modified code, so legal teams treat AGPL as too risky.

t: Driving technique that smooths traffic and saves fuel
w: Leave large gaps, keep constant speed, avoid braking; traffic becomes calmer, fuel economy improves, and others often follow.

t: Measured Go vs Rust results on a text search
w: Both programs were naive, yet Rust finished in about 4.2s versus Go's 6.5s with less memory; measure before trusting language-speed claims.

t: Practical ways to promote a new web app
w: Pitch smaller niche blogs with rapport, join competitor user communities, and seek interviews; small friendly blogs link more readily than big ones.

t: Quorum intersection is needed for safe federated consensus
w: Each node's quorum slices must overlap sufficiently for safety; without formal topology requirements or central trust, the protocol can fault, as Stellar did.

t: Investment bank analyst pay and career path
w: Bulge bracket analysts get roughly $70k base plus bonus; most leave after two years, few reach associate, and associates often come via MBA.

t: How to negotiate buying a domain you want
w: Don't ask for a favor; owners know their domain's value. Let them name a price, since a domain is worth only what buyers pay.

t: Why console unit sales mislead about profitability
w: Consoles often sell at a loss; profits come from games and services, so installed base and software attach rate matter more than hardware unit counts.

t: How AppJet pivoted to Etherpad and sold to Google
w: AppJet's developer platform had almost no users; the team pivoted to Etherpad, which earned revenue before the Google Wave sale.

t: Key-value and column stores trade away access patterns
w: Key-value stores lose lookups by non-key fields; column stores speed column scans but make fetching a whole row costlier.

t: Static typing can create errors with dynamic JSON
w: Forcing variable JSON into static types adds casting code and can introduce errors that dynamic languages would not have.

t: Clean-room reverse engineering and why it is legal
w: One team documents how the target works and a separate team implements from that spec, the process behind IBM PC clones.

t: Why declarative languages still run as instructions
w: Declarative code compiles to instructions; hiding them makes performance and bugs opaque once abstractions leak.

t: Why co-working spaces struggle: customer churn economics
w: Co-working revenue depends on customers who leave when they grow or fail; unpredictable churn and non-payment make revolving-door membership fragile.

t: Why Kotlin's multi-platform goals conflict with Java
w: Kotlin's low-overhead and multi-platform goals clash with Java virtual threads and Valhalla, forcing hard tradeoffs on Kotlin's design.

t: Peak oil scares recur and drive capital into costly reserves
w: Peak-oil alarms recurred every 25-30 years since 1859, spiking prices and pouring capital into uneconomic reserves like oil sands.

t: Women's share of CS degrees peaked in the 1980s
w: As a share of CS bachelor's degrees, women fell from 37% in 1984-85 to 27% in 2003; early corporate computing was more welcoming than startups.

t: Using SVG and Vue for interactive diagrams
w: SVG suits per-element mouse events and scales to high DPI; Vue interpolates values into static HTML without a SPA build.

t: Insider account of the Bitcoin block size fight
w: BIP 101 was compromised to 8MB; miners insisted on running only Core, so XT's adoption failed regardless of compromises.

t: Federated versus peer-to-peer social networks
w: Federated servers can control what you see; peer-to-peer removes that middle layer but needs a native client running locally.

t: SR-71 engineering: leaking fuel and fitting panels
w: The SR-71 leaked fuel on the ground so its panels could stretch and seal at speed; many parts failed, showing that effectiveness can beat minimalism.

t: Why astronomers hold code and data back
w: Short postdocs reward first-author papers, so collaborators guard data during proprietary periods; career incentives, not secrecy, drive the practice.

t: Why rootless containers trade off kernel attack surface
w: Unprivileged user namespaces expose rarely-audited root-only kernel code to users, so rootless podman is not automatically safer.

t: Why GCHQ destroyed the Guardian's devices
w: Insider explains that classified-network exposure legally required physical destruction of devices, so the Guardian was treated like everyone else.

t: Why Cuil, Blekko and others failed against Google
w: Cuil spent about $30M with no revenue model and weak tech; Google copied Yahoo's vertical search, so entrants struggled.

t: Why Tesla's bumper radar misses obstacles
w: Bumper radar is blind at windshield height, so it can miss stopped vehicles and high trailers.

t: Why very tall x-heights and plain forms hurt reading
w: Letterform distinctiveness matters; a very high x-height makes lowercase resemble uppercase, and serifs aid reading.

t: Common pitfalls in large make-based build systems
w: Large makefiles fail via vendor-specific supermake dialects, no debugger, and parallel builds breaking on library and generated-header ordering.

t: How intonation separates 'could care less' from literal use
w: Listeners tell idioms from literal phrases by intonation contour, as with 'black bird' stressed versus flat; the same words map to different referents.

t: Lessons from the Taos operating system startup
w: Tao's OS translated a custom portable assembly to native code at load; a proprietary language and hard-to-say name hurt adoption.

t: Pricing a fixed-scope web project on time and materials
w: Estimate hours, pad them, and multiply by a 100-200/hr rate; require written acceptance criteria up front and sell retainers to absorb changing requirements.

t: Why paid 'donations' for goods are sales
w: Donation has a specific tax meaning; exchanging money for a product is a sale, which can trigger sales tax and retail obligations regardless of label.

t: Why long-hours productivity evidence is murky
w: Pop-science claims confuse correlation with causation; health research supports limits on very long hours, but not productivity gains from working less.

t: Why blue light's sleep effects are more nuanced
w: Melanopsin responds to blue light regardless; equal-brightness comparisons and mixed human evidence complicate the simple story.

t: How an SNI-host mismatch let Lantern masquerade traffic
w: Cloudflare did not verify the SNI field matched the encrypted Host header, letting clients impersonate customers; fixed by matching them.

t: Why agent output overwhelms terminal UIs
w: Longer agent runs produce huge tool-call output, and terminals offer few pixels, one font size and inconsistent colors, forcing UX tradeoffs.

t: Why GNOME uses instant-apply configuration design
w: Explains GNOME's instant-apply settings choice, which drives a configuration service that notifies apps of changes, and the alt-drag workaround for panels.

t: Checklist for judging experimental claims
w: Applies Norvig's warning signs for experiment design, such as lack of randomized controlled trials, as a practical checklist for evaluating health claims.

t: Freelancer, contractor and consultant are different relationships
w: Distinguishes three client relationships by who sets strategy, and notice periods, so you can price and set expectations for each role.

t: Why parties sorted by issues, not extremity
w: Political science: polarization comes from issue positions aligning with party, shown by southern conservative Democrats re-registering as Republicans through inertia.

t: What likely happened in Air France 447's stall
w: The pilot never saw high angle of attack, and holding nose-up inputs let the tail trim reach maximum, delaying the response to stick-forward inputs.

t: Why ISP interconnects bottleneck streaming traffic
w: Last-mile upgrades raise core and interconnect load; gradual slowdowns point to congestion growth rather than a routing change.

t: How Knuth typesets with plain TeX
w: Knuth uses plain TeX as a formatting tool, producing DVI then PostScript then PDF, unlike LaTeX's semantic markup approach.

t: How Superfish broke browser certificate validation
w: Superfish's proxy accepted obviously fake self-signed certs and skipped revocation checks, so the attack didn't need the leaked private key.

t: Why Microsoft shifted Windows testing to telemetry
w: After dedicated testers were cut in 2014, Microsoft relied on developer tests, beta programs and telemetry; crash dumps find bugs testing misses.

t: How over-reliance on flight director guidance causes takeoff errors
w: Pilots trained on flight director bars can follow them into dangerous pitch; normal rotation is about 15 degrees nose-up, so flat rotation signals overreliance.

t: Apple Silicon benchmark numbers were Rosetta emulation
w: The published numbers matched x86_64 binaries under Rosetta; the arm64 build returned invalid results, so verify architecture before trusting benchmarks.

t: Why Lisp lost to the C machine
w: General-purpose infrastructure favors one standard; Lisp machines lost because C's compilers, stacks and formats dominated the ecosystem.

t: Why payday loans charge so much
w: Flat fees look like 1000% APR, but high default rates and costly operations make the price a function of risk.

t: Why CAD models need cleanup before game engines
w: CAD models carry unneeded detail like screw threads and hidden interiors that overwhelm game engines; strip everything not visible.

t: A 'Call Brian' message exposed memory corruption
w: A firmware error string meant for an impossible case fired in the field, revealing a processor bug writing corrupted memory; assertions can catch hardware faults.

t: Answering a cease-and-desist letter strategically
w: A litigator explains how principled, detailed replies deter overreaching IP claims from big companies.

t: Teaching data structures in Python instead of Java
w: Python lets courses skip Java generics and access modifiers, so students focus on structures, complexity and iterators before hand-compiling to MIPS.

t: Why telomere lengthening is not proven life extension
w: Telomere length correlates with aging but causation is unproven, and delivering genes to enough cells is hard.

t: Why significant misleads readers about effects
w: Significant means detectable, not important; large studies make trivial effects significant while small ones hide real effects.

t: Why non-bingeable spaced learning builds lasting skill
w: Exponential review intervals and daily stopping force retention; the design aims at durable learning rather than cramming.

t: Why Assange extradition was blocked on health grounds
w: Section 91 bars extradition if unjust or oppressive due to health; the judge found SAMs isolation would likely worsen his condition.

t: What AGPL section 13 actually requires for networked software
w: Clause 13 requires modified programs offering remote network interaction to share source; the license is not an EULA, and compliance is hard for ordinary developers.

t: Why Microsoft's Edit was written in Rust
w: The author prototyped in C, C++, Zig and Rust; Rust won on internal support despite weaker tree-building ergonomics, and scratch arenas replaced a general-purpose allocator.

t: How Hacker News selects and re-ups front-page stories
w: Software first-passes stories and reviewers handle the rest; past submissions matter, not karma, and reposts become re-ups with randomized placement.

t: How root cloud access went unmonitored at Ubiquiti
w: Root cloud accounts should be locked down with alerting; one engineer ran production AWS under a personal account until new controls were imposed.

t: Turning repeated client work into a sellable product
w: Package the piece you implement repeatedly as a teachable product, then sell to teams that would otherwise hire engineers.

t: How the Craig Wright Satoshi claim fell apart
w: Forged old blog posts, a PGP key added in 2013, and a fake SGI reference letter exposed the claim as fraud, showing how to check credentials.

t: How civilians coordinated Harvey water rescues
w: Volunteers used Zello, Glympse and shared sheets; drones were hazards to rescue helicopters, so airspace coordination is the real unsolved need.

t: How US law shapes at-will employment and overtime
w: US at-will employment is the default, with protective statutes carving out exceptions, including overtime pay requirements and their exemptions.

t: Science's exponential growth era has ended
w: Goodstein argues science's institutions were built for exponential expansion and are unsuited to the steady-state era that followed, so expectations must change.

t: Alan Kay's frame: most real-world code is pop culture
w: Pop culture is identity-driven and present-focused, which explains why new, hip solutions often beat proven ones in industry decisions.

t: Building Naughty Dog's games in a Lisp dialect
w: The author wrote GOOL and GOAL, Lisp-based runtime dialects that shipped Crash Bandicoot and Jak and Daxter, before Ruby replaced Lisp for libraries.

t: Self-study path for relearning undergraduate math
w: Master fundamental ideas deeply via Feynman's number chapter, then learn problem-solving tricks; probability and Bayesian reasoning matter most.

t: Taviso's Windows kernel disclosure fight with Microsoft
w: Microsoft refused out-of-band kernel patches; a simple disable-VDM mitigation was documented and published after four months of negotiation.

t: Heroku's reproducible deploys and why it's still admired
w: Insider view: Heroku made reproducible builds and deployments standard when most teams copied files to servers, long before 12-factor.

t: Maintainer burden of reviewing patches at scale
w: Reviewing contributions eats time needed for design; overcommunication and unavoidable decisions drain maintainers of large open source projects.

t: How Langstroth hives may harm bee health
w: Movable frames and top-opening hives enabled migratory, interventionist beekeeping that spreads mites and disrupts the colony's nest climate.

t: How grid frequency balances supply in markets
w: Spot prices come from dispatching cheapest generation until demand is met; grid frequency near 50Hz signals supply-demand balance.

t: Models can add bias beyond biased training data
w: Proxy variables can reconstruct protected attributes and design choices affect harm, so bias is not only a data-collection problem.

t: Lessons from running hundreds of mobile apps
w: Feature phone stores still matter; localize beyond English; non-SaaS apps are impulse buys with short lifespans; extend established brands for reliable profit.

t: Why chip teams formally verify circuits
w: Silicon bugs cost months and multimillion-dollar mask sets, so teams formally verify arithmetic like adders and multipliers, though few things are provable.

t: Subscription business funnel metrics for a solo founder
w: About 2% of visitors start a free trial, 70% convert, and churn settles near 5% monthly after a first-month drop of about 25%.

t: Why Tailscale's iOS client can't be open sourced
w: Network Extension entitlements are tied to Apple's corporate account, so even open source code wouldn't run without it; macOS dev setup is fragile.

t: What antitrust law permits among competing investors
w: Competitors may meet and share industry info; only agreements restraining competition violate Sherman Act; parallel conduct alone is not illegal.

t: Why classroom tech procurement is so hard
w: Schools must satisfy legal compliance, simplicity, price limits, long lifespans and layered bureaucracy simultaneously, which explains why vendors struggle.

t: Most tech founders were in their 30s
w: A running list of founders' ages at founding shows most successful tech companies were started by people in their 30s or older.

t: Practical advice for 501(c)(3) status for open source
w: Hire a nonprofit attorney rather than DIY, and explain copyleft to the IRS as public benefit, not private benefit to for-profits.

t: Leading AI researchers' views on AI danger
w: Quotes from Ng, Bengio, LeCun, Brooks and others show top researchers consider AI doom fears premature and distracting.

t: Why array languages avoid abstraction overhead
w: Terse array operations let code stay flat instead of splitting into many functions, which often improves readability in practice.

t: Why classical music often repeats so much
w: Pre-recording composers repeated ideas because listeners could not replay; modern audiences find that stretch overlong, and dynamic range matters.

t: Structural reasons US medical care costs so much
w: Employer-paid insurance is pre-tax while out-of-pocket spending is after-tax, and licensing and long residencies restrict doctor supply.

t: Practical gotchas for moving to Canada
w: Immigration consultants exist for good reason: apply for health coverage immediately on arrival, and expect to rebuild banking and credit history from scratch.

t: Quant traders versus engineers in high-frequency trading
w: Traders earn a share of profits and need steady psychology, while non-trading engineers earn salaries; the roles differ sharply.

t: Why patent pools reduce licensing risk
w: Pools let competitors share standards on fair terms, offload licensing work, and mitigate the risk of unknown patents.

t: Why Berkeley moved SICP from Scheme to Python
w: Insider account: the switch came from lack of Scheme instructors, not rejecting SICP ideas; Scheme lambda power comes from proper closures.

t: V8 isolates need OS sandboxing, processes add limits
w: Isolates in one process give weak isolation; separate processes with cgroups, namespaces or VMs give stronger limits.

t: Why AR glasses face optics, power, and latency limits
w: Focus sits at distance, so lens overlays blur; glasses lack power and compute, and ground overlays need recognition within about 11ms.

t: Where to get CS2/CS3 installers after activation shutdown
w: CS2 got activation-free installers and generic serials; CS3 offline serials came via Adobe Account until about 2020, then were removed.

t: Why card companies distrust new merchants
w: Merchants bear US chargeback liability and card-reader ownership makes duplicated cards cashable, so fraud systems err cautious.

t: Correcting common PHP language myths
w: Object equality compares contents with == but identity with ===; foo()->method() has always parsed; + is addition and . is concatenation, unlike JavaScript.

t: Research-backed hiring beats grilling on hobbies
w: Schmidt and Hunter's validity research shows job-relevant structured selection predicts performance better than unstructured interviews; a referenced FAQ collects the literature.

t: GrapheneOS versus CalyxOS network permissions
w: GrapheneOS's network toggle blocks direct and indirect access, while CalyxOS lets apps bypass its firewall through INTERNET-gated APIs; concrete privacy architecture comparison.

t: How Yelp review removal worked for sales staff
w: Sales reps couldn't remove reviews; removal needed customer service approval, and removals rarely changed sales outcomes.

t: Four conversation books converge on the same elements
w: Difficult Conversations, NVC, Crucial Conversations and Getting Past No share core steps; NVC's edge is concrete recipes, while the others explain why.

t: How Minimoog-style synth controls map to organ pipes
w: Footage labels like 16' and 8' are organ pipe lengths giving octaves. LO is a subsonic setting used for modulation on real synths.

t: Why lead toxicity varies: metallothionein production
w: Metallothionein proteins bind metals for use or removal. Genetic predisposition and environment explain why only some exposed people show symptoms.

t: Paul Graham's 2010 predictions: innovation, biotech, metrics
w: Empires fall when people cannot make money building things. Metrics shape behaviour, since you make what you measure, and efficient markets spread via information.

t: How a record gigapixel London panorama was shot
w: Four synchronized cameras on precision robots, 128GB cards, and laptops for copying; shooting took three days after two days of setup.

t: Why a storage system chose Rust over Go
w: Explains heap-size-driven choice of Rust: bit-packing, perfect hashing, stack allocation and FFI, with GC pauses irrelevant for non-latency-sensitive workloads.

t: How macros are used in a real Lisp application
w: Arc's codebase uses macros heavily, sometimes for code called only once, where a plain function would otherwise be the natural choice.

t: Banking liquidity problem and the 1918 leased wire
w: Banks lend customer deposits, so settlement systems must balance liquidity; each technical change created new exploits, such as the 1918 leased wire.

t: How Urbit's event-driven server OS works
w: Each input is a transaction that fully applies or not; persistent links give exactly-once messaging; identity is built in as the instance key.

t: Why big providers block small mail servers
w: Even with SPF, DKIM, DMARC, matching reverse DNS and clean IPs, large providers may reject a tiny self-hosted server, so reputation outweighs correct configuration.

t: Checking whether iPhone location logs really track you
w: Unique MAC and timestamp checks plus coordinate rounding show the cache is not continuous tracking; a reusable way to audit local databases.

t: Why Ruby is hard to optimize versus Lisp
w: Ruby's easy syntax hides scope, data representation and memory layout, making it hard to optimize; Lisp demands more precision while staying expressive.

t: Pilot reports of MCAS nose-down events
w: Pilots' ASRS reports describe MAX 8 nose-down pitching after departure with no obvious cause, which crews countered by disconnecting autopilot.

t: A minimal kitchen: what to buy and skip
w: Buy a cheap Fibrox knife, skip butcher block and sharpeners, and keep one color board for meat to reduce cross-contamination.

t: Why the semantic web failed in practice
w: Publishers got no payoff for semantic markup, most people model poorly, and reasoners were immature; the field kept rebranding failed ideas.

t: Hiring advice: sell the role before screening
w: Sell candidates on the role before demanding anything, and avoid subjective prompts like code you're proud of that cannot be benchmarked.

t: Why modern board games outpaced 80s designs
w: Modern designs such as Dominion and Puerto Rico cut idle time and dice-and-lookup overhead, with move selection enabling deep tactical planning.

t: Why builds should pin exact dependency versions
w: Builds should default to the exact dependency versions the author used; changing one must be an explicit user action, not an install side effect.

t: How starchitect skyscraper designs get built
w: Star architects sketch the shape while junior teams solve the real problems on tight, often unpaid, deadlines, which explains practical flaws.

t: Keep licensing contracts alongside source code
w: Source provenance depends on contracts; acquisitions scatter records, so archive rights agreements alongside copies of the code.

t: Why role-based hostnames beat theme-based names
w: Themed names encourage blaming machines and rely on memory; role names aid config management and alerting but need a service database at scale.

t: Why bug bounties lose to black-market exploit prices
w: Bounties work only if payouts are worth a finder's time yet well below criminal buyers' prices; otherwise bugs get sold instead of reported.

t: Why flat profiles and optimizing compilers still matter
w: Google-scale C++ profiles have grown flatter over time, and GCC beat experts on interpreter loops, countering claims that optimizing compilers are obsolete.

t: Stack ranking: why forced curves reward politics
w: Forced stack ranking predetermines firing and promotion percentages regardless of performance; asking whether a company uses it reveals its culture.

t: Why HN's comment markup rewrite was hard
w: HN's presentation was tangled with server logic, and scrapers depended on table markup, so changing markup risked breaking many apps.

t: Hiring by short take-home and live code review
w: A one-hour take-home judged for tests and clarity, then an in-person session on the candidate's laptop, screens for real problem-solving over years of language experience.

t: Survival tips for an unplanned freefall
w: Surface area is the only way to slow down, relaxing muscles greatly improves survival odds, and aiming for trees, snow or skylights matters.

t: Why Zenefits repriced shares: a fraud settlement
w: Repricing works as a de facto settlement: undisclosed compliance fraud makes prior-round purchases securities fraud, so the valuation is corrected toward what it should have been.

t: Why online reviews hit small businesses hardest
w: Reviews spread fast, persist, and get ranked; a few one-stars dominate small businesses' visibility, unlike word of mouth that faded.

t: German court ruling on Facebook's default consent
w: Default-on settings and buried imprint fail explicit informed consent; German law applies regardless of Facebook's Irish-jurisdiction claim.

t: AngularJS providers exist for pre-start configuration
w: Providers are configured in config blocks via the Provider suffix before use; services and factories build instances differently.

t: Why replacing comments with methods can lose context
w: Turning commented blocks into methods ignores shared variables and spawns classes and boilerplate; comments can carry context worth keeping.

t: Why IPv6 is harder to run on a LAN
w: SLAAC, multicast discovery, multi-homing and unmemorable addresses add moving parts that IPv4 LANs never needed, so DNS becomes essential.

t: Why IPv6 adoption lags despite address exhaustion
w: NAT, tunneling, and idle public address blocks reduce pressure on most users to adopt IPv6, so demand curves stay flat.

t: Why Shenzhen's dense supplier cluster speeds up hardware
w: Fabs, mold shops and distributors within 2km enable cheap rapid prototyping, and apparent redundancy carries collective learning across suppliers.

t: A gentle intro: pointers store addresses, star dereferences
w: A pointer stores an address; the star in a declaration only marks the type, while the star in an expression reads the value there.

t: Why Chennai's water crisis runs deeper than drought
w: Borewells mask the shortage for many households, while a leaky, unmetered pipe network and weak government ownership of water persist.

t: Why USPS delays come from the flats collapse
w: COVID collapsed letter and magazine volume while packages surged; flats sorters cannot handle packages, so USPS shut them down and cut overtime.

t: What startups and big companies each teach
w: Startups teach quick cobbling and uncertainty; large companies teach systemic fixes, scaling architecture, and research value.

t: Why second screens rarely beat a single display
w: Switching attention between screens costs time; an auxiliary screen must beat the same feature on one display to justify itself.

t: Tight campaigns and negative keywords make ads profitable
w: Match landing pages to exact keywords, add negatives every few days, and track sales back to cut wasteful clicks.

t: How SystemXVI's repository and restarters work
w: Init stays small; a hash-table service repository stores instance state and properties, while delegated restarters supervise services, similar to Solaris SMF.

t: Why roaming passkeys still carry phishing risk
w: Syncing passkeys to the cloud by design means attestation can't enforce device binding; they still beat passwords, but phishing resistance has limits.

t: Why early equity rounds can hurt founders
w: Equity rounds force a valuation when founders are weakest and add strings; founder loans, convertible notes, or services revenue may be better early options.

t: Why patent examiners reject impossible inventions
w: Patents must enable a skilled person to build the invention without undue experimentation; examiners reject perpetual-motion-style claims, though this one still issued.

t: Free TPU research compute for ML hackers
w: TPU Research Cloud gives independent ML developers free TPU access, enabling self-hosted inference APIs that once required institutional budgets.

t: Why native plugins like NaCl conflict with web standards
w: Proprietary plugins lock users in; Pepper's Chrome-tied API can't be reimplemented by other browsers, so standards must keep up.

t: Binary-trees benchmark: GC languages versus manual memory
w: Allocation-heavy benchmark shows C++ and Rust beat GC languages; Go trails most GC languages at 12 seconds.

t: Why cancer research has a decade-long feedback loop
w: Cancer research's OODA loop runs 10-20 years, so errors and irreproducible studies persist far longer than they would in software development.

t: Why dark themes strain some eyes: optics explained
w: Pupil dilation and lens accommodation explain how focus and depth of field shift with bright pixels on dark backgrounds, affecting readability.

t: Why EU privacy law rests on purpose limitation
w: France's 1978 SAFARI backlash produced the purpose-of-data principle that underpins European data protection law.

t: Why musicians earn little from albums and tours
w: Insider view: recording costs stay high, merch and concerts pay poorly, and most artists barely make money from live performance.

t: Distribution-free tests for zero-day anomaly detection
w: Multidimensional hypothesis tests let you pick a false alarm rate and get it in practice, when healthy behavior is statistically stable.

t: Twin and adoption studies show genetic vulnerability
w: Twin and adoption studies point to genetic vulnerability; researchers seek endophenotypes to guide treatment, but none are yet established for major mental illness.

t: Why hand-built common sense may not reach AGI
w: Manually adding common-sense rules to Cyc accrued heavy technical debt and lacked a self-directed learning path toward general intelligence.

t: Why Java's mobile licensing drove the Google lawsuit
w: Google implemented part of Java without a mobile license, undercutting Sun's main Java revenue, which is why the suit mattered.

t: Why Paul Graham's essays provoke so much reaction
w: Minimalist, vivid essay style strips out phatic reassurance and softening, so readers project their own passions onto the text.

t: Practical rules for building performant systems
w: Measure before optimising, prefer fewer moving parts, learn database tools like EXPLAIN, and understand the data before building schemas.

t: Why escape from Pompeii was nearly impossible
w: Pyroclastic flows travel 10-100 m/s, faster than walking, so escape needed a route perpendicular to the wind, uphill to the northeast.

t: Moving WordPress from Apache prefork to nginx
w: Prefork mod_php collapsed under traffic spikes; MPM worker plus pre-launched PHP over FastCGI fixed the scaling problem.

t: How Google mixes Bing links and its own modules
w: Bing supplies most traditional web links, while knowledge and local modules are Google's own; top-of-page modules get far more engagement.

t: Linux is the kernel; the userspace stack is separate
w: Linux is the kernel; systemd, glibc, GNOME and similar userspace are separate, so Android-based systems like GrapheneOS are still Linux distributions.

t: Why XMPP struggles: message IDs and multi-device routing
w: XMPP lacks unique message IDs and sends messages only to the last-active device, so multi-device chat needs fragile carbons workarounds.

t: Solar output varies and has driven past climates
w: Total solar irradiance fluctuates over daily, 11-year and millennial cycles, and has been a primary driver of Earth's climate history.

t: Why algebraic types make ASTs easy in ML
w: A few lines of ML variant types express an AST, while C++ needs tags, unions and manual memory management for the same tree.

t: Why always-online three-tier apps break on sync
w: Always-online architectures fail when connections drop and struggle with multi-client sync, often forcing full reloads to recover missed updates.

t: Why regulation slows biotech more than software
w: Human-safety rules encode old testing standards and punish errors harshly, so proven adaptive trial designs stay stuck at the FDA.

t: Why publishing costs drive ebook prices
w: Editors reject most manuscripts, so acquisition costs are high, and books lack perfect substitutes, which weakens price competition.

t: How standardized tests get written and why they're bland
w: Tests are shaped by legislation and many-stakeholder committees with cautious piloting, so distinctive teaching styles rarely fit the format.

t: Why traffic estimators misread TechCrunch
w: Third-party traffic estimates diverged from internal analytics; insider says the outlet accepts a 1-2% error rate to publish quickly.

t: How foreigners' names are registered in Japan
w: Explains Japanese official name rules, nicknames, and how a koseki family register conflicts with Latin-script names and passports.

t: Why datacenter-hosted darknet sites get found
w: Tor hides endpoint addresses but not traffic volume, so datacenter operators can spot high-bandwidth Tor servers and image them.

t: Disparate impact: discrimination without intent
w: Explains disparate impact from Griggs v. Duke Power, and why precise Facebook job-ad targeting by age or gender raises legal risk.

t: Common misreadings of heritability in intelligence research
w: Corrects common misunderstandings of heritability for human intelligence and points to behavioral genetics literature as the place to learn current research.

t: Why hospital computerization clashes with clinical culture
w: ER nurse explains how medicine's slow, safety-first change culture clashes with fast IT cycles, so computerized workflows can add risk.

t: How DVD region encryption sparked Linux DeCSS
w: CSS encrypted discs with per-region keys and no Linux player was offered, so enthusiasts reverse engineered the scheme, the origin of DeCSS.

t: Dissecting a malicious applet that robbed Mt.Gox
w: Shows the method: fetch the applet jar, decompile with JD-GUI, and find the obfuscated URL that logged victims' hosts and OS details.

t: Practical obstacles to moving a city administration to Linux
w: Windows-only specialist software, vendor drivers for ID hardware and staff retraining were bigger obstacles than the OS itself, per a former employee.

t: Employment is a risk swap; build a cash cushion first
w: Employers absorb business risk for most upside; holding 18-24 months of burn in cash lets you start a company without debt pressure.

t: Why blockchain can't settle contested land ownership
w: A blockchain only records what it is given; bribery, conflicting claims and court rulings still need institutions, so the ledger solves none of it.

t: Choose-your-own-adventure ML reading list for engineers
w: Organized by prerequisites, beginner and intermediate texts; Metacademy and Ng's CS229 are good entry points for practitioners.

t: Lotus Notes differential work factor explained
w: Notes' key strength was deliberately reduced for export, and the design was publicly documented at RSA, unlike covert backdoors.

t: How much Labor Commissioner rulings really mean
w: Hearings are informal and employee-leaning, so decisions carry limited precedent weight unless upheld in court.

t: Starlink as a planetary atmosphere sensor
w: Starlink's many radio links through the atmosphere can be inverted tomographically, like CT scans, to map weather in real time.

t: What standard technical interviews actually assess
w: Interviewers use standard problems to gauge how much hand-holding a candidate needs; strong candidates understand the purpose and think aloud.

t: How System76 prepares hardware for Linux
w: Vendors co-design products with OEMs, fix firmware for Linux kernels, then upstream fixes so all distributions benefit.

t: Mathematicians' critiques of US math teaching
w: Several mathematicians argue US K-12 math trails high-performing systems; their cited papers form a useful reading list.

t: Short selling versus manipulative squeezes
w: Shorting is legal, but the SEC prohibits schemes that manipulate price or availability to force a short squeeze.

t: Income-based repayment versus income share plans
w: A 30-year 6% loan costs about 216% of principal; IBR depends on discretionary income and spousal tax-filing rules.

t: Why logic proofs differ from textbook mathematical proofs
w: Logic proofs justify every line by a rule or theorem, unlike informal math proofs that skip steps; the aim is syntax-semantics precision.

t: How Japan's family register enables caste discrimination
w: Parish and temple records and the koseki family register can reveal burakumin or Korean ancestry, so churches refuse ancestry investigations.

t: CRUD line-of-business programming versus algorithmic systems work
w: Programmers split into LOB glue-code developers and algorithmic systems engineers; bootcamp advocacy reflects the first group's reality.

t: How public friend lists reveal private friendships
w: Friendships are two-way, so a public friend list on either side exposes the private user's friends; this is why the leak persists.

t: Reader macro for brace hash literals in Common Lisp
w: set-macro-character with read-delimited-list can turn brace syntax into a hash table at read time, though hash table tuning matters.

t: Most tech founders were not garage kids
w: Lists dozens of major founders with ages at founding, showing most were 28 to 50.

t: Why 90-day option windows hurt leaving staff
w: Standard ISO terms force leavers to pay exercise cost and AMT on illiquid shares; early exercise avoids this.

t: Why L6 promotions are deliberately hard
w: Stack-ranked committees and a lowered promotion target make L6 rare, and senior pay depends heavily on equity.

t: Why software markets tend toward winner-take-all
w: Zero marginal cost lets the leader reinvest, and one 40-hour developer beats two 20-hour ones due to communication overhead.

t: Mutable IOArray updates in Haskell, with working code
w: Haskell has mutable arrays via Data.Array.IO; readArray and writeArray give ordinary in-place mutation in IO.

t: How Android's permission model evolved toward granular controls
w: Early Android granted all permissions at install; background camera use lasted until Android P, and broad storage access until about Android 10.

t: How brokerage settlement float works
w: Sold stock takes about two days to clear; brokers fund trades from a float pool, so mass withdrawals can drain it.

t: Why Argentines turn to Bitcoin for savings
w: Capital controls and inflation make dollar savings hard to access, so people use real estate or Bitcoin to move money beyond restrictions.

t: How failed startups get liquidated and acquired
w: Failed startups liquidate assets under creditor pressure, and acquirers exploit founders and employees who are upside down on equity.

t: Immigrant founder share can mislead through aggregation

t: How ILR proficiency levels assess spoken language
w: Expert rubric-based assessment using ILR levels, separating pronunciation from discourse, circumlocution and sustained communication when judging a speaker's Mandarin.

t: Personal liability for unpaid withheld payroll taxes
w: Explains IRC 6672: withheld payroll taxes are held in trust, so any responsible officer can face personal liability for the full amount.

t: Why single-viewer streams can count as public performance
w: Explains the public performance doctrine: one owned copy repeatedly shown to individual patrons in private rooms was held a public performance in Redd Horne.

t: Why mainframes sell reliability and high-volume transactions
w: Insider explanation: mainframes target near-zero downtime for many short transactions, such as card validation, where economies depend on uninterrupted service.

t: Port scanning with an event loop in Ruby
w: Event-driven connects with a capped in-flight count let one process scan all 65535 ports without threads.

t: Why SQL resists composition and abstraction
w: SQL fragments can't be composed into larger expressions, so functions degenerate into redundant code; SQL is inspired by the relational model, not equal to it.

t: Standard math path from algebra to measure theory
w: Outlines the usual sequence from high school algebra and geometry through linear algebra, ODEs, topology and measure theory, with computing relevance.

t: What contracting really costs beyond the rate
w: Contractors earn more because they absorb unpaid networking, admin, taxes and downtime that salaried employers otherwise subsidize.

t: Go far outruns Node.js in an HTTP benchmark
w: On 10,000 requests, single-process Node took 46s, clustered Node 17s and Go 3.5s, with full ab output showing the method.

t: Reading football formations from TV footage
w: Count tight ends and backfield alignment to infer run versus pass; defenders' positions can be inferred from the offensive setup.

t: Why hits can't be predicted in music
w: Hits are usually surprises, and disrupting labels means understanding points, mechanical royalties and publishing, which the labels rely on.

t: Why cumulative diffs speed up apt updates
w: Debian does not generate cumulative diffs, forcing clients to fetch many small patches; at Cydia scale this makes a large speedup worth it.

t: Low returns hurt retirement more than mortgages help
w: Lower expected investment returns raise the savings needed for retirement, often outweighing the benefit of cheap mortgage financing for a buyer.

t: The four group axioms explained with addition
w: A group needs identity, inverses, associativity and closure; abelian groups also commute, illustrated with addition and matrix examples.

t: Go's toolchain descends from Plan 9
w: Go's compiler and linker inherit Plan 9's special C dialect and toolchain, which explains the self-contained build and its bootstrap history.

t: Why voluntary online polls can't describe populations
w: Self-selected responses are not a random sample, so HN poll results cannot infer the community's geographic or age distribution.

t: Why the shopping cart patent was invalidated
w: The Federal Circuit ruled on obviousness on its own initiative, despite a jury verdict and earlier patent re-exam approvals.

t: Why most Uber-for-X services fail on LTV
w: Infrequent services make customer acquisition costs exceed lifetime value, unlike Uber's frequent rides or Geico's retention-heavy model.

t: SAFe borrows heavily from Reinertsen's flow principles
w: A SAFe-certified practitioner says SAFe is about 80% based on Reinertsen's book, so reading the source is more useful than rigid training.

w: Starting with linear systems motivates vector spaces, since many proofs reduce to row-reducing a matrix; the textbook order should follow that dependency.

w: Provide init scripts with start/stop/status, drop root privileges, use config files not XML, ship deb/rpm packaging, and fix bugs systems teams report.

t: Why Bitcoin miners keep mining at a loss
w: Difficulty and hashrate track sunk costs and bets on future price, not current price, so much mining is unprofitable.

t: Why frameworks exist: the raw DOM is hard for state
w: Raw DOM suits static pages but stateful UIs are hard; React composes components while frameworks add routing, state persistence and builds.

t: Why unconventional engineering can win and still hurt
w: Radical designs can outperform, but their nonstandardness raises later maintenance and hiring costs; conventions are often just habits.

t: Monitor emissions: Tempest, Van Eck, and EMR
w: CRT patterns can broadcast audio to a nearby AM radio, and LCD cables leak signals; these emissions are real side channels.

t: How a photo startup squeezed its AWS costs
w: Insider account of cutting cloud spend by optimizing S3, EC2 and RDS, and the argument that large photo platforms run their own storage at scale.

t: A near-fatal rhabdomyolysis case from CrossFit
w: Rhabdomyolysis can follow an intense first-day workout; inability to walk the next morning is a warning sign.

t: Idiomatic Go uses interfaces, not type switches
w: Porting Rust-style enum message handling to Go with type switches over interface{} is unidiomatic; Go's small interfaces express the same design.

t: What makes Facebook's engineering culture distinctive
w: High hiring bar enables autonomy: engineers choose work, no OWNERS gatekeeping, and impact rewards productivity and removing bad code.

t: Reproducing Heartbleed private key theft on nginx
w: Heartbleed leaks server memory; the author reports dumping an nginx private key in one request, with setup steps.

w: Additive abstractions add capabilities to an underlying concept and tend to leak; aligning ones hide detail and model differently.

t: Why present-day innovation is invisible to us
w: McLuhan's point: we perceive an environment only after it is superseded, so the present always looks dull and ordinary.

t: Three real sources of competitive advantage
w: Durable advantages: secret roadmapped tech that keeps you ahead, customer habits and switching costs, and market leadership that attracts more customers.

t: Why CNC joinery mainly serves hobbyists
w: Professional shops rely on dedicated machines and jigs; a hobby CNC speeds results but doesn't build the hand skill custom work demands.

t: How the petrodollar ties oil to dollar demand
w: Oil sold only in dollars makes importers hold USD reserves, sustaining dollar demand and recycling surpluses into US securities.

t: CCR5 delta32 may stem from smallpox
w: Mice with the mutation still get plague, and several studies point to smallpox as the likelier selective pressure.

t: Who pays when Apple refunds an app
w: Developers must reimburse Apple for refunded sales, and Apple keeps its commission even when a purchase is refunded.

t: Java dual licensing and OpenJDK's GPL classpath exception
w: Java had commercial and GPL tracks; the GPL classpath exception means applications on OpenJDK are not bound by copyleft.

w: Commenter argues Rust and WebAssembly gains also rest on optimizer heuristics, not spec guarantees, and WebAssembly is still experimental in LLVM.

t: Four ways Tesla owners unlock their cars
w: Bluetooth, key card and fob work locally without servers; only remote app unlocks depend on the internet and Tesla's backend.

t: Why avoid hourly billing as a consultant
w: Hourly billing penalizes efficiency, hides ramp-up costs and multiplies invoices; price projects by value.

t: Training yourself to think in images
w: Bilingual thinkers form concrete imagery; whiteboard practice can build that skill, citing Sapir-Whorf research.

t: Why 21700 cells may trade power for capacity
w: Larger cells have lower power density for the same weight, so Tesla must cut performance draw or add cells and weight.

t: Halting is decidable for finite-memory machines
w: Finite-state machines must repeat states, so cycle detection decides halting in principle, though the state space can be huge.

t: Why game-based algebra can hide meaning
w: Students can manipulate symbols without understanding why or connecting equations to real problems; games risk teaching rules alone.

w: Sentences like 汉字好学 are not shortened copula forms; Chinese uses stative adjective predicates, so generic lessons mislead.

t: Racket's documentation and language-building strengths
w: Racket's Scribble docs far outclass Common Lisp's, and Racket's language-building tools shine for domain-specific languages.

t: Why SaaS vendors price out low-probability customers
w: Most new subscription businesses fail and cost more than they earn, so vendors either set high minimums or cheap trials as a bet.

t: Why bulk recording pays off in retroactive tracing
w: Recording everything lets analysts rewind from an attack to the bomber's staging site, turning surplus data into a tracing tool.

t: Storytelling as hacking investors' evaluation
w: Storytelling hacks investors' evaluation, so funding favors good storytellers over strong technology, mirroring schooling that rewards gaming bad tests.

w: Indefinite-length items force decoders to accept unbounded streams, creating unbounded memory use and ambiguity, unlike definite-length MessagePack-style encodings.

t: Why Bitcoin matters in middling kleptocracies
w: In countries like Argentina with capital controls and few savings options, Bitcoin offers a way to move and store value that local banks cannot.

t: Ancient farm tenure: owners, tenants and families
w: Ancient land was mostly small family plots, with rent in kind to tenants and few large estates, the largest held by the state.

t: Lippmann: moral codes rest on stereotyped facts
w: Each moral code rests on stereotypes about psychology and history, and the same view of human nature rarely persists across all of them.

t: What Wolfram's simplest-programs claim actually says
w: Wolfram's real claim is that the simplest nontrivial programs with space and time can produce complex behavior, which a rebuttal misread as trivial.

t: What systemd's service status and journal improve
w: Integrated status output with PID, cgroup and logs makes debugging services easier than upstart's terse status, as a Debian analysis argues.

t: Why seizing a chip fab wouldn't yield chips
w: Fabs depend on complex materials, software and staff; subtle contamination like the 1987 IBM Hera problem shows how fragile yields are.

w: Theatres keep about half of box office, marketing can match production cost, and home video has historically covered most profit.

t: Early text selection models: Cedar, Tioga, SunView
w: Cedar used three mouse buttons and modifier keys for consistent actions everywhere; SunView and NeWS offered a quick-paste mode preserving selection.

t: Why the TrackPoint was invented: hand travel time
w: Selker measured 0.75-1.75 seconds to move a hand between keyboard and mouse in 1984, motivating the TrackPoint.

t: How the Universal Postal Convention enables cheap shipping
w: UPU's 1870s-era agreement sets cross-border postal rates so importing countries' postal services absorb costs, making cheap imports possible.

w: Forth lacks standard dynamic memory, while PostScript offers homoiconic code, dictionaries and first-class functions, making it more Lisp-like.

w: Large applicant pools and committee discretion let schools fill niche needs like violas or regional quotas, so niche traits can decide admissions.

t: Why Alsup's ruling matters for API copyright
w: Alsup's ruling offers a clearer approach to API copyright than case-by-case Ninth Circuit structure, sequence and organization precedent.

t: Why experienced teams beat new grads in chip design
w: Successful microprocessor teams have long-working veterans; new-grad teams often burn $100M without a competitive product.

w: Cadence raises SWF's payload, history, and duration limits, runs on Cassandra or MySQL, and stays actively developed.

t: Spotting flaws in a dubious garage physics experiment
w: Check mechanical artifacts, separate modeled from measured values, and include baselines before trusting reported forces or fringes.

t: What Cloudflare's keyless SSL does and doesn't protect
w: Keeping keys on-premises stops passive reading of traffic and key handover, but the provider still sees all decrypted traffic, so the benefit is limited.

t: Why rule-based code beat ACLs for compliance logic
w: One compliance rule across 1,000 users and containers needed 270,000 ACL entries; 400 lines of Ruby were auditable instead.

t: How NYC rental brokers and the 40x rule work
w: Landlords expect annual pre-tax income of 40x monthly rent; brokers take 12-15% of annual rent, and fee-free listings are often bait-and-switch.

t: What running a high-volume assembly line involves
w: Adding capacity means working the bottleneck; sampling-based QA lets some defects through; labor balancing and forklift accidents can stall whole lines.

t: Why Hokkien text doesn't fit Mandarin-centric Unicode
w: Chinese varieties share written characters unevenly; Unicode's Chinese set favors Mandarin, so some Hokkien characters look unfamiliar to Mandarin readers.

t: Tracking mystery aircraft with RTL-SDR and FAA records
w: Obscure companies with PO-box addresses register many aircraft; an RTL-SDR dongle lets you log ADS-B pings to identify them.

t: Three routes into algorithmic trading
w: Break in through MIT-style hiring, join a prop shop and build tooling, or join a trading firm technically and move up; each route has trade-offs.

t: Index documentation by concept, not just function name
w: Reference manuals only help when you know the function name; concept-indexed docs let users discover functions by what they want to do.

t: Why many patents are mere implementations
w: Judged by skilled-in-the-art standards, many patents only apply obvious implementations that engineers reach independently, so obviousness tests are applied too loosely.

t: Work-sample tests beat puzzles for hiring
w: Research favors work-sample tests for hiring, since a manager who understands the job can design one that predicts good performance.

t: How Robinhood's order flow payments are disclosed
w: Brokers' Rule 606 reports reveal per-share payments for order flow, e.g. under $0.0025 from Knight; the disclosure is buried but findable.

t: How Amazon's stock comp amplifies share risk
w: Amazon sizes RSUs assuming 15% stock growth and caps comp at band ceilings, so falling shares cut pay sharply while upside is limited.

w: Interviews are hostile and depleting, so their results reflect stress as much as skill; hiring should expect limited signal from one session.

t: Why tags beat folders but still break down
w: Tags let items sit in many categories, but manual typing, typos and global-variable-like sprawl hurt at scale.

t: When Postgres full-text search beats a dedicated engine
w: Postgres search suits early projects, small teams and quick features without a second datastore; dedicated engines win on heavy search.

t: Silicon Valley's surplus electronics market in the 80s
w: Dealers bought decommissioned gear for pennies, letting hobbyists buy costly parts cheaply until companies stopped churning hardware.

t: Bytecode weaving enables green threads on the JVM
w: Quasar adds green threads and channels via bytecode weaving; ProGuard, JaCoCo and RoboVM show tool-level bytecode manipulation's value.

t: Why LED bulbs need heatsinks and certification budgets
w: Most LED bulb energy becomes heat, so heatsinks are needed regardless of WiFi; certification can exceed $100K.

t: Two levels of practical cryptography: design and software
w: Practical cryptography splits into cryptographic design and software design, and most people work at only one of those levels.

w: Haskell and Scala use static Hindley-Milner inference; Erlang and Clojure are dynamic, trading compile-time safety for runtime flexibility.

w: Unlike gold, a bitcoin's location is a blockchain record, so a protocol-level failure could hit all holders at once.

t: Robotics expert rebuts automation hype with specifics
w: Self-checkouts often extend store hours rather than only cutting staff, and self-driving cars remain far from broad deployment.

t: Why BFT consensus fits Libra's consortium design
w: BFT is standard in blockchain; Libra as a multi-implementation consortium protocol makes byzantine fault tolerance a logical choice.

w: Interns' feedback counts toward half their full-time interviews, a big advantage; even strong engineers might struggle cold.

t: Scaling contract review by materiality
w: Review effort should match what is material: routine contracts need little review, while material terms need customizing and protections for each party.

t: Serious postmodern works to read instead of Sokal
w: Recommends Deleuze, Badiou and Latour directly; many postmodernists were trained scientists engaging math and science seriously.

t: A simple model of educational success factors
w: Models success as intelligence, family, peers and teaching, suggesting teacher quality is only one of several factors.

t: Why spam filtering is a constant arms race
w: Spam is profitable on open trust-based email; filters need ongoing ML work, and insider bribery can defeat technical defenses.

t: Choosing math books that build intuition
w: Most textbooks organize the author's view; Pugh's Real Mathematical Analysis is written to be internalized, not just a list of theorems.

t: Julia at scale: missing interfaces and static checks
w: On a 10k-line Julia codebase, missing interfaces, static typing and error types hurt, and JET.jl struggled to scale.

t: Practical off-grid power and water system design
w: Off-grid living needs real capacity: solar, hydro and wind with lead-acid storage, plus staged water filtration; rationing often fails.

t: Core contract law principles behind online terms
w: Contracts need mutual assent judged by a reasonable-person standard plus consideration, which keeps commercial deals predictable.

t: Why FreeBSD's integrated base system matters
w: FreeBSD ships kernel and userland as one system; kqueue and tuned ports explain its historical web-serving performance edge.

t: Practical pros and cons of Crystal language
