t: Refinement as a lattice of abstraction in TLA+
w: Properties true at a coarser abstraction also hold at finer ones; TLA+ can state abstract algorithms that programming languages cannot express.

t: What jurisdictional security for email really means
w: Hosting location alone protects little; corporate seat, banking, officers, DNS and certificate authority all determine legal exposure.

t: Self-teach engineering from top-school textbooks

t: Elementary teachers lack area-multiplication understanding
w: Area of a rectangle underpins multiplication and the distributive law; many elementary teachers lack this, a clear training gap.

t: Why small cities struggle with public transit
w: Transit needs critical mass; low average bus loads make buses more polluting per passenger-mile than cars, undermining car-replacement plans.

t: Calling Congress beats emailing or petitions
w: Staffers tally daily call topics while letters and petitions are ignored; call both DC and home offices, and attend town halls.

t: How patent prosecution usually plays out
w: First office actions are rarely final; expect more rejections and continued examinations, and claim wording matters more than the spec.

t: Why type erasure helps the JVM host languages
w: Erasure keeps the runtime uniform for other languages; performance specialization can exist without reified generics.

t: Engineers reason about programs with TLA+
w: State machines underlie computation and simple math reasons about them; TLA+, SPIN, and Alloy suit engineers better than Coq.

t: Why visa holders cannot earn outside income
w: Work visas typically limit income to the sponsoring employer; tax reporting can reveal other income, risking deportation and a ban.

t: Speed reading claims versus research evidence
w: Controlled testing of champion speed readers, as cited here, finds the advertised gains are limited and comprehension is the tradeoff.

w: Developers ship duct-tape solutions, engineers build scalable systems, computer scientists chase theory; Google and Facebook cultures differ accordingly.

t: Budgeting for an ergonomic workstation

t: Why CouchDB map-reduce views are slow
w: Views serialize JSON twice through an external couchjs process on an old SpiderMonkey, with no streaming between steps.

t: Why Objective-C feels hard: C memory and silent errors
w: Objective-C mixes four memory schemes and C APIs; missing sentinels and @ literals compile with warnings but crash at runtime.

t: Why the fanless Sandia cooler transfers heat well
w: Heat crosses a thin rotating air gap; impeller rotation breaks the boundary layer and sweeps dust off the fins.

t: Why Symbian and MeeGo were not viable for Nokia
w: MeeGo was far from shippable by 2010, and Symbian's UI made basic search-as-you-type a multi-team engineering problem.

t: Definition of an operating system versus distribution
w: An OS is software that provides and limits hardware access; distributions bundle utilities, so naming follows who wrote what.

t: Why rendered video looks fake: light and color
w: Rendering multiplies colors, which has no physical basis; the eye averages photons, so approximations miss what real light does.

t: Why WordPress has an inherently risky design
w: Shared auth tables for admins and commenters, template code execution, and concatenated SQL create a broad attack surface for WordPress.

t: How the rat-neuron flight sim actually worked
w: The 'brain flies F-22' result sampled firing of two neurons mapped to roll and elevation error, with responses deadened over time to drive control.

t: Reading SBCL's inferred function type declarations
w: SBCL infers function types such as FUNCTION with VALUES and uses static analysis for optimization, delegating checks to runtime where types overlap.

t: Insider history of Guile at Cygnus
w: The author recounts earlier failed Scheme extension attempts and how Cygnus's free-software strategy shaped the project.

t: Why real systems value evolvable schemas over type elegance
w: The hard part of engineering is changing deployed code. Protobuf's evolution rules matter more than type-theoretic elegance, which does not guarantee safe change.

t: Lineage of realtime visual music programming tools
w: Traces Hookup, Image/ine and Isadora from MIT and STEIM, showing how early realtime visual languages shaped music performance software.

t: How AT Protocol signed repositories work
w: Each user runs a git-like repository of signed commits; signed records let anyone verify authenticity without polling the home server.

t: Why Node.js needs callbacks where Erlang doesn't
w: Synchronous waiting blocks Node's single thread, so concurrency must be continuation-based; Erlang's lightweight processes make blocking-style calls safe via message passing.

t: Why Markdeep breaks on raw < in code
w: Markdeep puts Markdown in the body, so browsers parse text like '<string' as HTML; TeXMe's textarea keeps input intact and parses more robustly.

t: How mmap cut model load times in llama.cpp
w: Memory-mapping weights avoids read() copies; 1D tensors in 7B models could be mmapped immediately while the file format was being redesigned.

t: Separate math input syntax from typesetting quality
w: Math quality comes from TeX's rendering rules, while input syntax and symbols are separate problems; Unicode and OpenType now bypass symbol lookup.

t: Lorentzian manifolds: signature and curvature
w: A Lorentzian metric usually has signature (1, n-1); flat Minkowski space is not hyperbolic space, which has constant negative curvature, so the two cannot be the same.

t: Why merging window manager and compositor causes problems
w: If the WM and compositor are one process, WM restarts kill the session and GC pauses hurt frame presentation and input latency.

t: Government funding behind TCP/IP and the early web
w: TCP/IP and HTTP were built with DARPA and CERN funding, not venture capital; open protocols depended on institutional sponsorship.

t: Mistake theory versus conflict theory explains baffling disagreements
w: People disagree either from misunderstanding (mistake theory) or wanting to win (conflict theory); assuming the wrong one causes baffling talks.

t: Back pain often resolves itself, confounding treatment claims
w: Acute back flare-ups usually clear within weeks, so people credit whatever treatment they tried; this explains the wide range of cures.

t: Adversarial Go AI shows alien playing style with gaping weaknesses
w: A strong Go AI can still have a non-human shape: a basic exploit humans would never miss, showing strength and fragility coexisting.

t: How Ricci flow's early path toward Poincare was recognized
w: Hamilton's Ricci flow was recognized early by Yau: neck-pinch singularities undo connected sums, offering a route to the Poincare conjecture.

t: Strong guarantees come from immutability plus type systems
w: TypeScript's type system is very advanced; Haskell feels strong mainly because immutability makes it hard to bypass types.

t: Why country rankings mislead for startup location choices
w: Corporate tax matters little for startups; at-will employment, constructive dismissal rules, and contract enforcement matter more.

t: Why TC39 struggled with promise cancellation design
w: Cancellation is a zero-sum design question; the committee gives constraints while champions craft solutions, with staged proposals building consensus.

t: Playbook for landing deals with large companies
w: Pursue only with a specific pain-point hypothesis and over 50% fit; then use senior-titled outreach and a sequenced email plan.

t: Flynn Effect: IQ scores rose faster than genetics explains
w: Raw IQ scores rose substantially worldwide over decades; environmental change dwarfs plausible genetic shifts from selective breeding.

t: US securities law regulates disclosure, not investment quality
w: Offerings can be junk as long as material facts are disclosed; exemptions reduce disclosure burdens for smaller issuers.

t: How the bitcoin block-size dispute led to SegWit
w: Congestion sparked block-size debate; SegWit was a soft fork avoiding a hard fork while enabling second-layer designs.

t: Why assembly countries capture little of product value
w: iPhone assembly earns a few dollars of a $1000 device; high-tech components capture most margin, shaping wage gaps across countries.

t: Most common Android app permissions by app share
w: First-hand static analysis data: INTERNET appears in 92.9 percent of apps, network state 83 percent, storage access about 60 percent.

t: Cold chills, ASMR and frisson are distinct phenomena
w: Explains three different sensory responses by trigger and emotional character, noting ASMR and frisson affect roughly 3 to 10 percent of people.

t: Cheap free tooling let the web outpace enterprise stacks
w: Enterprise suites cost thousands and needed heavy training; free Linux, MySQL and PHP let small teams build and ship, which drove web adoption.

t: Why containers are process isolation, not a fad
w: A container is essentially a process, so it is a useful abstraction; serverless requires rewriting apps and cannot hold long-lived server connections.

t: Interviewers screen to avoid the worst hires
w: Experienced managers aim to avoid bad hires rather than pick the best, so soft interview questions mainly test whether a candidate seems normal and reliable.

t: Useful but overlooked Unix command-line tools
w: A practical list of tools such as bsdiff, par2, pv, mktemp, glark and lshw, with a short description of what each one does.

t: Why autofocus and custom file inputs often hurt users
w: Autofocus disrupts desktop Space-key scrolling and pops mobile keyboards, and custom file inputs often break; only autofocus after explicit user intent.

t: Cached array length and critique of a Closure review
w: Shows caching array length matters in tight loops, and that Closure's own array code already caches it where it counts, refuting a naive critique.

t: Why 1990s scripting languages were inherently slow
w: Dynamic typing, boxing and hash-table everything make such languages fundamentally slow, so JIT gains like asm.js reveal what was left on the table.

t: Facebook's data export omits photos you are tagged in
w: The Graph API misreports tagged photos and blocks export, so the author scraped them with authenticated cookies; first-hand reverse engineering of the gap.

t: Why low-frequency spectrum matters for wireless coverage
w: Sub-1GHz signals travel farther and penetrate buildings better; T-Mobile lacked it, limiting coverage and delaying its LTE rollout.

t: Why intermittent solar still needs fossil backup
w: Solar output is free but intermittent, so conventional plants must stay on standby for the remaining demand, and their costs do not disappear.

t: Build a strong math foundation before a PhD
w: Pure math teaches stating and proving theorems, the core skill for producing research that is new, correct and significant; Knuth's critique of PhD training supports it.

t: Defending XML against common criticisms
w: XML verbosity comes from end tags and angle brackets inherited from SGML, and binary data needs safe text encoding for interchange.

t: How big-tech hiring committees make decisions
w: Committee rejections often mean not hired this round, leveling deadlocks are common, and recruiters' relayed reasons are often distorted.

t: Why ARM sued Qualcomm over Nuvia's licensed IP
w: Nuvia's ARM license required approval for IP transfers, so ARM sought control to block licensees from later dropping its architecture.

t: Back-of-envelope scale of replacing fossil energy
w: Replacing fuel-based transport needs over a thousand 1 GW plants by this estimate, and home solar rarely covers EV charging plus cooling.

t: Why P=NP would not mean practical algorithms
w: A polynomial-time algorithm can have huge exponents, so proving P=NP would not automatically make NP-complete problems practically easy.

t: Cognitive fundamentals before considering supplements
w: Hydration, sleep consolidating memory from hippocampus to neocortex, and exercise support cognition before any supplements are considered.

t: Why per-phone royalties favor premium phone makers
w: Royalties tied to device price make identical cellular tech costlier on high-end phones, giving Apple a strong reason to negotiate hard.

t: Learn sysadmin basics before running Docker in production
w: Docker is an optimization, not a substitute for Linux, networking, backups and security skills; production needs automated provisioning and deploys.

t: When genetic algorithms are actually a good fit
w: GAs suit specific classes of objective functions; judge them against competing optimizers on speed rather than trusting biological analogies.

t: How big companies misuse startup trade secrets
w: Promising a firewall then passing secrets across it is blatant misappropriation, and startups dependent on one big partner face severe risk.

t: Why battery chemistry limits grid storage
w: Chemistry caps capacity and lithium is scarce, so abundant thermal or molten-salt storage may scale better.

t: Why in-browser crypto trusts the server
w: Crypto code served by the server you guard against can leak keys; only signed, reviewable clients fix that.

t: Login CSRF and how PKCE helps magic links
w: Login CSRF logs victims into attacker accounts; PKCE binds the link click to the requesting device, though webviews complicate it.

t: Practical fundraising insights from investor behavior
w: Investors court founders early, so plan to raise zero dollars for leverage and have one founder handle fundraising.

t: How Sandstorm isolation limits app vulnerabilities
w: Sandstorm gives apps an unspoofable identity header and isolates each grain, so private apps are protected even when the app has bugs.

t: Why Dutch cities make cycling infrastructure pay off
w: Compact cities with short trips make bike lanes efficient; sprawling cities built for cars lack that trip-length profile.

t: Payment accounting is harder than payment processing
w: Reconciling fees, refunds, chargebacks and VAT across providers takes months; the charge API is the easy part.

t: Migrating a live service between datacenters
w: A reverse proxy with dynamic backends, a VPN between sites, and database replication let backends move with zero downtime.

t: Starting points for audio programming
w: WebAudio supplies building-block nodes, Tone.js abstracts them, and AudioWorklet runs custom DSP, though performance and plugin limits remain.

t: How sodium/lithium-sulfur batteries discharge
w: Metal anodes shed electrons into the wire, ions enter the electrolyte, and sulfur at the cathode accepts electrons; ion buildup stops discharge.

t: NFS originally trusted clients to name their hostname
w: The server never checked the client's claimed hostname against its IP, so mount access was trivially spoofable.

t: WebDAV needs many round trips to find versions
w: Shows WebDAV needs PROPFIND plus XML parsing and a separate history URL to find a resource's version, versus a simpler Braid request.

t: Why ripgrep skips AVX-512 support
w: Most recent consumer Intel CPUs lack AVX-512, so AVX2 reaches more users; ripgrep is weaker on compressed data.

t: Why LIGO's gravitational wave detections hold up
w: Independent groups replicated LIGO's analysis, and the 2017 neutron star event was located optically, answering doubts about the detection.

t: Recovering from a crashed service manager
w: A separate service manager keeps PID 1 simple; orphaned daemons are reparented if the manager dies, trading recovery for simplicity.

t: Heat pumps cost more per watt saved than solar
w: Heat pump costs about 39 cents per saved watt versus about 7 cents for panels, before counting seasons and storage.

t: Why a small site feature could change norms
w: Pinning a link turns a subtle gesture into a superslot; small social features have counterintuitive effects only operators can see.

t: Reversed index column order makes inserts far slower
w: Two identically filled MySQL tables with reversed composite-index order: one loads in 25 minutes, the other takes over 37 hours, with matching checksums.

t: Why Munich's LiMux migration struggled
w: Insider notes: aging desktops with 256 MB RAM swapped constantly, slow SDSL site links and immature office software made the Linux migration look worse than its causes.

t: How Croquet grew out of Smalltalk and Squeak
w: Croquet extended Squeak with 3D hardware acceleration and transparent networking via the Teatime protocol, building on Smalltalk's GUI goals.

t: Adding end-to-end encryption to any Matrix client
w: Pantalaimon proxy gives E2E encryption to clients without native support; several major clients already have full E2E.

t: Why Tesla's cameras fall short of human vision
w: 20/20 vision is about 1 arc-minute; 20/40 needs about 30 pixels per degree, and Tesla's forward cameras are compared against that.

t: Why starting a personal blog pays off
w: Blogging accelerates learning, boosts hiring prospects, builds a searchable record of your thinking, and establishes credibility on topics.

t: Where Windows enforces the FAT32 32GB format limit
w: Format dialog lacks the limit; Windows 2000 formats then errors, so enforcement sits in lower-level code, per leaked NT sources.

t: Practical path to conversational Mandarin through self-study
w: Total study hours matter most; look up unknown words in example sentences, aim for about 10,000 passive words, and use transcripts for media.

t: How UK contractor agencies behave in downturns
w: Companies source contractors from preferred supplier lists, and agency CV quotas can hide whether you were actually submitted for a job.

t: Learn a language by writing a program per feature
w: Write a small program for every language feature and run it under several compilers to expose real differences; sustained daily practice builds fluency.

t: Practical steps to check medical insurance bills
w: Wait for the explanation of benefits before paying, match it to the invoice, and confirm providers are truly in network.

t: Threat-model campaign security by how documents flow
w: Choose security approach by storage model (office, cloud, hybrid); hybrid setups inherit the weaknesses of both, and end users shouldn't own security decisions.

t: Insider view of IBM's late cloud transition
w: IBM was still manually building physical servers in 2013; the layoffs reflected a slow cloud transition plus cost-cutting, not only performance.

t: Modeling arguments as typed premises and conclusions
w: Represent claims, premises and arguments as data types, letting conclusions become premises and enabling a wiki-like catalog of structured arguments.

t: Sparse graphs versus adjacency matrices in APL
w: Adjacency matrices make neighbor lookup O(n) for sparse graphs; the APL Tarjan implementation shows matrix code is expressive but awkward for sparse data.

t: Why convertible notes and SAFEs suit early startups
w: Convertibles let founders bridge to Series A without a low-valuation dilution hit; caps protect investors from abuse of uncapped notes.

t: Splitting sequences into monotonic runs with groupby
w: Use itertools.groupby over pairwise comparisons, with a closure or tee-based window, to segment a sequence into increasing and decreasing runs.

t: TN, IPS and VA panels compared for monitors
w: TN is fast but has poor color and viewing angles; IPS suits bright offices and VA suits dark rooms, and IPS variants need checking in specs.

t: Calories versus macros for body recomposition
w: Calories drive weight change, but macronutrients decide whether loss is fat or muscle; eat enough protein and train for strength to lose fat intelligently.

t: Useful bash aliases and functions for daily use
w: Small functions like mkd, extract, plot via gnuplot and mksum via paste and bc save time and show practical shell composition.

t: Refactoring callback-heavy Node code into composable APIs
w: Hide cache-then-database logic behind one lookup API and standardize success and error continuations so async flows compose and stay testable.

t: Building a cheap used-hardware storage server
w: Used enterprise chassis, SAS drives and ECC memory are cheap; electricity costs can shift the best choice to newer drives.

t: Clojure on App Engine with a live REPL
w: App Engine forbids threads, so Clojure's concurrency is unused; the REPL-driven workflow via dev server and SLIME is the payoff.

t: git reset --hard can destroy uncommitted work
w: reset --hard discards working-tree edits never added or committed, and the reflog only tracks commits, so they are gone.

t: Why furniture quality tiers hollowed out
w: Buyers cannot perceive construction quality, so makers use veneers and cheap woods; the middle market vanishes.

t: How simulator practice transfers to real racing
w: Steering, slide correction and throttle control become subconscious through sim practice and carry directly to real cars.

t: Why number systems took millennia to develop
w: Negative, fractional and irrational numbers were hard to accept; arithmetic became easy only after good notation and representations.

t: Meeting a whole new team in week one
w: Send a detailed intro email with questions, then ask each contact for three referrals; the chain yields 30 plus meetings quickly.

t: Comparative advantage assumes immobile labor and capital
w: Ricardo's trade gains assume fixed factors; when capital and jobs move abroad, the employment effects differ from the textbook story.

t: Navigating a large .emacs with outline headers
w: Consistent section comments plus occur on that regex give an instant outline of a 1200-line init file.

t: Why Japanese x264 contributors stayed insular
w: Language confidence and intimidating channels stopped contributors upstreaming patches; making them comfortable fixed collaboration.

t: How chips are assembled from licensed IP cores
w: Most SoC makers license CPU and interface cores, then wire them in block diagrams or GUI tools rather than designing transistors.

t: Top-k word counting across languages
w: Hash-map counting then sorting is idiomatic; naive list.count approaches are O(N squared) and slow in every language shown.

t: Why the plasma dipole drive cannot work
w: Ion clouds build up outside the plates and cancel the net electric force, so the device cannot sustain thrust, as in a perpetual motion machine.

t: Bitcoin malleability and the normalized txid fix
w: Transaction IDs can change before confirmation; exchanges adopting a normalized hash index can track withdrawals reliably.

t: How fair use's four factors applied to Google Books
w: Shows fair use turns on four statutory factors, and why whole-work copying for public benefit can still qualify.

t: Why hiring defined impact as shipped code
w: Interviewers equated getting things done with writing shipped code, leaving designers and other non-coding impact unmeasured.

t: Why canvas-based GUIs hurt accessibility and integration
w: Canvas and WebGL widgets bypass the DOM accessibility layer and lose native scrolling, clipboard, and zoom behavior.

t: Why lock files still matter despite functional package managers
w: Pure hashed builds are powerful, but application developers still need resolution and easy config swapping, not full-graph specs.

t: Where expert-level science and foreign policy analysis lives
w: Primary sources like IPCC summaries and think-tank publications beat popular coverage, which often gets the questions wrong.

t: Why CMS backends should expose APIs, not pages
w: A content tool should only serve an API; rendering and page composition belong to separate components, improving security and decoupling.

t: Why HP's printer business is really an ink business
w: Refill ink is cheaper to sell than cartridges, so ink revenue shapes HP's printer and cartridge strategy in ways outsiders miss.

t: Treat hiring as a tracked funnel with mission
w: Track hiring funnel data from the start, write candidate-focused job descriptions, and measure how screens predict later success.

t: Correct framing of random variables and distributions
w: A random variable is a quantity measured across repeated experiments; its distribution is given by probabilities like P(X <= x).

t: Identity-aware proxies to avoid repeated logins
w: A proxy can sign identity tokens so apps need no login logic; securing bring-your-own devices is the hard part.

t: Why US metros struggle: parking, sprawl, and density
w: Suburban stations with parking decks draw few riders, and driving often beats transit, so ridership stays far below dense systems.

t: Three reasons copyright is hard to get right
w: Laws simplify reality, courts create uneven precedents, and most people hold vague notions of what copyright actually permits.

t: Why early hackers resisted timesharing
w: Hackers at MIT resisted timesharing because losing full machine control felt aesthetically wrong, not merely slower.

t: How flexible office space business models work
w: Landlords use long leases to service debt; flexible-space operators take risk on vacancy and charge more to compensate.

t: How state insurance borders exposed UFO cattle claims
w: Cattle-death evidence followed state insurance-law boundaries, suggesting human causes rather than alien visitations.

t: Why flotation devices and sightlines hinder lifeguards
w: Non-approved floats make children harder to spot and can trap them; poor pool sightlines hide drowning victims from lifeguards and parents.

t: How Japan's job-hunting system shapes startups
w: Rigid one-path hiring and lifetime employment expectations make deviating hard, which explains the startup scene's obstacles.

t: How ICBM interceptors and false alarms work
w: Interceptors destroy warheads by direct kinetic collision, and flight-time arithmetic shows whether a Hawaii alert could match a real threat.

t: Why adults struggle to hear foreign phonemes
w: After puberty, learners stop perceiving sound distinctions absent from their native language; they need deliberate, painstaking perceptual training.

t: What Web Components standards actually comprise
w: Web Components is an umbrella of W3C standards like custom elements and shadow DOM, not a single framework feature.

t: Building chemistry up from quantum basics
w: Electrons cannot collapse into the nucleus because of the uncertainty principle, which sets the orbital structure that drives chemistry.

t: Handling out-of-memory in systems languages
w: Allocators can return error values, but the real design task is budgeting memory for the platform so the system never runs out.

t: S-expressions have a canonical spec and binary form
w: Rivest's Sexp spec defines a canonical binary encoding that maps one-to-one with a readable text form.

t: Emacs is command-driven: learn commands first
w: Teach M-x and named commands before keybindings, since each key just invokes a command that learners need to understand first.

t: Why vectorized operations solve the two-language problem
w: Vectorized operations move loops into compiled code, giving high-level languages near-native speed with simple semantics.

t: Choosing a security specialty: four distinct fields
w: Security careers split into network, application, incident response, and general practice; each needs different skills, so choose deliberately.

t: Why RDF implementations are hard in practice
w: RDF serialization, datatypes, and blank nodes make real implementations hard, and tooling quality varies widely across libraries.

t: Resources for learning math for understanding
w: Points to Epsilon Camp's FAQ on problems versus exercises and Stillwell's Numbers and Geometry for deep mathematical understanding.

t: Social proof and asymmetry in hiring pipelines
w: Candidates need one strong signal such as school, employer, or known work; pipelines are asymmetric, so rejections are expected.

t: Comparing Clojure, Racket, Scheme, and Common Lisp
w: Dialects differ on purity, concurrency, performance, C interop, GUI support, and libraries; these axes help pick a first Lisp.

t: systemd OnCalendar shorthands and normalized forms
w: OnCalendar shorthands like daily and weekly each normalize to a fixed calendar form, as systemd.time examples show.

t: How Japan's Fifth Generation project affected Prolog
w: The Fifth Generation project, centered on Prolog, reshaped AI funding and mindshare in the 1980s, shifting attention away from Prolog.

t: Why Unix skills and tools persist across decades
w: Unix tools change incrementally with drop-in replacements and stable scripting interfaces, so learned skills keep paying off.

t: Python's approach to encapsulation and readability
w: Python signals privacy with naming conventions and name mangling, relying on documented convention rather than enforced access control.

t: Why self-hosted crowdfunding beats Kickstarter for hardware
w: Self-hosting captures long-tail sales after the campaign, gives you account and shipping data, controls branding, and lets you pick payment processors.

t: Why chipmaking expertise is hard to copy
w: Fabrication needs design software, about 40 equipment types, and decades of tacit engineering knowledge across the supply chain.

t: Alan Kay on ten-thousand-line systems
w: Complication can exceed essential complexity by thousands of times; PARC built OS, language and UI in about 10k lines.

t: What CS study adds: maintaining invariants
w: Formal training builds habits of enforcing invariants and constraints, which self-taught programmers often miss in API design.
